Danny Barker Interviewed by Milt Hinton, April '80 (Tape 1):

I'm sitting here in New Orleans, Louisiana, in the Hyatt-Regency Hotel, talking to my dear friend, longtime companion and musician, Danny Barker -- Daniel Moses Barker, as we call him. And if you hear an unusual noise on this, because outside of the hotel... What do you call what they're doing out there, Danny?
Piledriving.

They're piledriving, and they're keeping it up and up and up and up. So it stopped for a minute to get us started, but if it's in there, you'll understand what we're about. Now, Danny, what is that Social Security Number? Do you remember your Social Security number?
And your New York Union Card number? Do you remember that? B...?
Uh-huh. You just go ahead on... First let's start with where were you born, Danny?

I was born here in New Orleans, in the French Quarter. That's on... If you have ever been to New Orleans, you will see I was smack dab... I'm a smack-dab original native of the city. I was born right in the section where the city was founded. It's called the French Quarter, the first square mile of New Orleans.
Barker - I-2

My grandmother and grandfather resided there, and my grandmother was my wife's midwife. She was a midwife for Vernon(?) Hand, and midwife for most of the women who would get calls of emergency. Most of the time they would call old Miss Barker, because she knew how to handle situations of childbirth and distress and panicking. And she was my mother's midwife. My mother was going to...prepared to go to the hospital to have me and make the (?). She said, "Don't worry about it; I'll be your midwife." So just about when the confinement came up, Mother went and resided with her. And my grandmother brought me in this world, Mrs. Barker -- Victoria Barker.
Victoria Barker. And what year was that? What's that date?
1909, January the 13th.
January 13, 1909.
Night people. Born at night. 9:30 my mother.
[LAUGHS] Uh-huh. And your father's name?
Moses Barker.
Moses Barker. What did he do, Danny?
What did he do? He was a common laborer. Not exactly a common laborer, but he worked at any kind of job you can get. He didn't finish high school...
Barker - I-3
Unskilled, yeah.

Yeah, unskilled. His last job was driving a dray truck, which was called a float. It's a peculiar early instrument to have drawn by mules or horses, or one horses... There was a float, a flatback, like you have the flatback trucks... It was a flatback, heavily constructed, low-slung, flatbedded vehicle that could hold maybe a ton.
Did it have two wheels or four wheels?
It had four wheels.
Because some drays had two wheels, didn't they.

Yeah. Yeah. This was a long thing, and it could bear... It could carry like four huge barrels of cotton. It could carry like eight barrels of wine, which was a variety of wine that you would bring to barrooms and what you call grog shops, which there was many of them in New Orleans, because this is a town that doesn't have a curfew -- so there were many wine-houses, called honky-tonks [hunky-tunks] and dives.

And he drove this truck, I mean what they called a float. And his work-mate was a white mule who was very inconvenient, who would decide to move his bowels right in the main part of town, which embarrassed my father, who sat on this wagon. He had to go through this procedure. The
Barker - I-4

mule would never wait for him to get back in the stable or in some sparsely settled area. He'd wait and get right at the corner of Canal and St. Charles (that's like at 50th and Broadway), and stop -- and you couldn't move him. And he would do his business right there. My father would sit there and have to go through this scene. It was very embarrassing.

This mule seemed to have a grievance against my father. Because when he got involved with the Nightlife People, people used to kid him. Every time they noticed what this mule was doing. Because different mules... Mules were very... They were as popular as people. Mules live a long life for animals. Certain people had certain wagons, and they had certain animals, and people admired the animals. "That's Willie's mule" or "That's Sam's horse" or "That horse belongs to that wagon." If they saw the kid bringing the mule or the horse to the blacksmith's shop, they could tell. They knew these animals, like they knew so-and-so's car. If you knew a kid had a goat and a little wagon, you knew that was little Willie's wagon and his goat.
That was the scene. That's part of the reason why my father went into the fast life.
Uh-huh. What kind of fast life was that?
Barker - I-5

Well, there was the Red-Light District. And his route was bringing wine and beers and stimulants in the Red-Light District, which was infested with all kinds of strange people, fast women, pickpockets, shoplifters, and what you call "night people," who were indulging in everything that is illegal.

There was a special section in New Orleans that was called the Tenderloin, over at Basin Street... You hear "The Basin Street Blues," says, "Why don't you come along with me." And over there you went... You went into there because there was no curfew. I keep repeating that there was no curfew in New Orleans. And the city decided to put all these non-conforming people over in that section, and do what you want, 24 hours around the clock, but just stay over in there amongst your bunch.

My father used to deliver this wine, and heavy liquors, whiskey and beers, other stimulants, over to these joints. And all the joints, most of them had a piano. And he could play a little piano. And he met this woman, this fast woman there named Ruby. She had seen his mule, him and this mule. And he played these Blues on this piano, and he was pretty nice to look at -- and she inveigled him why he wanted to be foolin' around with that mule and that old truck when he could be over there. And the usual procedure was the woman
Barker - I-6
taking of a man, because fast women need some kind of protection. Because you could get kicked around if you didn't have a man to protect you.
Well, who played the piano? This lady?
My father played a little piano. But she was a fast and sportin' woman. She was a hooker.
Oh, I see. Yeah.

And she inveigled him and kept enticing him with the easy life, and "Come on over," and you know... And he got involved with her, and next thing he starts shacking up with her and he stopped coming home, see. And he went into that life.
Now, what was your mother's maiden name...?
Rose. My mother's name was Ridley(?) Rose Barbarin, Paul Barbarin's sister.
Ah!
There were nine in the family. And...
So your mother was Paul Barbarin's sister. That's how he's your uncle.
He's my uncle. And he's my godfather. There's this thing that you call like baptizing...you call it... With the Baptists, it's baptism; with the Catholics, it's christening.
Christening, yeah.
Barker - I-7

Well, he was my godfather. They always do that, see, if you're a little youngster whose (?) is not capable of taking care of a baby, an infant... You know, nine years...he'd be nine years older than the infant, and you could help him or sponsor him, christen him, take care of him if something happened to the parent. That is the procedure of the godparent. And he is my godparent.
And he was beautiful in doing that, because he helped me all through my career.
Sure.
You know, he bought my first banjo for me, because he was with King Oliver's band. Well...
And did you know your grandparents on both sides?
Yeah, sure. They lived to a ripe old age..
Well, what was your mother's parent's name?

My mother's father's name was Isadore John Barbarin. His wife, his maiden name was Josephine Auphidore(?). Her grandmother's mother had came from Haiti. She spoke French, she spoke Creole, she spoke Patois and Cajol(?). All of them is different versions of the French, all of them spoke by different people. French was spoken by the Whites. Cajol(?) was spoken by the White Cajuns who were living in the country -- from the Acadians. There was
Barker - I-8

a little deviation in all them versions [voizhins] of the French language. And she could speak all of them. Sometimes you could speak French, but you couldn't understand a Cajol, see, because they spoke French, bad French with a southern accent. See, French is a fluent language; you know, it flows.
In other words, your father's people came from Haiti...?
No, no. My grandmother's grandmother came from Haiti.
Which one on which side?
That's my mother's mother I'm speaking about. Josephine...
On the Barbarin side.
Yeah, Isadore Barbarin.
Uh-huh.

Isadore Barbarin's father was a Frenchman. Nobody saw him. My grandfather's mother raised him. I don't know what status you would put him in, but his father was a Frenchman who owned a schooner. A schooner just supplies trade between the new basin, like this, over to Mandeville, and they used to bring produce and things from the country out there, the little country towns, into the city to be sold. Spices, herbs, roots, skins, coons,
Barker - I-9
possums and rabbits, and everything that could get...they'd add some pine. A little small boat.
That's exactly what New Orleans was like, I mean, as far as the mixture of races.
Yeah. Well, they had...
And you're a direct descendant of that. French and Spanish and...

Yeah. And they were descendants of all these people. And there was a whole lot of Chinese came from here. The peculiar thing about New Orleans was that the Whites could pull the hat, or whatever you would call it, with all other women -- everybody's women. But nobody of another race should catch his woman. So this whole Creole business is most times White...
The master's (?).

The White and the Black woman. The Black woman was subjected to all kinds of abuse. See, she could be raped, she could be seduced into giving her something, and she'd come up with a child. But generally, they'd never give up their children. See, they don't go too much for orphanage. Whatever the scandal in the family, if it's White man's child, she kept her child...
Sure.
Barker - I-10

...by hook or crook. So that's what you see (?). We don't be abandoning' our children, regardless. So you'd get a Black woman with a snow-white child, see. Now, before that, years ago, they had what was called the quadroon balls, where Black women purposely would have a White man to have a White child, because there was something about the gene, that the blacker the woman and a White man, a blond White man, generally you have a blond child or something like that. And these old women knew that. So if you're subject to slavery, so you try to breed something that could help you. So thousands of women had these kids, and you'd have these girls praying for a girl all the time, because they could raise this girl, and this girl, by being White, looking White, she could go into upper strata, out of slavery. There was all kind of ingenious ways (if that's the proper word) to get out of this slavery thing. See, and she could always say she is the maid in the house. Or she says she works for this girl, or she's this girl's gardener, never mentioning that that's her child. And if the girl married White, or with somebody who was similar... There was a whole breed of this thing going, this Creole thing. If she married somebody her color who wasn't White, passing for White they called it, they brought up a breed that brought on the Creole and the free man of color. And you'd see
Barker - I-11
these Black women in the house there with the Mack (?) or whatever you call it in the house... They had a secret sort of a way.
That's probably where that story Imitation of Life came about.
Yeah.
It's that type of thing.

Yeah. Well, Imitation Of Life was that the girl, she was ashamed. And of course, many times you have it here, whereby they leave here and they go to California. There was a discussion last night at the church... Well, I should have brought them papers; I'll bring them to you -- and we will continue on this thing.
Mmm-hmm.

What Black has to do... Like, in my case, it was all around me. I was raised with my Black grandparents, and I was about seven, and then I'd go downtown with my Creole grandparents and I'd see all this intrigue(?) with Whites. Like, kids would meet one another in the street, you'd see a bunch of kids playing, and you'd go over there to join them. All of them would be (?) playing tops, or they're throwing [t'rowin']...pitchin' to the line with coins or something And you'd go in and join two or three kids... And it happened to me. I didn't get aware of it til
Barker - I-12

later. They was light kids. I know they were Colored. By the time I joined, saying, "I'm going to...let me get in this" -- they picked up the coins and walked away. See, they were told "Don't mingle with the Black brothers."
Yeah.
You know, to my amazement! Like, "What the hell is happening here?" And it happened two or three times til I woke up, because when you're young, you don't know.
Sure.

But you see, because a Black has to... When you're a Negro in America, you have to learn to be a Negro. You have to go through a schooling. You don't know. And you constantly shop, but you can't do this and you can't do that. And in the case of New Orleans and the South, you had to learn to read the signs right away. White Men's Room, White Gentleman's Bath, Negro Man, White Ladies Dressing Room or Toilet or Black Women's Toilet.

It was always a putdown. So you're raised with a putdown from the beginning. So if your skin ain't tough, you're in trouble. You have to be watching all these.. You spend half of your time seeing can you go in somewhere. And you've got the money, the same as everybody else, but you've got to watch with this caution to keep out of trouble. Because any bum, a White bum, no matter if he's a wino, he
Barker - I-13

can holler, "What are you doin' in here, you?! Make him get out of here!" The lowest bum you probably can find. It was his prerogative because he was White. So you had to learn how to roll with the punches, and all them scars is on your personality. If you're smart and listen to what older people tell you, then you learn how to survive.
Mmm-hmm.
So that's what you had here in New Orleans, a multi...a triple multi-level society.
Right!

And the Black was the lowest upon the totem pole, the last run. So for you to survive, you had to be very alert, you know... Watch them seven holes in your head. I got some kids, I'll be teaching them. I'll ask them, "How many holes you got in your head?" They don't know what the hell I'm talking about. I ask them, "How many holes...?" They say, "One, two..." But there are seven. One, two, two eyes; two nostrils...
That's four.

And your mouth and your two ears. So you've got to keep that in coordination at all times. In fact, I did... Today they have all kind of openings for them. They don't see no signs. They don't know what it was to have a sign on a bus or on a streetcar. And you had to maneuver to
Barker - I-14
put the sign in front of yourself. That's the way it was rigged up.

And that's the way it was in Jazz! No matter how much you could play, you'd have imitators, imitating you, getting triple the amount of money you was making. The very people that you would teach and taking lessons from you and call you "Mr. Barker" or "Mr. Hinton" or "Mr. Coleman Hawkins" or "Mr. Ellington," and turn around after the lesson, and they'd go on and make some money, and you'd find that you'd almost have to call them "Mister," because they got all the money and you got the crumbs off the table.

So if you learn how to maneuver with that, you can survive. But a lot of musicians died, you know, at the bar, you know, right next to the spittoon and the sawdust on the floor, drank themselves to death because they couldn't stand up under the pressure.
What was it like as a kid, Danny, around here, other than that...?

Fantastic music. At six o'clock in the evening, you heard the calliope on the riverboat, in the summertime -- and in the wintertime. Then Fate Marable was out on the Marquis(?)... Fate Marable I can remember from like 1915, I'm six years old, in the evening. They didn't have all the noise that you have today, like automobiles and
Barker - I-15

trucks, and it was quiet, and you could hear that beautiful calliope on the river, Fate Marable was playing the latest melodies that the Streckfus people always made it their business to play... Like, "Twelfth Street Rag," you'd hear him playing that, or whatever, or playing "The St. Louis Blues." And he was the kingpin on he river, off of New Orleans to St. Paul, Minnesota. Fate Marable was the boss on the river. You'd hear musicians, White musicians, Black musicians, fellows(?) who hadn't played a while on the riverboat.
What complexion was Fate Marable?
Fate Marable looked like Scoville Brown. That kind...
Marines(?)...
Yes, Marines(?).
He would be a light-complected Black.
Didn't say much. Great piano player. Great full-handed piano player of that time. A reading musician. The Streckfus people had sent him out...
Who was the Streckfus people? You mentioned about them before.
The riverboat people. That's the people on the Streckfus Line. They were Germans. Had iron discipline on that boat, or on those boats. They owned the St. Paul,
Barker - I-16

the Capitol, the Admiral... Oh, through the years they must have had like fifteen or twenty boats. Their boats plied the Ohio River, the Missouri River out of Kansas City, and the Arkansas River -- all the rivers in the Basin, the Mississippi Basin.
And they had these bands, big...these coaster bands. Bix Beiderbecke worked on the band, Jimmy McPartland and them people.
Is that so?
Yes.
They worked in bands with them.

Yeah, out in Indiana. They joined them bands. There's a picture, you're supposed to see...a painting that's supposed to be Louis Armstrong and Bix Beiderbecke discussing music on a wharf that's by some bales of cotton.
Well, that's what you heard in the evening. Now, other than that, you heard...
You'd hear the calliope thing.
Yes.
What did the thing look like?
It's a piano with a copper fingerboard, and it's steam, it has steam pipes. It's the same as an organ in church, them big pipes you see with the organ in the
Barker - I-17

church. But it's run by steam, and the pipes are copper, and the whole mechanism is copper, because it turns green and it's steam. And Fate used to play it with a raincoat on because the steam is poppin' all around you.
Oh, he wore it.
He put on his raincoat and his rain-hat and he'd go and sit up under this canopy, and play this calliope on the riverboat.

He was a master. A calliope, there's something about it that the chords seem unfinished, because it's generally two notes of a triad, and you're hittin' at it, you know. You hear it in the circus. But Fate Marable could somehow play it full, so you... He could mix them chords. Nobody's supposed to play a calliope like Fate. He let the tones run into one another, to cover up what was what -- which was a scientific phenomenon to do that, to know how to make those chords, which modern people are doing today, making them hit on organ, to cover up its misgivings. So you heard that.

Then there was these guys with the piano. There was the organ grinder, but it was a piano, and he got in a thing... It was like a shaft, like a wagon, and he pulled it about to different bars of the time and played. You heard that. Generally, this guy had a kid with him, and this kid was taking a bucket. And when he'd play a couple of tunes,
Barker - I-18

he'd send the kid inside of the bar. Because the bar-flies and the neighborhood chicks who frequented the local bars, they would hear the latest tunes, and it was a novelty. And they would come by to listen, or come out the barroom and listen. Some monkey would come out and do a little step. You heard that and you stop that.

Now, every peddler... You had charcoal peddlers, you had vegetable peddlers, you had the milk peddlers. Then you had the contraband fish and shrimp and seafood peddler, who generally had a fast horse and a light wagon, who could run. Because you weren't allowed to sell seafood out in the public. It had to be under supervision because of the spoilage. But these guys would come along on Friday, which was the fast day. They had seafood; they had no meat. They had a wagon, and inside this wagon they'd have, they'd have shrimps, they'd have a vast variety of fish, a couple of turtles -- (?) more than one. But they were always on the move, looking out for the cops. Because the cops would generally try to catch them, to confiscate all the fish, bring them to jail, bring them out to the Fifth Precinct (in this neighborhood, in my particular neighborhood), and when they'd get there, they'd take all the provisions and split them up amongst the Police Department. The old folks said, "Oh, the police got the poor man. All that good fish, all
Barker - I-19

them policemen's goin' to take all that fish and bring it home." Whatever he had, man. They didn't have no refrigeration in jail, so they'd keep in jail overnight. Because it's against the law, the sanitation law. And generally, he had to get somebody to speak for him...
Get a (?).

It was a racket. You'd lose your day's provisions, and they might send you home. So the Negroes generally had fast horses. See, the police had horses, too, you know. So if you was on foot, you had a chance. But generally, when automobiles came along, them little Fords just pulled right up, right in front of the horses, they'd stop and go to jail. "What you got in there?" They'd look under the cart, because sometimes he'd keep some shrimps under there.
So you're seeing all this intrigue and all this, and on the corner, all the... Among the cats on the corner, you always had a great whistler. [WHISTLES] Trill like a mockingbird.

See, everywhere you went around, there was music. There was the praline lady. She'd come down the street: "I got pralines..." -- she'd sing it in tune, and you'd listen to her, she'd get that same key every time unless she got a cold. You'd hear her singing. Then you had the milkman in
Barker - I-20

the morning. He had the cowbells, and you'd get familiar to the different sounds of different cowbells. The great big old cowbells, went DONG, DONG, or they went DING-A-LING-A-LING-A-LING. There were different varieties.

Everywhere you'd turn around, there was music here. You'd pass the house and you'd hear people inside singing. You'd see women washing clothes, and they would be singing with beautiful voice, they'd be singing in the choir in the church. Housewives. You heard singing. In spite of the oppression...

That's why when you see Louis Armstrong... Louis Armstrong, when he spoke of New Orleans, he forgot the bad things he suffered as a youngster. Everything to him of New Orleans was the good things. He was fortunate(?) that he could differentiate it, to match(?) my home town. He always spoke of the pleasure out of it, not the time when they locked him up and put him in this waif's home, because they shouldn't have -- or maybe they should have, because he had a weapon. But he was not there shootin' nobody; he was (?) a shooting gun. But he always speaks of the town as the pleasurable thing, and hearing the music all the time.
You'd pass people's houses, and you hear somebody playing the piano. The first time I heard the "Twelfth Street Rag," I passed a house and I heard this piano. It
Barker - I-21

was fascinating to me, because you heard it in the barroom, but you didn't dare to go look in the barroom. And I just stopped by this house and listened to this piano. The piano was a player piano, and the lady was sitting there... The door was partly open, and the lady was sitting there playing the "Twelfth Street Rag" on it, using her feet.

So there was music all around. Then you heard all them different steam...all them riverboat horns. WHOOO, way into the night. Then you could hear train whistles. [TRAIN SOUND] This was a trunk line, and about fifteen or twenty different railroads used to come through, L&N, the Sun-Pacific -- and you heard that at night .
So it was just music, music, music, music...
Some kind of sounds.

It went on and on. Some sounds. It's not like you're in some little country town. Because this was a business city. And there was commerce and things going on, and you observed it. And then they would advertise... There was a plentiful supply of musicians, so if you would open up a little store, you would get a little local band, whether it was a Spasm band or a Jazz band or whatever you... And there was a band out there playing. When the people heard that bass drum beating that bass line, they'd run outside, left their food burning on the table, just run out there to
Barker - I-22

see what the hell is happening. And there on the corner would be maybe the Superior Band, or Buddy Petit's band, or Chris Kelly's band playing out there. And you'd go out there to look at the music. Because there was music. Everything was music.

You'd go on the riverfront, where I'm going to take you this week, and you'd see the camps on the riverfront, on the stilts, like you see in an Oriental country. There were camps out there. It was just loaded with camps, and every camp on a Sunday had some kind of a music. And they went out to play out on a picnic; they'd have a picnic at such-and-such a camp, at Little Woods or Milenburg or West Bend or Seabrook, all along there -- each two or three miles there was a little village. And there was music, and you'd see guys with their horns.

My stepfather told me one day... I saw this guy when I was with my uncle. He said, "That's a trumpet player." I said, "How do you know?" He said, "Well, you see his lip? He's got a red lip spot on his lip." So I said, "You don't have to be a trumpet player..." No, a cornet player. "He don't have to be a cornet player because he's got a red spot on his lip." So I criticized(?) my stepfather. He said, "It might not, but he's a trumpet player." I said, "Who is he?" He said, "That's Long-Haired Bob."
Barker - I-23

So I've got to put Long-Haired Bob in there. I had never seen Long-Haired Bob play. But they told me about him. Long-Haired Bob had this funky Blues band. He played nothin' but Blues. A real professor of Blues. He played four styles of Blues. Blues, Slow Blues, Fast Blues, and the Slow-Slow-Slow Drag. When you hired Long-Haired Bob, all he did was play the Blues. And that Slow-Slow-Slow Drag was the fightin' Blues, because you'd do a whole lot of wigglin' and shakin'. And he played for people that was on the real lower level of the strata, who didn't give a damn. They drank... They worked hard, they lived hard, and they drank, and they wouldn't have nobody's music... They wouldn't hire no Louis Armstrong, King Oliver, nobody else they'd hire but Long-Haired Bob. Because Long-Haired Bob played Slow Blues, Fast Blues, Medium Blues, and the Slow-Slow-Slow Drag.
You mentioned your stepfather...

Yeah. Well, after my father split and went in the District, see, met this woman and that life that you had nothin' to do... She told him, 'You come over here and get from behind that old jive-ass mule [you didn't say "jive"]...'
Uh-huh.
Barker - I-24

"...and come... I've seen that mule embarrass you at Royal and Canal Street, all them White folks sneakin' a look at you sittin' up there while that mule shit all over the place, right in yo' face, and you sittin' there, waggin' his tail in yo' face, and you have to sit there embarrassed. Why don't you get off the wagon?"
What was your stepfather's name?

My stepfather was Chris Columbel(?), who was a Cajun, a Creole who'd come from out the swamp-land. Handsome. He became a baker. He was a baker. My mother was working for the baker, B.C. Fronsang(?). She was a housekeeper.
Your mother was a housekeeper.

Uh-huh. For B.C. Fronsang(?), who was a popular baker downtown. And my grandmother raised me until I was seven. Grandma said, "I'll take.... That's my son's little boy. I'll take his place." Because when my Daddy went in the District, his mother said, "Well, I know my son ain't gonna make old bones." Which he didn't, incidentally. When you live that fast life...
She said he ain't gonna make what?
Old bones.
That means you ain't ever gonna get old, huh?
Barker - I-25.

That's right. 'Cause you're gonna die, because it was dangerous in that District. And very few young people made old bones (that's what they'd say), living that fast life. Because if you went in the District, the theory was you did nothing. Nothin'. You picked up nothing heavier than a slice of bread. You don't do nothin' but live a fast life and wait for the suckers, for the day people to bring you that money and (?). So you set up all kind of traps -- card games, cabarets.

My grandma said, "Jazz music is nothin' but the Devil's music, because it entices people to live a fast life. Danny, that's not no life," she told me when I first started... "Son, you're going to be a Jazz...play that music? That ain't no way to make no honest living." My grandmother, Miss Barker, had never seen a movie. She said that was a Devil's contraption. People go there, nice, good people go and see that, and it puts notions in people's heads to do the things they see in that thing.
That's amazing. They lived for quite a long time, until you were grown, didn't they?
Both of them.
I remember when we were talking about that. That's amazing.
So you got all this music. You understand?
Barker - I-26
Mmm-hmm.

So my mother got a house and she got a husband. Mrs. Chris Columbel(?). Chris Columbel(?) knew everything you ever want to know about the swamp. You'd go out hunting and he'd come back with fish. You'd go out fishing and he'd come back with rabbits. He'd come back with alligator. He'd take me out in the woods with him. When we were walking in the woods, I'd get me a stick, and we'd make a steak right away. He'd tell us, 'Okay, now you watch, because you've got the snakes out here.' When we were going through the blackberries, he said, 'Watch them blackberry bushes. Snakes like blackberries. They get up in there, and they suck the juice.' And you'd see a bush, and you'd see all those blackberries that's been squashed, all of them ripe -- you'd watch that for snakes. He'd say, 'Watch over there. There's a snake over there. You see him?' I said, 'No, I don't see him.' He said, 'Look, you see by that yellow flower? You see his head over there? Look at it.' And sure enough, it's snake laying over there.
My grandmother told me about that blackberry thing. Boy, she went to pick a blackberry, and picked a snake up by the seed(?).
Yeah, they love... They go after the blackberries, because all of them are in the ground, and
Barker - I-27

they suck it in. Now, certainly the rock reptile is something else. They are very wise. That Bible scene, you know, where they say, "For doing what you did to Adam, you shall have your head stomped into the ground."

So he and I, we took up right away. He was a master baker, which is called... He was an oven man, which is the baker that goes to the oven, raises up the hood and puts the bread in and takes the bread out. Time. It's got to be timed perfectly, or you lose a batch. I should have been a baker. But I wrapped bread for a while. You'd wrap the bread... They'd bring it out, you'd let it cool, then you'd wrap it.

He was a master baker. He was a master hunter. He was a master fisherman. He knew all about the water. If we were going fishing, we'd go out on a lake, if you heard a skip(?), he'd say, "Come on, let's go. There's a Northeastern coming in, or a Northwestern." And sure enough, off on the horizon he would see the darkness, and next thing you know, you'd see that water doing the chopping." Then we'd get to land, where we may have been a block out in the water, and get to the land just in time, or that water start choppin' and turn that boat over. He was great.
He seems to have been ...(?).
Barker - I-28

Yeah. His brother was... There was brother who had a camp on the lake, dealt from it all his life. Dealt in fish and crabs for the restaurants in town. So while I had Creole food with my French people, my mother's people, and I had Country food with my grandmother and my father's people. They came out of New Iberia. I'll tell you how they got here later on.

But getting back to this music, there was music all around. Everywhere that guys could whistle. There was a strollin' guitar [gi-tar] player, a guy who played guitar who was known in the town -- Black Hamp and...Black Nolan(?). Helluva guitar player. That Folk guitar, that Leadbelly (?) that you play with your fingers.
Mmm-hmm.

And they had a guitar [gi-tar], it just dawned upon me, because it was a great guitar -- it was called a Washburn. It was a finely chiseled instrument. And them cats could play them guitars and play them Blues. There were Blues about... They'd heard about this thing about the Titanic going down. They'd go into a bar, and they'd tell these folk tales in song. And Stave-and-Chain(?), when the people wasn't around, this super Negro who'd make love to women. They had him on a plantation, and they'd they'd bring Stave-and-Chain(?), five women, then
Barker - I-29
he'd make 'em all happy...
That was his name?
Yeah, Stave-and-Chain(?). He's a legendary character.
Like Mandingo, huh?

Yeah. Stave-and-chain(?). Because there's a stave, and you have a chain on it to tie off it. You have them in the circus. It's a big long one you put it in the ground. He had some more of (?) this pipe down in a hole.
You'd use him like a stud, right?
Yeah.
You told me about Mace...
One-Eyed Bill. Big Bill?
Yes. He's the one who started drinkin' wine, and he used to go out and play.

Drunk Bob. Bob? No, not Bob. A little fat cat with the bass. It's a three-string bass that's made out of twine. And his buddy. You'd see them together. That cat played a whole lot of music, but it would be jive, you know. And he played for ofays. He'd go in White ballrooms, no nigger ballrooms. They'd go in White ballrooms. But they were two funny niggers to see. And they'd play Irish songs, and play ...(?)... -- you know, whatever the Cajuns wanted.
Barker - I-30

No, George Jones. George Jones and Cornelius! They was two buddies. George Jones was fat, a little fat cat like Abbott and Costello, but fatter than them. And Cornelius was a sleepy-eyed cat, you know, like that other cat that worked with Costello [SIC: HARDY] . What's the name of the guy who always does... Stan...Stan...Stan... Stan... Stan Laurel. One of them kind of cats that, you know, they was pickin' on. It would look like George gave him hell, and he's playing all the time.
But you had all those different kind of cats, and you'd see them on the street.

Then you heard of Sundays. Sunday you would see them great bands on the wagons, on the tailgate the trombone and that bass would sit there, and you would look to see who that was. And about midway(?) the wagon... They used furniture wagons, which was a long wagon. You've seen them. They're trucks, but they're laid on the... All that comes in a big van. But the little one... The furniture stores used to have a long wagon, maybe about 15 feet long, that they'd put mattresses on, the mattress and the bed. You don't see those wagons. But they used to use them and rent them from the furniture store. They had some guys who was draymen who rented wagons... It was a big business, what do you say, a drayman, because you could go in and rent different kinds of
Barker - I-31
carts if you wanted to haul something. Like a U-Haul today. You'd go in and hire a horse-and-wagon from Mister So-and-So. He's got the drayman's yard.

So they'd rent them wagons, then you'd see on the front... You'd see Chris Kelly's band, you'd see Sam Morgan's band, you'd see Lee Collins' band, Kid Rena's band. At that time, when I was coming up, when I was kid around 10 and 11 and 12, you'd see the Chameleon Band and you'd see the Olympia Band. And sometimes I'd see a band that I'd never see no more. There would be some band come out of a little country town, and it would be Slidedale(?) or one of them little country towns -- and all of them had bands. And all of them played the tradition without a piano. That way you could sing, because the piano would be out of tune, and you don't want to fool around with a piano that's out of tune, and it hasn't been used when it's been there, and the keys is out...
Where would they come to play, Danny?
Hmm?
Where would they come to play?
They'd go out on the corner, to the corner and stop, and play on the corner.
Well, of course, you couldn't use a piano there, because you're on the wagon, huh?
Barker - I-32

On the wagon... But I mean, the bands, as a rule, never used a piano, because it just was a good sounding thing. A bass, a good guitar and a banjo and a drum, with a good-sized drum that had a boom to it, which was tuned. And it was a sound that was fascinating, because you had the (?) marching, a trombonist that could play. The trombone, the clarinet and the cornet playing the melody, and the trombone giving them the slide...
Yeah.
You could hear Kid Ory's mute(?); him and Preston Jackson did that to perfection.
Yes!

They knew where to come in there, and don't get no (?) on a man's note. The clarinet would just noodle around, and would make the filigrees all around -- don't touch that melody. And you'd watch that, and you'd hear the rhythm with that guitar. Good guitar players, generally, and good banjo players then had the figure-eight stroke. They kept a rhythm going in there, stating that beat. And that big bass drum had a good sound. And the bass player that had a (?) bass that played, you know, the... Well, you had something there.
And they'd get off the truck, on they'd get on the sidewalk in front of the hall, and they'd play that. And
Barker - I-33
then nobody asked where is the piano or who...
They would play out in front so they'd invite the people to come in.

Yeah. They'd play a little program out there, maybe a half-a-dozen numbers. They'd find a chick out there, the trumpet player or the clarinet player, who would ask them, "Play me another song before you all go in there. I ain't ready for you'all to come in there yet. I might go home and wash up and dress and come on and be out there with you...you know, the way I feel towards you. Please play me another tune."
[LAUGHS]

The cat is going to be obliged to play another tune. Until the guy who is booking it says, "All right, that's enough out there. If they're coming, they're coming." Then someone says, "They ain't comin', they ain't comin'." "Come on in here, let's get this band going." Because the people inside would be waiting...
Yeah.
You had this abundance of halls! Downtown, I'll show 'em to you. You had the Economy Hall. You had the...
Where was that?
Barker - I-34
...Cooperators Hall. On Ursuline and Drury. Two blocks away was the Cooperators Hall.
What street was that on?

On Liberty and Marais. Two blocks from that, at Lafitte and Orleans, was the Globe Hall, which ceased to be a hall, and became a gambling house. Then you had the First Veterans Hall. Then you had... All these halls were about four blocks from one another. I'll show you where they were. And then there was the clubs. The San Jacinto Club right in the midst of that, a great big club. And two blocks away was the Lions Club. See? All that's in about...
Six or eight blocks, huh.

In six or eight blocks there's all these halls. You see. And a certain number of people went to them halls. The people at the Lions wouldn't go to the First Veterans Hall because they was different color strata. For every color of the rainbow, you had a hall.
You had ladders(?)?

Yeah. Everybody had their hall. Similar to New York, you'd see the speakeasy, where they'd peep through the hole, and they would say, 'Well, yeah, we'll let you in.' Well, they had that down in New Orleans. Because if you knocked on the door, they had a hole to look through to
Barker - I-35

see if you're the (?) color or if anybody know you. They say, "Okay, wait until (?) gets up. Do you know who that is out there? There's somebody out there wanting to come in." They were very careful(?) and particular who they associated with. So if you had a stigma of being anything that's unnatural or being any kind of character, certain people would have nothing to do with you. That was your backside. None of them would associate with you. You were relegated to get on the outskirts and get out. Don't be coming here. Because you're not invited. They'd let you know.
In Vicksburg, Mississippi, we had Blue Vein Society...
What is that?!

...where they could see if you're light enough for them to see your veins. If they could see the blue blood through your veins, then you could come to their (?), but a guy like me, I didn't have a chance!
Well, you have your own thing. It was like the blue bloods.
No. We would let them have it.

You know, so that is the strata. So as a kid in New Orleans, you went through all of that. "Oh, they have a dance at the Jeunes(?) Ami(?) all night. I think I'll go. I heard they've got a dance." You wanted to go to
Barker - I-36

everything, because you'd want to hear the bands, when you could (?) with this band. My mother would say, "You don't want to go there. Those people aren't to let you in there. That's a private affair."

Tio was the brother-in-law. He married one of the Bocage sisters. Now, Cottrell, the drummer, was a cousin. Leroy married one of his cousins. So they was all intermingled with the whole family. So you didn't get into that band unless somebody died. Because they're all depend on... Their wives and their families depend on that band as... And everybody was particular who came in the band; you know, who was taking whose place. You had to be respectable. You had to be able to read music, and you had to be what is called a gentleman.

Now, Steve Lewis was the piano player. It was an orchestra. It wasn't in the sense of a Jazz band. This was an orchestra. And they played in opposition to Joe Robichaux and Papa Celestin. They had to lead three orchestras.
Papa Celestin, yeah.
Barker - I-37
Yeah. They played the polite music, and played for all the people, all the White folks, they'd play all the colleges in Mississippi and around here -- and they was the top band...reading band.

But then they had the funky bands that played for the people, like Buddy Petit and Kid Rena. Buddy Petit was a fantastic musician. Reminds me some of Charlie Shavers. He was called "The Diminished King." Louis got all them diminished things, that's what everybody said, from Buddy. Because Buddy was older than Louis. Buddy was the boss after King Oliver. See, Bunk disappeared, so it left the mantle to King Oliver...
Bunk Johnson.
Yeah.
He disappeared, huh. Where did he...

He went with the circus. He took some money for a gig with some Irishmen on the waterfront, that Jefferson City Buffet(?) Gang. They was a bad, rough gang of Irishmen who acted like Negroes and danced like Negroes, who could jump just like the Negroes, they'd act like Negroes, and they was rough and rowdy, and they fought -- they're still up there now in the Irish Channel. They work hard, and they do all the...all the work just above the work that they would give Negroes. Driving trucks, they got the
Barker - I-38

gangs on the riverfront, they're foremen... And Eddie Halliday, a tough Irishman who would pull his coat off and fight, and one got the gang...you know, test Eddie Halliday's Negroes, you know, insult them on the river, because Eddie Halliday would come over there and cap the joint.

They had a thing going. All the element of people, the poor oppressed Irishmen come here, starving from the potato famine, they settle in New Orleans. You have the Negro here. They're both working. They're rivals for the hardest work, uneducated work in town. But they have a common thing in one another. They were still longshoremen. So you don't say nothin' about these Nigger longshoremen and you don't say nothin' about them Irish longshoremen. They come over there and...
Hard-working.

Yeah. They (?) hard work. Don't talk. Put up or shut up. Make it. And they'd work together. They use different toilets, just so they got so (?), and then they let them all use the same toilet. They respected one another, and they wanted to know if you was a man.
Many times they had fights on the river where a White longshoreman made a remark to a Black longshoreman, and they said, "Well, go out and settle it out on the (?)." And
Barker - I-39

they'd go out at twelve o'clock, and the two (?) would get out there and fight. And all of them would sit around, the Black and White, and look, and the best man wins. We ain't talkin' about no goddamn color now. Just fight. You're a man, I'm a man. So many times that's been on the river(?).
So Bunk Johnson...

Bunk Johnson booked a date for the longshoremen. And he forgot it! And the parade is waiting to go on, doin' with the umbrellas just like the Blacks. Same thing. And all of them rough Irish chicks is out there in the bar, and the band ain't comin'. And them sumbitches just... Heh...
They weren't on time, huh?
The sent word, said, "If we catch Bunk Johnson, you tell that son-of-a-bitch we're gonna tie him in a sack and throw him in the river."
[LAUGHS]
Bunk Johnson heard that, and left for Crowley.
Crowley!

Yes. Two hundred miles from there! They said, "They're looking for you, Bunk. Everybody is agitating for you. Bunk, them sumbitches out on the riverfront, all them longshoremen, say, oh, if they get hold
Barker - I-40

of your ass, that's the end of you." Bunk Johnson got nervous, cut out and went out to Crowley, and went away with the Black Eagle Band, Evan Thomas' band, which was a funky band out there. He went to Crowley...
Evan Thomas was killed out there. He was going with a cat's old lady who was in the penitentiary.
Who's that?

Evan Thomas. The Black Eagle Band. It was a helluva band. They used to come to New Orleans occasionally. And Evan Thomas was going out with some cat's old lady. Cats went to the penitentiary and told... It was a freaky thing, like a country club down there, the penitentiary shit, you know...
Mmm-hmm.

He went up there and told this cat, whoever he was, that Evan Thomas was going with his old lady. And the cat said, 'When I come out of here, I'm gonna kill him.' Sure enough, he got out, and he got a cane knife, one of them machetes, and walked in the hall, and just walked... Evan Thomas was up there blowing his horn, and he just went up there and chopped him down. There was blood all over the place. Killed him right in front of the people.
Bunk Johnson was there playing second fiddle to Evan Thomas. Bunk Johnson split from there, and went on the
Barker - I-41
circus...
He was moving!
He went on the circus. Then he went with the (?)Shell Float(?) touring, that other circus, that went all over the world.
Is that so?

Yeah, and he come back to New Iberia, and stayed out there. He was a legend in (?) parts. That son-of-a-bitch, boy, you should have heard that man. Bunk Johnson! King Oliver, none of them was playing that shit then. See, he wasn't powerful, but the shit he played on his horn. See, he was always running that third valve. See, you can't (?) that very few trumpet players play with that third valve. That's where you get them accidental (?) sharps in your line.
Well, when we were with Cab Calloway, you took me back up in (?), where we found him back up there.
Yeah, yeah.
I took pictures of him there. I still have those pictures.
Yeah. And then...
Later on they were ...(?)...(?)...
A couple of years later.
Barker - I-42
You took me down there on one of the (?) ways. That's amazing.

So that's the legendary Bunk Johnson. (?) used to be in the parade with him. He said King Oliver had a funny eye. He said, "you bad-eyed sumbitch, you won't listen when I'm playing!" He was a little sassy, ratty(?) or something, tatty... (?) tells me he'd wear his cap on the side. Everybody got their position of the cap...
The (?) is tight, yeah.

Yeah. He's got his cap on the side! And he got hold of one of the chicks to hold his horn, and another one holding his bottle. And that's how he walked in the parade. And everybody was looking at Bunk. That's a helluva a thing, man, to see that. When you'd hear, like, Lee Collins and them would play...
Yeah.

You'd see little kids, you know, who were just fascinated by what they were playing in the street. And you would have to watch for a (?) stone or a she-brick. Now, what you call a she-brick is when it rains. See, in a loose brick, the water is under this brick...
And you call that a she-brick.
Yeah. See, it will piss on you!
[LAUGHS HEARTILY]
Barker - I-43

See, if you walk under... [AWAY FROM MICROPHONE, NOT AUDIBLE] ...all over my pants(?), we have a she-brick. Or heave(?) a stone, see. See, my grandfather was a master at watching stones, Old Man Barbarin. See, he could dig back around the stone(?)... [BOTH LAUGH]
What did he play, your grandfather, Danny?

Mellophone and alto horn. He had played trumpet to begin with, but they told him to get off the trumpet. But he was just about as Creole as you could get. He used to eat dinner every day at 12 o'clock with his bottle of wine. He was French as you... He'd never say nothin'. He never said nothing, except (?)"If Negroes start a fight or something, they're lucky to (?)."(?) Didn't move a muscle. He was the first... He drove... He was a carriage-driver, which was a profession in the South.
A hackman, yeah.

A hackman. And he drove the hearse for the undertaking parlors. They called him "Joe Never Smile." Sit on this hearse... You had to have this beaver or this derby, and you'd sit on a hearse, and you had to not get emotionally aroused by nothin', because you had them kind of funerals where the wives and everybody go hysterical and they start screamin' and howlin' and runnin', and then
Barker - I-44
breaking up the place because they just closed the casket, and they come out and there's pandemonium. So Grandpa said, "don't never smile, never move a muscle."
Just sat there. That was Paul Barbarin's father, right?
Yes.
Uh-huh.

His attitude was be cold! [DISSOLVES IN LAUGHTER]... Stay cold! No matter how much a woman screams. "Oh! My baby's gone. My husband's gone. My mother's gone. Lawd, they done closed that casket! I don't care what happens." "Don't never smile, don't move a muscle." And he'd tell his horses. He'd go, CLIP-CLOP, hit them horses on the rump with them lines (?), and the hearse would pull off. Don't move a muscle.
He was a...
Three undertaking parlors he worked -- funerals. Always, most of the time with that hearse.
Well, that's...

Now, there was he and Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez was a contemporary of King Oliver. He was the boss in the street parades. Played a little fat cornet, him and Pottot(?)...Pottot(?)... Joe...I can't think of his name right now... George...George... Pottot(?) was the leader of
Barker - I-45

the Olympia Band and the Excelsior Band.
They had Excelsior Bands all around the country. That was a big name for bands. They had one in St. Louis. They had one in Memphis. That's the bands that played for the Black Masonic temples, and they had these bands in all these cities like St. Louis and Kansas City, that played for affairs of the Black people -- the Elks, the Moose, the Masons.

Well, Manuel Perez was the boss of the street. Well, he and my grandfather were tight. And they were on...like, the boss in the background of the Onward Brass Band, which was the greatest brass band. If you heard that brass band...
Which was the greatest brass band?

Onward. They had Kimball, this fantastic trumpet player who used to play in the theatre, and he played like King Oliver. Those people were great lead trumpet players then. You know, it could be said what... They had them all over the country, you know. But there were so many of these super trumpet players.
Strong, yes.
Yeah. You see, you worked with Lee, you heard Lee. Well, Lee was just another trumpet player here. So we had (?) when the rest of them died. Andrew Kimball,
Barker - I-46
he had the respect...Andrew Kimball... He had the respect of Mister Manuel Perez.
How about Freddie Keppard?
Freddie Keppard was fantastic. You heard Freddie.
I played with Freddie.
Well, Freddie was a Ragtime trumpet player. Am I right?
Yeah.
He seemed like he played ragged.
But he was strong, boy. He was so loud, man. Whoo!
With that little bit of (?).
Knocking walls down.
Yeah, he would blast the horn. Well, the people would look at him, right.
Yeah, whoa. I played with him at 35th and State Street, up there where that Jesse Benga bank was. Do you remember that bank in those days?
I was over there.

Oh, he was fabulous, man. He lived on up by the Vincennes Hotel, 36th and Vincennes over there. I think that's where he died. Because he was getting... He was sick when I was playing, because he was on...you know, he was on
Barker - I-47

Well, he had been on the Orpheum circuit for about ten years, from about 1909, the year I was born, until, what, 1918 or 1919, when the Dixieland Band recorded... Them people had been on the Orpheum circuit, him and Big-Eye Louis, a band from New Orleans...
Who was Big-Eye Louis?
Big-Eye Louis [Nelson] was a great clarinet player, who was somewhat of a rival of Tio. Big-Eye Louis and Picou, they were masters of that style of playing, that improvisation...
Was Jay-Joe(?) from here? A clarinet player named Jay-Joe(?).
No, I think he was from Cuba.
Oh, yeah. He came to Chicago.
Yeah, Jay-Joe(?) and the other one, the one who plays clarinet upside-down.
I can't think of his name. It wasn't Cliff Keene, was it?
No. It was another guy. Later Paul showed me him in New York. He was a master clarinet player from one of them islands.
[PAUSE]
Barker - I-48
I just want to get back a little so we won't digress too far, Danny. When you were a kid around New Orleans, when did you first start to think about getting into music?

Well, I didn't think about it too much. I was going to school. And I'm hearing this music all the time, and I'd see these musicians, they're celebrated. I've got four uncles -- Paul Barbarin, Louis Barbarin, Lucien Barbarin, Willie Barbarin. We live in the neighborhood, in the Seventh Ward, where there's quite a few halls -- the (?) Hall, the Jean Ami Hall, the Franz(?) Ami Hall, the New Hall. And on Ledgerfield Avenue there was about four or five White halls. And there was music all the time. And I'm listening to the music...

And my uncles... My grandfather being in the brass band, he played the funerals with the Onward Brass Band, which was the greatest brass band at that time. And there was a rivalry between Manny Perez and George Moret(?), who was the leader of the Excelsior Band. And I'm hearing this. And my uncles, they're talkin' about who's who and who ain't. And it's a celebrate thing, and everybody is celebrated. So they would talk who could play and who couldn't, and who rated... Like most people, the kids in town, they would be involved with baseball or basketball or
Barker - I-49

other sports. But in New Orleans, when I come up, other than playing in the street, when you got down to something you want to do that you aspire... Like, today kids aspire to be, if they're tall...to be a basketball star. If he's heavy, he's going to be a football star. Well, I had no... none of that I was involved with. Everything I saw, everybody, they wanted to be a musician. Because you saw the musicians walking there. Everything was music. Music. Music. Music...
And they got the best of everything, too, didn't they?
Yes.
The best chicks...
Yeah. Well, everything was good... It was the glamour... The glamour stick(?) was not a Jackie Robinson or a Joe Louis or...or Abba-Dabba, that...
Mmm-hmm.

None of them people. This was who was... Mister Manuel Perez, when he'd blow that trumpet...cornet in the street, and everybody said, "That's Mister Manuel Perez blowing." Or you saw Chris Kelly on a truck, playing them Blues. You'd say, "I'd like to do that." You'd see how them people get affected by that music. You'd say, "Mister Chris really blows. Did you hear him play? Yeah, Mister
Barker - I-50

Chris, Lordy." See? And you heard that. And you'd see Kid Rena, and you'd see a battle of music -- Kid Rena and Kid Ricotti(?), cousins, but that don't make no difference, 'cause the blood's gonna fly if they meet today. And they're both advertised in the same neighborhood. And here come Chris Kelly. And here come Long-Haired Bob with his truck or on his wagon. And them cats meet on the corner, and they're battlin' to draw a crowd of about four or five hundred people. They stand there and they blow. And they were so into his blowing, but "He should go home because he's no...he can't compete with so-and-so." And you're hearing this all the time.

And then they have a party in the Pecan Grove, and you go in there and you get on a fence and look down at... Pecan Grove is a yard that had a large pecan tree in it, and the people from the lower coast, the people that work hard... And they was all dark people, you see, because in New Orleans you get them different color strata, you see. But these were all dark people, and they all look alike, and they're all dancing, and they're having fun. And Chris Kelly is playing for them, and he'd playing them low-down Blues, and you can hear it from the neighborhood, and you'd get up on the fence and you'd look down there. And you'd see Mister So-and-So is (?) dancing with Miss Lucy, and
Barker - I-51

you'd see them in the corner, and they'd be grinding and belly-rubbing, and you'd see that, and next thing you know, they're (?) and drinkin' and they're signifyin'. And you'd see that, and you'd say, "Yeah, Mister Chris Kelly, the greatest... Mister Chris Kelly, will you have a drink? You boys want some sandwiches?"

Everybody was so nice to the musicians. You're something special. You see that. So what the hell you gonna do? Now, you're a youngster, a Black youngster in New Orleans, and you figure, well, what'cha gonna do? From a kid you start shining shoes. You never even think of stealin' or takin' nothin' from nobody. You're not (?). You get a shoe-shining box, you can sell papers...
Go to work, yeah. Work.
Yeah. You can work piling brick. You can work for the grocery store...
What do you mean piling brick?

You get red bricks, and you pile it, because people use it to clean their sidewalk. And you'd take this brick and pound it, then you'd pound it, and then sprinkle this brick, and when you'd walk, it... It would smash(?) and give a coloring to the front of your house.
To the front of your house.
Yeah.
Barker - I-52
And kids would pound it up into powder at the time.
Yeah, powder it.
Get with the (?).

Yeah. You'd powder it... You'd say you were going to pound some bricks. So you'd wait until you see... If a kid in my neighborhood... If you saw a pretty red brick with a soft brick, an old ancient brick, you know, or even the plaster part of it. But you could tell, because the brick is almost pinkish, it's so pure, made out of this red sand. But it's red brick. And not a fire brick; a fire brick is hard. But this brick is...
Porous.

Yeah, it's porous. And you'd bring that brick home, because later, on Saturday, you'd see some bricks in the street. Or if they were building and they were knocking down the pillars, and then you go in the foundation you'd take two or three of them bricks. Because you could always sell a bucket of bricks to somebody in your family. See, you got six or seven ...(?)...
You'd get you a big old stone or something, and just pound it up til...
Then you'd get a hammer and you'd get a stone, and you'd take the brick and you'd wet it, and you'd
Barker - I-53

put it in the bucket wet. Then when you hit it, it cracks quick. And then you just pound the brick. You don't pound it into a powder. You pound it into a small grain by a little digging(?) in the rice and the pea and the bean.
Oh, I see. And then they spread it all on the sidewalk in front of the house.

And then throw it around after they've washed the steps, and then they use the yellow ochre. I don't know what the hell that was, but you could buy that yellow ochre at the grocery store. So when they washed the steps, they'd throw this yellow ochre in the bucket. And when they scrubbed them steps with the lye or whatever it was, high-powered soap or cleanser... It was a yellow octagon(?) soap. And the yellow ochre and that would make the steps be steps...as the pure wood, but it would have a yellow tinge. It's a decorating thing. And then they... All around the South, the bricks are even and everything, because people keep their bricks in front. You'd sprinkle that brick around there, and it makes a nice picture.
Oh yeah. Like little stones around there.

Yeah. But you see, when you step on them, it makes a powder and it's spread. So when you've done that, you sold papers. And you went and you worked with a peddler on Saturdays -- Fridays and Saturdays you worked with a
Barker - I-54

peddler, and he might give you fifty cents. You had your little spending change. And it wasn't so easy to spend your money like kids today. I see kids with two or three dollars, and they throw it in the pinball machine. There's no way in the world you could have got me, hard as I had to hustle for that money, to go playin' no pinball machine. I'd wait until the ice cream comes, get my ice cream, then when the doughnut man comes, get me a doughnut...
Yeah.
And I wanted to go to the show.
Yeah!

Now, as far as me going through [t'rou] my money, I'd never gamble, because I lost my money once shooting dice with some kids. This little cat could shoot dice, and I didn't know, I just wanted to be a smart-aleck, and he just won my money. I don't know how to shoot dice until today. I never did like gambling. I can give you some money, but I ain't into gambling. I never had that lustful feeling about it.
You know I went through that. I lost every dime I had in Cab's band. Then I finally got hip and quit.
Yeah. Who used to do all that winning up there when you all'd be gambling?
Barker - I-55
Oh, Illinois Jacquet and those guys. Ike Quebec. Jacquet was always winning.
Yeah, he was...
Russell Smith was cheating. When he'd play cards, poker, he used to stick cards all up his sleeve.
[LAUGHTER]
So who were some of the guys that turned out to be musicians along with you when you were growing up?

Well, you'd see them, you'd see all the kids. Well, I didn't pay him no mind, but there was one little youngster, he's about what...about fourteen -- Crump, they called him. ...(?)... Charlie Barbarin's wife; he was his uncle. Crump. He was a little-bitty cat, a little light cat who looked like could be a Spaniard, had pretty black curly hair with big waves in it, and he wore sideburns as a... He didn't have them then, but later on he had these big heavy sideburns. But he played clarinet and saxophone, and I remember going to the Crescent Star Park and I seen him up there with these professional musicians. And he was playing. And they kept featuring him and sending him out for... And he was playing "High Society"; he must have played it about three times during the night. Because this is the hip(?) tune. This is like "Sweet Sue" in New York or "Liza." You played, you know, "High Society." He played
Barker - I-56

"High Society." And he was celebrated(?). But he didn't ever amount to much as a musician, because at a different level... You could stay, you know, and if you didn't improve, it didn't matter. You were working. But there's still a certain element, and you...

So, in the (?) the ukelele craze had come out. So I'd see these little kids around in their little spasm bands in the French Quarter makin' money, the White Folks throwing [t'rowin] them money -- and I see that everybody was makin' some money with this music business. My grandfather, he's supplementing the money. He's playing like maybe two funerals a week, sometimes three, and he's working as a coach driver... It put him out of business when they changed from horses to limousines; it throwed him out the whole business altogether.
My grandfather was a hackman in Vicksburg, too -- my mother's father.
Yeah. So that was quite a... It was a good profession.
Yeah. That was a high-class gig.
Yeah. Because you had to be careful with them people, you had to have responsible horses in order to let them ride comfortably, and be careful how you drove.
Barker - I-57

So that was that. So it was just a matter of you picking up music if you wanted to. So a little kid in the neighborhood was playin' the ukelele. His Daddy was a mailman, and he had this ukelele. He could play it -- somewhat. And the ukelele craze had come on, and everybody had ukeleles. My aunt bought a ukelele, a banjo uke from Grunwald(?), which was nice, and I saw it. They had no money. And she tried to play it, couldn't ever tune it, and she left it around my house. My grandmother got (?), and I saw the ukelele then.

So I see this little boy one evening, and he's sitting there playing the ukelele, and all the little girls from all around there, all the little boys, looking at him in amazement, how he could play this ukelele. And he was playing, and singing a little song. His name was Ashton Murray, a big supervisor in the school department. Ashton Murray. I used to see him. But he was always with little girls. He would never play with them little roughnecks in the neighborhood. So, "All right," I said...

There was another one, Herman Henderson! Sharp little cat. He lived about three blocks down from me. I never saw him much, but I saw him one day, he was playing that ukelele, and everybody around him saying he was great, "That kid is wonderful." But he was about what, fourteen, and he
Barker - I-58
could drive an automobile, he would drive his father's car, he could fix the car, he would cook... After I got to know him, he would cook the dinner for the family...
A real bright kid.
Yeah, just a little smart cat. He was a wonderful little kid. He died with appendix.
Hmm!

So I said... Well, I saw this ukelele. So I asked Ma, I said, 'What did you do with that ukelele?' She said, 'I'm not doin' nothin' with it.' [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE] I said, 'Why don't you give it to me.' She said, 'I'm not goin' to give it to you.' She said, 'I'll sell it to you.' I said, 'What do you want?' She said, 'I paid out fifteen dollars for it.' She said, 'I'll sell it to you.' I said, 'What you want?' She said, 'What you giving?' I said, 'I ain't got nothin' to give.' She said, 'Well, I'll let you have it, but you got to pay me something.' I said, 'What you want?' She said, 'Pay me half of what I paid.' Half of $15 is what? $7.50. I said, 'All right.' She said, 'Well, how you gonna pay me?' -- she was putting me on. She said, 'Give me fifty cents a week.' I says, 'Yeah?' 'Yes, that's right.' I said, 'I'll give you a quarter a week.' That's (?) money, you know what...
Yeah.
Barker - I-59
When you said fifty cents a week, that meant I'd have to pound a whole lot of brick, and I'd have to sell some papers...
That's right! That's half of your fun.

So she said, "Okay, give me 25 cents a week." And I got that ukelele. And I made a beeline to Ashton's house, and knocked on the door. His aunt was very (?). She said, "What do you want?" They were sophisticated, nice and reserved mulatto people. So you'd go through that again. It was hurtin' for me to go in there and ask them for anything. I said, "Is Ashton there?" She said, "What do you want with Ashton?" I guess she had seen me out there playin' with them little girls, talkin' trash, because I was a smart-aleck even then. "What you want with Ashton?" I said, "I want him to tune my ukelele." "Well, he won't be here until after school. Then we have to go somewhere. You can come back later." I said, "Okay."

So I finally caught Ashton, and then Ashton tuned that guitar...that ukelele for me, and he showed me a couple of chords. And I said, "Well, I (?) Ashton." Herman Henderson could play it better than Ashton. So I go... Between Herman Henderson and Ashton, I'm learning the...
The changes, yeah.
Barker - I-60

The changes. And three chords, C-F-G. But in the meantime, I had been around my uncle Paul between his visits from Chicago, and my uncle Louis and them, and they all got this drum set up, and they'd play... All of them played the drums. So I could get by on the drums, too. They showed me how to hold the sticks properly and they let me play. And my aunt had bought a victrola, and they'd go borrow the victrola in (?), and they'd play against the victrola. And they'd let me play. Then I thought about all them drums you have to carry.

So my Uncle Paul has got a clarinet. He's foolin' around with the clarinet. Can't play it. He's foolin' around, but he's learning to... I found out later that he was learning so he could count, count notation to write, because he wanted to write. So he figured he'd play a little melody and he'd be able to. So he let me blow the clarinet. A lift-off(?) point. He told me, 'Go take some lessons.'

So he sent me to Barney Bigard. They were working at ...(?)... So I went to see Barney Bigard, and he gave me a little book, and I started figuring out them notes -- and they still all, some of them, the same to me today. So I worked with him for about what...about three months -- when I could catch him. But my God, he would sit down and play
Barker - I-61
and...
Now, he must have lived in another part of town, too, didn't he?
Lived right around a couple of blocks from me.

Now, across the street from me is Don Albert, who is going to school taking clarinet lessons. And on the next block is Herman Henderson. He's taking clarinet lessons. And all around you, every day you could hear horns. You'd pass the street and listen to some kid practicing a horn, practicing the clarinet, or somebody playing the piano. It was just music, music, music, music, music, music, music. No football, no basketball, no nothin'. It was nothing else but music. So little Herman Henderson, he showed me how to get them three chords, the foundation, and how to sing, and to get the song "Chinaman and Mabel."

Charlie Costain(?), I meet him. He was another little kid. He played a little ukelele. And I go to his house, and he's in there, his mother's hitting him on the wrist(?) because he wasn't playing the piano right. If he was playing the piano right, what ...(? )...(? )... He sang, "Chinaman and Mabel/Sat down at a table/Down in a cabaret..." He had learned that at the bar. "He wanted his Dinah/She couldn't be finer/Well, those were the words I
Barker - I-62

heard him say..." His mother said, "Shut that up, boy, and play your lesson instead of singing them old rowdy songs." "And these are the words I heard him say:/Good-night little girl, good-night/I hope you get home by the light./Your kisses were fine/With each drink of wine.../Couldn't be finer/But it's still some..." -- I can't think of all of it. "Good-night, little girl, good-night/Good-night, little girl, good-night./Because that ring on your finger/Tells me not to linger,/Good-night, little girl,/Good-night." He was playing... That's a honky tonk tune, with all those lyrics. So I played it with him...
You played the changes.

I played a little bit with him, and then we got a little thing going there. Charlie Costain(?), his mother was a Creole, a real Creole woman that talked French and did everything like a Frenchwoman. She ran around with French people. And Charlie Costain(?) was a little like what someone would maybe call him a Mama's boy -- they thought he was a Mama's boy. Charlie Costain was hip to it; you know, how(?) the gang would see him. So he and I was buddies, see.
[LAUGHING...]
Charlie Costain could sing Creole, sing little Creole songs, and he could talk Creole, and he was a little
Barker - I-63

hustler. He had started drinkin' wine then. We were about fourteen, and Charlie Costain(?) would drink a glass of wine. Because his mother used to buy wine for his daddy, and he'd drink...he'd get his wine at the table. His daddy said, "Water is no good for nobody. Wine is good for the digestive system." So Charlie Costain was a little wine-head then. He's a wine-head now. He'd stand in front of the jukebox all night, and play the jukebox and dance by himself.
What, now?
Every Louis Armstrong record. "Some day/You'll be sorry."
He's still around, huh?
[MIMICS] Sitting at the jukebox. [SINGS REFRAIN] "Some day/You'll be sorry..." Heh, you'll see him at the jukebox, nine at night til three at the morning. He'll put all them nickels in that jukebox.
Still doing it, huh?
Drink wine. He's around there in the neighborhood. Charlie Costain(?).

So we're sitting on my steps. Now, Joe Francis Ely(?) is on the corner. He's a presser's son. He gets the kazoo, he comes around. Then with the ukelele, I'm drawing a crowd. I've become a little celebrity with the ukelele.
Barker - I-64
Joe comes with the kazoo. Russell, another friend of ours, he's got the drum. He gets the top of a cheese-box and had a little drum. And we're sitting on my steps.
Now, every evening there's a concert. And the people would stop, because we were beginning to sound good. "Little Liza Jane"...
Yeah!

We've got a beat. We've definitely got the beat. Because you would learn that beat from the street parades, that funky beat, the snappin' the fingers. The second... All the little cats on the street are second-lining, you know, with "The Saints..."
Yeah.

So we've got this group. So here comes Ervin Butler. Ervin Butler's a hustler in town, a young cat, a roughneck, fight anybody anywhere, any time, and go anywhere -- because they had them gang wars with youngsters. Well, Ervin Butler would go anywhere. He'd go to Cherokee, you know, and the various streets where you have them gangs. You know, like on the South Side of Chicago, man, they have certain neighborhoods that you don't go if you're out of bounds. Well, Ervin Butler would go everywhere.
He sees us. He sits there and listens. And he says, "Man, you'all got a gold mine here, man. We could make some
Barker - I-65
money with this." I said, "How?" He said, "Well, come on with me, and I'll take you to the balls(?) on Saturday, and we'll make us some money."

Now, Herman Henderson was an aristocratic little kid, see. He was there, and... But his people didn't want him hustling or none of that. They had aspired for him to be a little college kid, and his mother was a midwife and his father worked as...he was a helluva mechanic with a big machine company, a machine design... And his grandmother was a midwife. And he was high-class. But he... He had a little thing with him, but that's what his parents did.

So I said, "Well, man, we're gonna make it. Let's organize a band." So we called the band the Boozaire Kings. Because what you say... Them people down there are having a ball or party, you say "they're having a boozaire(?) down there." Now, that's a "boozain", that's a good time in Creole patois, in Cajun...
So "boozaire" is patois for "a good time."
Yes. Now, "baza"(?) is a humbug. So you had the "boozaire" on that (?), and it turned into a "baza." You know a bazaar? A regular bazaar where all the...
Yeah!
Man, it's a "ba-za." "Man, they had a boozaire(?) last night, and man, a cat got drunk and turned
Barker - I-66
that place into a baza(?)! A humbug!

So I named the group the Boozaire(?) Kings. So Ervin Butler, sure enough, comes and get us. We started right at the corner of the house. We played out on the side of the street by the bar, by the door. We played ..[SINGS REFRAIN] Charlie Costain(?) sang "Apple pie ..[INAUDIBLE].." [SYNCOPATING] Man, all the people come out the barroom to see this music, because they're used to itinerant... Then they say, "You'all can come on in here." So they send us some money. So we made about fifty cents. Well, then Butler got the hat, he passed the hat -- he's hustling hard. We go to the next bar, kept on going.
We made like two dollars a piece. Men was makin' like ten dollars a week and raising their family!
Sure.
So then we're in business. You dig? Next week's... Now, I know what Ervin(?) Butler ain't givin' us. We got about maybe, say, three-fifths of what we made. He kept that other.

Next week... Next week he takes us in the District. We just go. And the police come and say "Take them kids out of here. They ain't got no business in here." But we was coinin'(?) (?). Boy, we must have made about seven dollars a piece. I didn't get home until about, like, around 11
Barker - I-67

o'clock, and when I hit the door, my mother said, "Boy, where you been?" I said, "Well, I went and made some money." She said, "You made some money?" [LAUGHS] I just thought I was gonna get smacked upside the head. And she said, "You made some money? Where could you go and do that?" I said, "Well, we was playing for them people, playing for them rich White people." "Them rich White people?" I put that "rich White people" to let her know I was around a nice place! [LAUGHING HELPLESSLY] Then I went inside to count that money. I gave her $4, and I kept one I'd stashed before, and it left me with $3. She wasn't mad.
Boy, the next day she told the whole family. Shit, I made more money than my uncles who was playing in the bands! She only gave me three dollars!
[BOTH LAUGH HEARTILY]

So after that, man, I could kind of stay out late. And that went on. The Boozaire(?) Kings, we get popular. Now they want us for house parties. They say, "We could pay you all two dollars if you all come around, you'll all be at the party, all them little girls are gonna be there, and you'all can have all the cake and ice cream you'all want." So we played a couple of them.
Then a woman, her daughter was named Manuella, she was a good-time woman, nice, you know. But she knew all them
Barker - I-68
chicks that love a good time, all them cats that love a good time. She gave a party and printed tickets, boy, and her house and yard was loaded.
A ticket to play at the house, huh?
Yeah, that the Boozaire(?) Kings would be there. And we had made this name, our reputation. So we made what, made about five dollars a piece, man. That was a whole lot-ta money then, man.
Oh yeah.
And we got this name, then everybody wanted us. Then they wanted us in the Tremais(?)...
What's the Tremais(?)?

That's a section up there, above Esplanade. But we couldn't go across there, because you had to fight them little thugs up there. Then over the bridge was another section, and they couldn't go up there. You know, they had the gangs of kids...
Territorial.

Yeah. Same gangs as Chicago(?). So Wilhelmina Breaux(?) was a piano player, and she heard about everything in the whole Downtown, in this section where we had a (?) section, an eight-block section was the Boozaire(?) Kings. Because we'd be out there on Claiborne Avenue under the trees playing in the evening, and there
Barker - I-69

would be a crowd around us like this. Man, we celebrated. So she gave a dance at the Franz(?) Ami, which is the big Creole hall where all the muckamucks go, real staunch-down Creoles, Free Men of Color, all that shit. It said, "Wilhelmina Breaux Presents the Original Boozaire(?) Kings." And she gave this thing. And man, that fuckin' place was packed and jammed. And I didn't set no price for it. I should have known it; I'd been doing this long enough.
