When she got through, she gave us a dollar-and-a-half a piece. Boy, these place was loaded, and she was charging 50 cents...no, 25 and 35 cents to come in. And that place was packed and jammed. And it was a great big hall. My mother said, "What did Wilhelmina Breaux(?) pay you all?" I said, "A dollar and a half." She said, "That dirty bitch should've gave you'all more money."

But then we went to the Lyric Theatre. And the first time we worked there, we stopped the show. They had an amateur hour, and they used to have all the same little kids come every week. You've seen that.
Sure.
The same little bunch of little (?)s...
Yeah.
And they brought us on and put us on, and we did "Little Liza Jane." For an encore we did "The Chinaman
Barker - I-70
and Mabel."
"Chinaman and Mabel"!? [LAUGHS]

A whole (?). "Chinaman and Mabel/Sat down at a table/Down in a cabaret." That's a story of a Chinaman, a nice Chinaman, he's seeing this woman, and he's out with her, and he's gonna make it with her, and then he sees that she's got this ring on her finger. It's a legendary song like "Frankie and Johnny" or "St. James." But it's "The Chinaman and..."
Mabel.
And it says the Chinaman seen that Mabel had a husband...
She was married, yeah.

Yeah. He told her, "Oh, goodbye, little girl..." A nice Chinaman. It's a sentimental thing. You know, someone would go, "Yeah, that's a good Chinaman. He's ...(?). . .(?). . . The woman is weak, but he saw it and told her to go home..." [LAUGHS] So that's a legendary...

See, that one and "The Titanic." I used to sing "The Titanic." I can't sing it no more. The Titanic went down, and the Captain begs... Yeah, I forgot it all. "Slim, please save my wife and my daughter, the Titanic's gonna..." Slim jumped in the ocean and ...(?). . ., and swam faster than the sharks, he was dippin' and dodgin', savin' people all
Barker - I-71
through the dark. You can recite that almost for two hours. "The Titanic." Drunks loved to hear "The Titanic." They wept on it.
[LAUGHS] Yeah, that was at that theatre... The Lyric Theatre? What was the name again?
The Lyric Theatre was like the...
Like the Apollo, sort of, huh?
Yeah. Well, it was bigger than the Apollo. Actually it was bigger.
Like a regular theatre.

The Lyric. We went on there for the Amateur Hour. The stage doorman was Chinese. And I remember he had a fight with a cat named Charlie, a one-legged guy who sang like a tenor -- Charlie Henderson. You might have seen him in Chicago. He came out with a white full-dress suit and one leg. It was a cork leg, you couldn't see it. But he sang tenor. They got in an argument. They had an argument backstage about some woman. And the Chinese threatened to kill him and all that shit, and he was going to get his pistol and all that... The second night.
So we won the amateur prize, which was five dollars...
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE B]
Danny Barker (Milt Hinton, 4/80) - (Pt.2, Tapes 2 & 3):

...Petit, Buddy Petit... See he goes off, and he's with... He goes to Chicago and he's with King Oliver. Gee whiz! Then he leaves King Oliver and he goes with the Tennessee Ten. I didn't know what the hell they was talking about. I found out later that was one of the best vaudeville acts that ever happened, the Tennessee Ten. You know about them.
I've heard the name. I didn't see them.

Yeah, out of Chicago. It was a fantastic act. Then I asked my Uncle Louis. He's in New Orleans. He's with Papa Celestin, Sidney Desvignes, and he's probably one of the best young drummers. And I got my other Uncle Lucien, he was a drummer, he played in ballrooms, he played in honky-tonks, played at house parties everywhere. He got... They said Lucien's got more personality than all of them. He'd play a street parade. He'd play for advertising on a truck, he'd get out of the truck with his cymbal in the street, and go play all up and down the street in front of people's buildings.
Just a stick and a cymbal, huh.

Yeah. He was a showman. And he'd create a big scene in the street. And I got Willie, he's about two years older than me, he's trying to play trumpet. And he's playing with the little band. Everybody's playing music.
Barker - II-2
Estee Bijou, who was a great vaudeville performer -- she was a cousin of my grandfather. And all of them...

You were entangled all around music. And everybody's proud. Ain't nobody to tell you, "Don't fool with no music." They're saying, "Yeah, so-and-so is doing wonderful with the music." It's encouraging...
Sure.
...to get somewhere, to get any esteem.
That's beautiful, Danny. This is unbelievable.
[PAUSE]
Yeah, Danny, to continue our conversation about the early days: You mentioned the vaudeville act, the Tennessee Ten. What did they do?

Well, when I got to New York, I found out about the Tennessee Ten. I forget the name of the people. But Florence Mills was the star. She later starred in The Blackbirds. Florence Mills was one of the stars, dancers of the girl performers, what you call a soubrette. She came out front and she done her thing, and she danced with the little chorus there. There was ten people, but they were very compact, what you would call a revue, a small revue or a small tab show. You could play the side-show in a carnival. You could go in a nightclub in town and do an
Barker - II-3

act, a compact hour act. But they generally did, like twenty minutes or thirty minutes on the Orpheum and the Pantages circuit. It was considered one of the greatest acts. And especially when you mention this name of Florence Mills. She later became one of the greatest Black performers there ever was. And you mention her in awe when you say "Florence Mills." She lit up a stage. She had this charisma that people have, when you see them they just upset a stage, and it's natural. That was Florence Mills.

That was the Tennessee Ten. They had Little Broadway Rastus, who was a terrific drummer. They speak of him. He went to Europe and stayed over there. He could run and jump and slide, slide and sort of... It was mystifying how he could run across the stage and slide, and made a spread eagle on the stage, and just continued to move. When you'd look at the momentum to think he had stopped, he'd slide some more.
Oh, yeah.
You know, like a rubber band pullin' him. Yeah, yeah. And he later... Later on I saw him with a septet. I can't think of the name of that septet. They were great in vaudeville.
But the Tennessee Ten was one of the greatest acts in vaudeville. They played the big-time Orpheum circuit.
Barker - II-4
Never went on the TOBA circuit, which was the Black ...(?)... attraction. It was Tough On Black Asses; that was the name of TOBA. It started at the Pekin Theatre and went down South.
And I had a cousin, Estee Bijou, and you mentioned relatives...
Yeah.

She was a star. She was Irving C. Miller's wife. She was a very beautiful Creole woman. I have a picture of her at the house, and you can see. and she was a star. They called her The Creole Songbird. So I saw Irving C. Miller about 1940 in New York, and I asked him about Estee Bijou, his relationship. He said she was wonderful, a beautiful woman, but she was a little off in her head. He said, "She nagged me. I couldn't sleep. She nagged me, accusing me of winning all the time. And the other thing with ...(?)..., she'd call and disturb me. She was superstitious. And I couldn't stand it no longer. I had to let it go."
And I had a cousin, Big Belly Five-Ball. He played trombone. That's the Tapo branch of the family. He was famous for...
What's his name?
Barker - II-5

Tapo [SPELLS] His name was... I can't think of his last name, but... Yeah, it's Tapo. Yeah, that's right. Tapo. He played trombone, and he did it in a comic manner. He was big and fat. And his nickname was Big Belly Five-Ball. And he worked in the bands around. So you saw him.

Now, there was Manuel Perez, who was the top trumpet player around here, Downtown. Like, everybody respected him as a reading musician. He went to Chicago. He went up there and joined Charlie Elgar's band.
Oh yeah.
Charlie Elgar transported some musicians.
He had a society type band, didn't he.

Yes. And that was... You looked up on him; you saw him in the street. And these people were all celebrated when you'd see as a kid. My little uncle, Willie, would whisper [SOTTO VOCE] "That's Mister Manuel Perez. That's Mister Buddy Petit. That's Kid Rena. That's Chris Kelly. That's ...(?)...." (?) had this great band, you'd hear him. And I'm listening to all that.

So there's a funeral. And it's a Masonic funeral. You never seen nothin' like that. These guys got these soles and these aprons on. Because a minister died a few blocks from my house. So we say "They got second-line; let's go
and see them." I was... That's about 1917, so I was about eight years old...
When you say they got a second line, that means there's going to be a line behind the funeral.
That's the people that follow the funeral.
That follow the funeral. Second line.

They was inquisitive and they want to see. It's just a crowd. Here's something happening. They'll see who is going to perform, see how loud the widow screams, and who holds the widow. There's all kind of intrigue at a funeral. What kind of casket the late deceased, and who is there, if his woman is there, or if his wife is there, his first wife is there. There's always something.

So they'd say, "Well, let's go down there." My Uncle Lucien and Willie, the younger ones, said, "Let's go down there to the band(?) and see the funeral." So we go down there and see the funeral. I don't know what it is; all I'm seeing is guys with aprons on. So I said, "Man, they must gonna serve food. I see all these waiters.
[LAUGHS] What about this guy Willie, what's his name, Pagaud... How do you pronounce his name?
Willie Pagaud. [SPELLS] Willie Pagaud was one of the first bands...
He's one of the first guys you played with?

Yeah. He's a trumpet player. He was a Creole trumpet player. So he talks this French and he's Creole. Manuel Perez is today what you'd call a Creole musician. Picou, Tio, all them people down there could talk a little French. Like, if you went in a band, they could talk on you, and you wouldn't know what they said. "Qua t'est ca? Metta quoi...?" -- "What is he playing?" They thought they could put you down, because...
Yeah. "What's happening?"
Yeah. They'd do it behind this thing. And they're all easy-going and cool, and nothin' faze 'em, because they could play their instruments. See, they put that music up there.
Now, they had just loads of musicians in New Orleans who couldn't play no music. They was all saying, "Nobody pay you to read no music; they pay you to play!"
[LAUGHS]
That's what they said. As long as you could play like Chris Kelly -- and I don't think he ever had his hand on a piece of music.
Who was Chris Kelly?
One of the greatest Blues trumpet players ever happened. He used to go from New Orleans to Mobile. And when I seen Cootie playing that plunger, that's what
Barker - II-8

Chris Kelly used to do. Because when you'd go to Mobile, they'd talk of Gomez's Auditorium you played in. And when you played there, all the Mobile musicians went there and stood in front, just about ten deep looking at you, to see what you were doing. Because then they couldn't understand what this New Orleans thing was all about. Because it was hard for people to fake.
Well, that was quite a trip to go from here to Mobile.
Yeah. They used to go... Chris Kelly was going to play the weekend. He and Sam Morgan, they all went on the road. Every weekend they'd go to ..(?)..
Was that Al Morgan's brother?
Yes. Sam Morgan. There was four of them. Isaiah Morgan, Sam Morgan, Albert Morgan... There was five of them. They come down off the Magnolia Plantation, down in Magnolia, Louisiana, in ..(?)..(?)...
Did they all play bass? Were they all musicians?

They all played trumpet. Two trumpet players, tenor saxophone.... Andrew Morgan played tenor. Albert played bass. Sam played cornet. Isaiah played cornet. Two, first and second cornet players, two brothers. But Albert, he sprung up last, and just jumped in with
Barker - II-9
Sidney Desvignes, out of Sidney Desvignes to Fate Marable, from Fate Marable to New York.
And he went with Cab Calloway's band.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Cab Calloway.
He was my idol. He was the one that I followed in Cab's band. Great bass player.
Yeah. Mmm-hmm.
In fact, I took his place in Cab's band. That's where I came in.
Yeah. Well, the reason(?) when you say about bass... See, I know about Chester...
Chester who?
Chester Zardis.
Oh, Chester Zardis, yeah.

Little short Chester here. But Simon Marrero was considered the boss. But his Daddy had been the greatest, you know, Rag to Jazz bass before him -- Billy Marrero. That's what they called him. Old Man Billy Marrero. Simon Marrero, John Marrero, Lawrence Marrero and Eddie... Four brothers. Two banjo players and two bass players. And that was Old Man Billy Marrero's sons. Now, when you'd see John and Simon, they were masters. Eddie was great, but... And as for Lawrence, he wasn't much of a banjo player. But as of today, all of a sudden, with the George
Barker - II-10
Lewis, he was in that band, the band that Bunk Johnson became a legend with...
George Lewis, huh?

Yeah, George Lewis, the clarinet player. Well, Bunk Johnson picked up this band, and they played a sort of...I don't know... A strange beat. A slower time New Orleans beat. You know, they wasn't too proficient on them instrument, so they played a certain tempo. You know, they never went into nothin' like no "Chinatown or none of them things -- or "Limehouse Blues." But that was the emergence of the Bunk Johnson revival, and all the European Jazz bands began to copy this band because it was easier to copy. There wasn't an abundance of notes.
Yeah.

See, you even have it today. This little White boy that's a great actor, makes his own movies, he's got a band, a funeral band in New York he calls a funeral parade band. Little White boy who makes the greatest movies, what do you call him, with the long nose...
I'm trying to think of his name.
He's supposed to be a genius. Makes these movies. He's in there playing...
Oh! Oh, he plays in Michael's Pub on Monday night.
Barker - II-11
Yes, yes. He owns Michael's Pub, I think. He's great.
Yeah. He is. I know who you're talking about -- Woody Allen.

Woody Allen plays in the theme of George Lewis. It's a sad thing that... It's a lamentable thing, the way he plays. In fact, this guy... There's a whole cult behind George Lewis' band. That's one reason why I fell out of the Preservation Hall, because I played spirited banjo, the Figure-Eight stroke and...you know...
Mmm-hmm.

But them's people that play a straight, static beat -- BLUMP, BLUMP, BLUMP, BLUMP, BLUMP. A flat beat. That's what that band plays. Well, all them Europeans, it don't take you long (or the Japanese)...
Sure.
...to play that.
Yeah.
Because it's the primitive beginning of playing. Almost... It doesn't even reach the Swing Era.
Yeah, you can duplicate it easily.
So that became... You can have the whining, the vibrato on a clarinet, and you got the slow, you know, Jim Robinson trombone...
Barker - II-12
Yeah, the slide...

And you got the trumpet with just a minimum of notes. But it's a sound within itself, with this (?). We use it for a youngster to form himself(?). Now, you give him a Duke Ellington record with Barney and Braud, like "Check and Double Check" or "Stompy Jones," where them people is really swinging -- well, they're in trouble.
Uh-huh!

So when I went to Preservation Hall, they told me, said, "Well, play it straight." That's what Jaffe told me. I said, "What do you mean 'play it straight'?" He said, "They just want you to play a straight beat." I said, "I don't play a straight beat. If feel it, (?) it needs a little rhythm in there." I ain't rushing tempos. I don't want to sell(?) myself, you dig? Because usually, when you want to play (?), you (?) you don't know to do that. Just play straight like you don't know what you're doing. That's what he's telling me. So I'm too advanced for the atmosphere.
Yeah, I understand.
It's too shocking. They want it placid and just play it with a bland face, you know.
Dig that, yeah. I hear what you mean.
Barker - II-13
them things in there -- "Oh, no." So they don't use a lot of musicians(?) there. [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE]
You mentioned Jim Robinson, a trombonist. Who was he?

Jim Robinson was a trombone player who became...supposed to have been the greatest New Orleans trombone player after Kid Ory. Now, he was in that band. He was probably out to ...(?)... that band. But the Australian trombone players, they all got something from Jim Robinson -- which is the same pattern he plays in every chorus. [SINGS TWO BAR REFRAIN] He played the bass trombone.
I see.

So you know, if he was playing something in the first register, that to people is way out. That don't mean nothin' to these people. So when you're playing in the first position, like Jimmy Harrison or Higgenbotham playing up there, using all different (?).
Yeah.
Well, that's not Jazz.
[LAUGHS]

See, you have to listen to what these people will tell you, and they will beat you down and fight you, almost want to shoot you, if you say Jim Robinson ain't the greatest trombone player. And Slow Drag is supposed to have
Barker - II-14
been the top bass player.
Slow Drag.

Slow Drag. (?) Joe. See, you know... Like, I'm from New Orleans, and I will give credit where it's due. You know, a lot of these people what you think... You had levels. Like, when I started playing here, you went with this little jive band. You went to the first grade. Then you went Primer or Kindergarten. Then you jumped up here to this band. Then you went to that first grade, then you went in the second grade, third grade and the fourth grade. When you'd get somebody like Lee Collins, who was playing funky with a band, or David Jones, them people would be playing.
Tell me about Lee Collins.
Well, we'll get to him.
Yeah, okay.

Well, you got all these relatives, see, and they're telling you who is who. Who is on first base and who ain't, who to work with, and who would be beat somebody out of money, and who was the bandleader who is crooked -- and you'd hear all kinds of intrigue of the business. You know, like I'm listening and listening, but I like it, because you're somebody. You sit on a sideline, nobody know you. If you're a longshoreman, or you're a plasterer, you're a (?), whatever. If you play one of them
Barker - II-15

instruments, there come the women, there come the people, and you see the people giving the dances, offering you something -- and you're celebrated. And it's human nature to want to be somebody. So here was a chance for you to get a little exposure and to be somebody and to make a living -- and it's fun. Because I noticed right away, when I wanted to...getting my mind set to be a musician, every day you're going somewhere where people are having fun. Everywhere you go to play, it's people having...
Happy times, yeah.

Yeah. And it's a happy life you're living. Until you start to get stranded when you get out on the road. Even then, your life isn't (?). They want you to get out, don't hang around. So you see these people, and you look at them, and they're talking about you. It's like you see Ted Williams or Jackie Robinson or Ty Cobb, speaking in baseball like a reference...
Sure.
And right away you begin to learn who carries weight, and who can play and who can't play and who is copying. Well, right away, when I looked around, I saw Kimball.
Who is Kimball?
Marvin Kimball, a sensational banjo player.
Barker - II-16
Marvin Kimball.

Yeah. He was a sensation around 19... He was with Papa Celestin. He and Guy Kelly. The first [foist] time I heard [hoid] this band, I was shocked into insensibility when I heard those two. He was playing that banjo. He played "The World Is Waiting For The Sunrise." And he had this Paramount banjo. And he was a showman, and he played this banjo, he twirled it up and down, he played it behind his head. And the people were just looking at him in amazement. He came back... He must have learned that up when he went on the road before, and then he came back.

And there was Guy Kelly playing identically like Armstrong, and almost looking like Armstrong.
Trumpet player. I knew him.

Yeah. And I went out to the Fairgrounds, and they had Guy Kelly come to play. And I had never seen him before, where the hell he had come from. And that was a good sounding band. It was Jeannette Key(?), who was a woman about twenty... No, she wasn't twenty, she was about sixteen. Beautiful young girl, sitting right next to Kimball, and she's smiling at Kimball and playing, and all the time...
Now, Kimball played banjo and she played piano.
Barker - II-17

Yeah, she played piano. And they were sweethearts, and they eventually married. And Papa Celestin, he was there playing his beautiful sweet trumpet, you know, playing with the mute. He wasn't a hot... He played beautiful sweet trumpet. He played like first trumpet. He played beautiful melodies. And a reed section. Now, I had been hearing these Jazz bands with one clarinet. All of a sudden, I hear this full-sounding orchestra. Goddamn, they sounded good. Simon Marrero on bass, man. And they're playing. And that girl playing that correct piano. And Kimball. And Joe Strawder was on drums. He was a great drummer. Immaculate, good-looking, and he played them drummers, and everything was with taste. This was a whole new thing. I thought, 'If I can get to something like that. Look at this band.'

And Guy Kelly had started playing Louis Armstrong's thing. 'Everybody Loves Ma Baby' -- he played that on the trumpet. And he played 'What Did I Do To Be So Black and Blue?' [SINGS REFRAIN] And he was playing, and just like it was so easy... And he had a straw hat, and it was pulled down all around him. And he was an outstanding figure. He played so masterfully. See, these other guys, they played with the trumpet on the side of their lip or they looked like they were searching for something. Not Guy.
Barker - II-18
Everything he played was perfection. Not Louis Armstrong, but this was a man that sounded just like him. The image of Armstrong. Fantastic!
And the people were spellbound at the Fairgrounds. There was about a thousand people just standing around. And when you get a thousand Negroes to stay quiet, you have accomplished something.
[LAUGHS]
Ain't nobody movin', ain't nobody sayin' nothin'. They're just looking. A thousand, just sitting there, just compact(?), quiet out there. Gee whiz, if you want a peace (?), it's Guy Kelly!
He even used a handkerchief, too! Because his face was very bumpy, so he used to wipe his face.
Yeah. He had that, too.

Yeah, he had this big bump that would come up on his face, white bumps when he would blow, and they would break, and he always kept a handkerchief. He was very sensitive to it, because he was a very neat man...
Yeah, yeah.
...and a sharp dresser.
Oh, man. With his (?) shoes.
Shoes. Didn't he have pretty shoes?
Barker - II-19

I know. He was nice... And so he knew me. After I met him, he knew me. And then, when I went to Chicago... Let me see, this was '32. I went there with Bud Harris. We stayed at a hotel of that a man owned that owned the Grand Terrace.
What?
Yeah, we were staying at a hotel on the corner.
The Ritz.
Yes.
The Ritz Hotel.

Yes, we stayed at the Ritz. I've got an aunt there and two or three cousins there. I'm not stranded. I just didn't visit right quick, you know? But I'm with the band. Because the band is stranded. We go there, and they wouldn't let them play the Palace. What was it, the Palace? They wouldn't let us play the Loews State... No, we played the Loews State. So then he was going to come up to the Regal. So they said "No, you've got to use the house band."
What's the name of the band? What band is it?
Bud Harris' band.
Oh, Bud Harris.
Bud Harris was a vaudeville star, a big-time star in vaudeville. He decided to get a band...
Barker - II-20
That was your first trip to Chicago, huh?
No,, that was my second trip. I had been to Chicago in 1921 with my little uncle.
Oh, with Paul?

No, with Willie. My aunt went to visit my aunt, who lived in Chicago. He lived on 40th and State. And my grandmother went to visit, so she was taking Willie, the youngest boy -- so I wanted to go with Willie. My mother said, 'Well, we'll take you.' So they brought me up with him.
So what we used to do, we'd get up in the morning, like, around seven o'clock, after we (?). We'd go around back up on Federal Street, just bumming, you know, like kids...
Sure.

And my uncle had this thing where he could walk in the gutter, you know, in the business section or something, walk around and pick up money. He'd walk in the street and see money, and I'd be right behind him, and I didn't see nothing! Ain't that somethin'?
And we walked to 40...34th and...some street which had a nightclub. It was Jack Johnson's nightclub. And he used to put out (?) gold spittoons.
35th Street, I guess.
Barker - II-21

Probably so. And he put these spittoons out, and the guy would wash them. We'd never seen that. And it had this rug, a ruffled rug from the door, from the sidewalk to the door. There was a whole thing. The guy washed it in the morning, and it was clean and beautiful, then you looked there at the facade where you could see the four(?) doors. And it was a helluva nightclub. And we would stand and see the guy clean the spittoons. We had never seen nobody take all that trouble. Then he'd polish them and (?)... One of them things.
And the first time we'd seen a guy get a manicure.
What street was the Vendome was on?
The Vendome was State Street and 31st. 31st and State, yeah.
Because they had a lot of...a cluster of theatres around there.

Yeah. Well, they had the Grand Theatre across the street. The Grand was over on the west side, and Dave Peyton played over there -- he had the band. Erskine Tate had the band at the Vendome, which was on the east side of the street.
That was the business section.
Yeah. And Indiana was another... You know, down on 31st and Indiana, too.
Barker - II-22

The first time I'd seen a manicure. I seen this cat sittin' in a barber chair, me and my uncle. He was getting a shave and getting a haircut, and had this woman playing with his hands. So me and my uncle, we ...(?)... [LAUGHS] We were lookin' in the window...! And the woman looked at us, the barber looked at us. "What are them niggers doin'...?"
[LAUGHS HEARTILY]

So we looked. There was no (?). So we went back home and told her what happened, this lady was playin' with the man's hand while he was in the barber shop. She said, "She was giving the man a manicure."

First time I seen the word "delicatessen." Some delicatessen. Because we were going to school and learning to read. D-e-l-i-c-a-t-e-s-s-e-n. That's a big word. Delicatessen. And all we seen was bologna and ham and cheese in the window...
Well, from 31st Street, where the Vendome was, you'd come down State Street to 35th Street, and that's where the vaudeville house was. It was called the Monogram. Do you remember that?
We went to the Monogram.
That's where all the...
There were two of them.
Barker - II-23
Right.
There was another one. A little smaller theatre.

Across the street was where they had the movies, and at 35th and Wabash was where Jack Johnson lived, in that apartment building. He used to have that big old Stutz car sitting out in front. We used to come around and stare at it and look at it until he would come out and get in it. An open car.
He was a big man.
Yeah, he was a giant. He was something.
Yeah, yeah, he was something. Yeah, that Chicago was something.

And we'd play all up in Federal Street, and we'd play up in the lots up in there, and had this big pile of corn, about seven feet high. A big dump truck we saw come in the morning and dump this corn. We wondered what it was. It was sour mash that the racketeers were making at the still. Instead of going out on the dump and be exposed to it, they'd just find the first open dump, a lot with high weeds in it, and they saw it was abandoned houses and it was... You know, it was a slum. And they'd back this truck up in there and dump this; that dump truck would dump that corn, and you could smell it all over the neighborhood.
Barker - II-24
You sure could.
Huh?
Sure could. I remember that.

Now, there was another little cabaret we used to go and peep around 7 or 7:30, maybe around 8 o'clock in the morning, on State Street. We'd go there and we would lay on our stomach by the side... You'd go in there and you could look down and see these people in there dancing, still having a good time at 8 o'clock in the morning. I forget the name of it, but...
Was that the Entertainments? It might have been the Entertainments.
Probably could have been. Around 47th...

No, it was not that far. We hadn't got down to 47th Street in those days. It had to be 35th Street, 35th or 37th Street. 37th Street. Because we didn't get down to 47th Street until the Regal days. That's 1927.
Well, in 1921 my aunt lived at 48th Street.
But over on South Parkway, which was Grand Boulevard...
Oh, not over there.
Yeah. Well, we weren't out that way. The cabarets weren't on State Street until... I believe. I don't remember any cabarets out that far. But it could be.
Barker - II-25
It wasn't a great big cabaret. It was like a little dive! A little club, like those places where Ollie Potter(?) played. What did they call that little place?
Like a bookstore.

Yeah, one of them little funky joints. And you'd see them people in there with the women. We'd be up there looking down, layin' on our stomachs. And you had the window, see, right down here near the ground, just enough. And if you'd look down there... And we'd stare down. I guess people must have looked up and seen these two faces up there. I mean, we were on to everything, man.

I used to do that coming back from my newspaper route, and I would see the guys packing up their instruments, and I'd be looking in the windows, and the musicians would be standing around -- and it would be five or six o'clock in the morning, and I'd be out with my newspapers. I did the same thing.
Yeah. All right, now we go... State, Federal, what's the next one?
Well, you had State Street....
There was the railroad tracks over there.
Well, you got State, then you had Dearborn...
Yes.
Then Federal, I believe.
Barker - II-26

Yes. Right there on Federal, that was where all them inter-urban trains come in. I'd never seen that many trains! Every minute a train's pulling out, and one's coming in, one going out, and one... I said what...
That was the New York Central.
One was kind of kind of urban.
The commuter trains, yeah.
The commuter trains coming. Well, that was my first taste of Chicago. Then they took us... My Uncle Paul taken us to the ballgame, the White Sox Park, which was on the South Side.
Still there.

And I went there with him and King Oliver. They all were going to see some helluva game. I didn't know nothin' about no baseball. And we went there, and there were all these people. I'd never seen that many people. And we sat up in the top, and I hear him talking about Harry Hooper. Harry Hooper this, Harry Hooper that. He was a White ballplayer who was supposed to have been a sensation, a great center-fielder. Well, that was the music business, see...
Right on 35th Street there, right by the White Sox Park, past... Well, 39th Street was where the Black ballplayers had theirs, over in that same direction -- 39th
Barker - II-27
Street. The Giants. I can't think of their name.
Rube...Rube...
Yeah, Rube somebody.
Rube Walker?
Yeah.
The Colored Giants.
Yeah.
He was the man. So he was a big man in Black baseball.
Right.
That was a great, great city. Great. Still is, I guess.
[PAUSE]
Well, what's the first band you came up to Chicago to work with? You had worked with Lee Collins down in New Orleans.
That was the first band, Lee Collins.
Oh yeah?
Yeah.
Where did you all get(?) the excursion?

The excursion came up... Like, they used to have an excursion from New Orleans and other parts on the I.C. It was nine hundred miles from New Orleans to Chicago, and they would give you weekend excursions to Chicago at a

cut rate. And people would pack the trains, and go and spend, like, maybe a week up there. You'd get there... Leave on a Sunday and you'd get there Monday, and you'd stay over that week, and come back the following the week. And they used to bring a band most of the times. There would be a reunion of some kind.
Was the excursion on the train or the boat?
On the train.
On the train.

Yeah! On the IC. And we'd meet at Canal Street, and I went... Lee said, "We've got a chance to go to Chicago." I'm working with that band. He said, "We've got a chance to go to Chicago. Professor Cook is promoting it."
Sherman Cook?
Yeah.
Professor Sherman Cook?
Oh, you know him.
Sure. He used to go with my aunt. He was from Vicksburg, really.
Yes...
He would come down... He was a jive cat, wasn't he, from... He was kind of (?).
Yeah, that's right. You know, they tried, but they were limited. See, you were limited. You know,
Barker - II-29
you had to have a bankroll to do things. You'd get bankrupt and you'd get a bad name. Because the weather could knock you out. It was...
Yeah, Professor Sherman Cook!
Yeah. He was a (?). He had all kinds of vests and walking canes, and he'd drink(?) ...(?)...
Right. That's right.
And he couldn't read and write. But he would get back up for more.
Smoke them cigars.
Yes. And say 'Cool it'; you know, he was cool with it. And he was dedicated for more(?) ...(?)... But the man didn't have the education.
He had a con.

It was limited what you could do, because you could send a band out and get stranded. Like, many times you're playing the South, and you'd leave New Orleans and you'd say you're going to play Vicksburg, Hattiesburg, you're going to play Calverton(?), Alabama, you're going to play Pensacola -- you make a little tour. And you're going to play each night or every other night. And man, you get to the town, and nobody comes to the dance because it ain't payday! People ain't got the money. Everybody go out on Saturday. If you don't catch them on a Saturday or Sunday,
Barker - II-30
You're right. It's amazing how a guy like Professor Cook, who didn't play anything, but he had that gift of gab... He kept a lot of musicians working, man, around Chicago...
He did. He did. He did.
He had the gift of gab.

He put on a show. He was a showman. And he was a showman on and off stage. Because when he wasn't on stage, he had something that denoted that was no working man. He had some kind of sharp costume on, and that cigar.
And the gold in his mouth.
He had a gold smile.
Mmm-hmm.
Like... He was (?) loved Barnum. Like, you had to look at it and say... Well, he'd call you. He wasn't a braggart. Just cool. But just this... It's a great man, but he didn't have...
I mean, it was limited what you could do in the South. Limited.

He fascinated me when I was a kid, because he was coming to see my aunt, my mother's younger sister, Aunt Cissy, who we called Alberta. And we didn't have any of this; all we had was church people around there.
Barker - II-31
I'll bet.

And he'd come around with them sharp clothes on, you know, and I was looking at him, and he had all that gold in his mouth, and he looked...you know... And he was talkin' big, you know: "I got a band that's gonna play so-and-so, and I've got some fellas there." And I'm kind of... You know, I'm interested in getting started in music anyway. He fascinated me. Sherman Cook!

[CHUCKLING] Yeah, Sherman Cook. You had them all over the country. They all knew one another. They all had been in vaudeville, and then they tried to promote. So he'd call you when you'd go to Chicago.
And you'd sit up all day. You got on the train at nine o'clock in the morning, the train pulled out, and you got to Chicago the next afternoon.
Who was in that band that Lee Collins had with you, Danny? Do you remember?
Joe Robichaux...
What did he play?

Well, Joe Robichaux played piano. Joe Robichaux. Fats Martin on drums. We had Earl(?) Pernell on clarinet and saxophone. David Jones on tenor. Ernest Kelly on trombone. Ernest Kelly was a great man to play the Dozens. He'd actually talk about your mother in an uncouth
Barker - II-32
way right away. But I put a stop to it.
[LAUGHING] You did.

And that's why Lee kept me. He said, "You straightened Ernest Kelly out." When I joined... They needed a banjo player, so they sent... They knew that I could play a little bit. They was always lookin'... Because a lot of... When you said, "I'm going on the road," a lot of musicians said, "I ain't going. Where are they going? It's going to be a bazah(?)," which mean ain't nothin' gonna happen. "So you're goin' out there? They ain't gonna make enough money. You're wastin' your time. 'Cause it ain't payday out there in them little old towns." So they tried another banjo player.

Now, (?) me, I wanted to...I would go anywhere, whether I get paid or not. This is a trip for me. I ain't gonna sulk and I'm not a big eater. So I could get me a slice of bread and some water, and make it -- and I don't care where it's at. And I wasn't afraid to go anywhere, because I could run like hell, and I figured if I got into trouble, if I could get in the woods, they ain't never gonna catch me. See? So I was never worried about going nowhere.
So... Well, we go to Chicago. Now, when we get there, Lee Collins was... He said, "Well, we're gonna be at... Professor Cook said we're giving a dance at the Warren Hall,
Barker - II-33
so everybody can come meet there."
The Warren Hall was at 47th Street between Vincennes and St. Lawrence.

Yeah. So we played the Warren Hall. And that night the hall is packed and jammed with people. "And they say Louis is gonna come." "They say Louis is gonna come?" Yeah, Louis Armstrong is coming to meet Lee. That's his buddy. Cook said, "Yeah, Louis will be here." Sure enough, man, around ten-something, here comes Louis in the place. We're up on this bandstand. So Louis is there, they're talkin' to him, everybody's screaming, "There's Louis!" Man, Louis is a star, and the (?) wasn't much. And he's so happy to see Lee, and Cook is ...(?)...

So we sat down a while. So he said, "Let's play something!" But nothing happened. They're just going to wait and look at Louis, and talk about it. Then they asked him to play something. He ain't got no horn. So they had this band up, I forget which -- another band was playing. But we had blown them out, so they were just around there. And they had this little trumpeter, a little dark trumpet player, Swift, or Swaft...Swift...
Hughie Swift?
No, another one.
Bob Shoffner.
Barker - II-34
No, not Bob.
It wasn't Bob Shoffner?
No, not Bob. It was another little dark cat, very evil(?). I can't think of his name. So I'm sitting...
Henderson? It wasn't Henderson.
No. He could play. But he wasn't so fond of Louis, because Louis...
He wasn't a hunchback, was he? There was a guy named Mitch who had a hunchback.
You almost said it. Not (?), but a little cat. Looked something like Shad Collins. He had a name around Chicago.
It wasn't Tick Gray? Tick Gray.
Could have been.
Yeah, Tick, he was a little guy...

Well... So they kept begging Louis. So I'm by the bandstand, sitting up by the bandstand, looking at him, observing everything. And I said, 'Give him that horn!' I gave him the horn, and it ended up Louis and the band got on this thing...got around there, and they started playing. So Louis played 'When You're Smiling,' I think. Man, he just tore up the house in pieces, boy. People screaming. Then he played another one. And he was fingering the horn and looking at the horn like it was his
Barker - II-35
horn, you know, with (?) the number he played. So he got through (?) the horn and put it back.

Then we got off intermission. This cat come up on the stand and told me, "Who the hell gave you permission to give Louis Armstrong my horn? I don't let nobody play my horn. Don't never do that no more." He's getting ready to fight me. "Don't never give nobody..." I said, "But that was Louis." "I don't give a goddamn who it was. I don't let nobody put their lips on my horn." So I felt real bad, you know, you know, because I had no business doing that. But who the hell would think a son-of-a-bitch who was this good blowing his horn.
Well, so that's that. Then we come back to New Orleans. And you're laying off, then you begin to know what it is and to imagine(?). So we had about...
What year was that about, Dan? Was that in the Thirties.
Oh, that's 19...what? 19...
About 1930?
About 1930. Right after that, I went to New York.
So where did you play with Dave Nelson? In 1931 was it Dave Nelson you were playing with?
That's when I came to New York.
Barker - II-36
Is he the guy that wrote the "Mule Faced Blues"?
Yes.
That's the guy?
He was a composer. He was a nephew of King Oliver.
He was..
Yes.
I knew him. He was around Chicago for a while, too. I knew him in Chicago.
Yes.
"Mule Faced Blues." He wrote a couple of things. Dark guy.
Yeah. He was a little fat(?)...
He was a trumpet player. He played trumpet, too, didn't he?
Yeah. But he messed up his chops?) playing that soft... You saw that? Soft pressure.
Oh yeah. Non-pressure.
Non-pressure. So he wasn't considered to sit in the band, so he had to do something for himself.
Mmm-hmm.
All right. So I'm playing. This is New Orleans. And there's all kinds of things going on. And you
Barker - II-37
begin to play for White folks. You play house parties. You play lawn parties. You play on the riverboats.

There were millions of house parties. You play the ....(?).... There was a woman in ...(?)., a White woman who used to give parties. And me and Lawrence Tocca(?), we played a series of parties for her.
What was the name?
Well, I don't know this White woman's name.
But you said Lawrence Tocca(?). Who was Lawrence Tocca(?).

Lawrence Tocca(?) was a trumpet player. This was one of the first little(?) bands. We had about six numbers we would do, and we'd play them repeat... The people didn't know. A lot of them was drunks, and it was Blacks, so they... As long as you had a Black Jazz band, you was doing something. "Them Colored boys," or whatever, they could play. So if you knew six tunes, it was all right.

So we played the parties, and that's when I began to see how people are like, you know. They had all these fast... They weren't out-and-out whores, but they were fast women, good-time women. Or maybe they weren't. And they had all these guys from the riverfront with the money, acting like... I saw them like gutbucket White folks. And they was drinkin' hard and talkin' loud, signifying. We
Barker - II-38

played them kind of tough(?). Then from Lawrence Tocca(?)... He played so badly, they heard him and they said, 'Well, you are...' After the Boozaire Kings, I got the reputation(?) with this banjo, so I'm looking to play with little bands. So there's little groups all around, playing and rehearsing. You could hear rehearsals all around town, in my neighborhood, the Seventh Ward. And you'd get to know who's playing and who is improving. And you'd go to rehearsals. When you'd go to rehearsal, you'd get in the (?), or it's in the yard if it's early. They had nobody telling you not to play no music, nobody's complaining about the music is loud -- none of that. I mean, you never got that. Only way, if it's late in the morning, the police come around and tell you you're making too much racket. Because this is a good-time town, and they don't have a curfew here. So if the neighbors are having a party and they're raising hell, you know, loud... You know what whiskey and music will do.
Sure.
It's hilarious, and in the hilarity people are hyped up.
Well, when you played with Albert Nicholas, was it just in New Orleans?
No, I never played with him in New Orleans.
Barker - II-39
Oh, where did you play with Albert?
In New York.
Oh, that's when you came to New York.
No, the first time I went to New York.
Oh yeah, that's when you worked with him.
The first time. So to get back to....
Yeah, excuse me.

At the rehearsal... Because when you have a party at your house, your neighbors generally don't care. They might knock on the wall if gets too loud. But if they get to cursing and starting to fight, then whiskey will bring on... You've always got somebody who wants to come to somebody's house and start some shit, you know. Because the next night, they might want to have a party. That's the way it is in New Orleans. So you let them people ball, because next week you might have a party, and you don't want nobody coming. Because that's a part of our scene. And it's no curfew. I doubt if they ever had a curfew, even during the wartimes. Most times you go in Chicago, the town would close up. The clubs close when?
In Chicago now?
Yeah.
One o'clock.
Barker - II-40

One o'clock. In New York it's four o'clock. All those gin-mills are ...(?)... But in New Orleans, as long as somebody is spending money and popping their fingers, you can have entertainment until daybreak.
That's beautiful.
So you know, this is an active scene.
The scene continued here, too.
Mmm-hmm.
I didn't want to say it... We're sitting here, and you hear on that tape that noise, [WHAP]... The steamrollers are still building. That's pile-driving.
Yeah, that's a pile-driver.
Because his is soft land here...
Yes.
And they have to dig pile...
Wooden piles, mmm-hmm.
Wood is like logs...
No, that's pine.
Pine.

Pine. It's full of pine, raw pine, and the water don't corrode pine. It just (?)ticks up(?) the wood around it, but that pine stays. So they put pine sticks in there. "Long and tall as a Georgia pine."
Yes.
Barker - II-41
Well, that might be a 50-feet, 75-feet...
Log.
...pole. They got special trucks, long trucks that they put them on sometimes...
[END OF TAPE 2, SIDE A]

...these poles. And they stay there. They've got big wires on them, and they can resist the wind, they don't break or bend. The stone railings you see is them trees split in the middle. They split a tree, but the railing just be...they bust one of them pines.
So when you hear that pile, that's driving it into the ground.

That's driving it for the foundation, so you can hook the cement and the concrete and the pig iron and the steel onto those beams, so it will sway. See, in a time of the wind, that pine will give a little bit with the earth. The whole complete structure.
That's amazing.
Them engineers know what they're doing.
This hotel is built ...(?)..., this Hyatt House is looking right over the Super-Dome.
Yes.
Barker - II-42
Because you told me about this. You told me this used to be all old warehouses down here.
This was warehouses and floats. See that float? That's what you see, a float there. Them two-wheelers that have two mules?
The picture on the hotel wall, yeah.

The picture on the hotel wall, there's two mules. See, that's about maybe, say, 16 to 18 feet long, that they ....(?)...., and they used to roll in with the cotton. They rode in with big casks of molasses...
They'd ship it to Natchez.
Yeah, to the riverfront. They'd have these mules, and they'd have these Negroes with these mules, and that was a big business before the big transport trucks came in and took over that.

And there was so much for you to see in this town. You saw a big ocean liner, you'd see all these Oriental people coming in here on those ships. And we began to play in the nightclubs and the little honky-tonks on Decatur Street. When I was 16 and 17, I didn't use(?) any (?)s. We had ...(?)... out in the District with a Spasm band, and we used to... I used to take the kids out, and became a little promoter myself. I found out if you want something done, you have to do it yourself. I learned that early. And I had
Barker - II-43
this little Spasm band, about six of us, we'd play...
So you call it a Spasm band.
That's what they called it. You know, those makeshift bands?
Yeah.

Cats take a box and put some tin pans on it, and there are big jar covers like cymbals, three or four of them together. They're noisemakers! And we had a cowbell on that. And one of them had a washboard. They'd have a kazoo. We'd have a ukelele or a guitar. And you'd go in and sing the songs! We sang the (?) to "Chinaman and Mabel." Did I do that for you?
Yeah, you did that. You sang it, but you couldn't remember all the words to it.

Yeah,, this is somethin'. You got all these railroads here. You got to see these big engines on those railroads. See people going away when you're by the railroad station. You'd long to go away yourself. "Some day I'll get a chance to go away. Maybe I'll get a chance to get on that ship and go somewhere." You're young and you've got this wanderlust. You want to go somewhere. You want to see things.
They got these trains... The L&M Railroad was about four blocks from my house. I'd see this fast train leave
Barker - II-44

out in the morning, come back in. Jeff...what do you call it, Jeff Holloway. Do you remember that? The L&M Indian out there? And you'd go up to the IC, and you'd see the station, people...people well-dressed... You'd see people happy and well-dressed, not people sad, going to some towns in Georgia and Mississippi, the little small towns. And you'd see everybody relaxed, you know.

The late Arthur Stanley called New Orleans the Metropolitan City. And I got to understand what that means. It's not all White and Black Baptists, like you would go into Beaufort, Georgia or something, or you were going to Calverton(?), Alabama, or somewhere in Mississippi, where all the people... And there's two people -- White and Black. Because you have to always observe that when you're playing music, who you're playing for and what kind of music to play for them, and how to please and satisfy these people.

But in New Orleans, you look around, and there are some French people -- they're talking (?). There are some German people, they talk to you. You see restaurants. And you see people with class, you see people well dressed. You go to Canal Street and you see women getting out of their limousines and getting out of the carriages with the horse early -- and they're well-dressed. You see people that's got something. You look at the clothes and you see success,
Barker - II-45

and you're watching that. You've got something to emulate. That's why youngsters sort of get in trouble. They never learn that you have to wait your turn. Your turn will come in life when you can do this thing. Don't try to force them to try to take something from somebody and try to force your way. All you're going to do is get in trouble. See, we learnt [loynt] that, don't take nothin' that don't belong to you. Your day is coming. All the folks would tell you. They'd say, "Well, this ain't your time yet. You wait, and when you get old enough, you can buy the same things them people have." And you listened to that, because you'd know you was in trouble. If something happened in a town, like one of the kids would get in trouble, or a girl or a boy was shoplifting, would take something or stole something, and the police...

They would tell you that as an example. "You see? You keep out of trouble. Don't be touchin' nothin' that don't belong to you, because you're going to end up in jail. Because you ain't smarter than them people. They got ways of trickin' you and catchin' you. So you just go on and do without. It ain't no sin to be poor. How many other poor people you see? So you're with the rest of them. So you just wait til your time. When you want something, you wait til you get the money to buy it. Don't be go touchin'

nothin' or takin' nothing. People don't respect no burglar." A burglar is worse than a murderer. They'd tell you that. People will talk to a murderer, but a burglar they don't want nothin' to do with. "Don't be takin' nothin', bringin' nothin' into this house that don't belong to you."

And they'd keep preaching that in your ear, so you should know that. You learned that. You learned that your day is coming. And it took me a long time to finally arrive to the point where I could relax and buy what I want. I went through a whole gang of years, sixty-some years -- I'm 71. And it's up til I got to 60 when I could stop and go to a store and see what I want and buy what I want. Many times, raising a family and trying to provide in New York City, I would look in a window and I'd see things, and I couldn't afford it. I didn't cry. I didn't grieve. I'd say there's a day coming when I would be able to do these things. I wanted another instrument, but I couldn't afford it -- I played with what I had.
So when you learn that you're (?)ing with yourself, and you ain't got to worry about nothin'. You can sleep. If you're going to grieve and worry what somebody else has got, you're in trouble.
That's very true, Danny.
Barker - II-47

So, like right now, I... My wife said, "You bought that (?) and you ain't wearing 'em. I said, "I wore it and I bought it and I'm going into the closet to look at it." I'll look at it, that's what I want, and I can go and buy it. I bought a hat last week for forty dollars, fifty dollars -- $49-something. It's a bad cut, the finest grain straw you can get. It's a beautiful hat. I saw it and I bought it at Weinstein. You don't go into Weinstein unless you got some money in your pocket. And I bought that hat. And if I wait until September, I can get the hat maybe for thirty dollars. But I wanted it then. Because I've got this fifty-dollar hat. And I know what you're doing... I went down to Weinstein's(?) and went and got the hat. The box is even different. It's an elongated box, and it's a... You'll seen the hat.
I've got to see that hat, Danny.
Yeah. Maybe you'll get you one when you're here.
I'm telling you.
And she... She showed it to the neighbors. And the grain of the hat is knitted so fine that it's remarkable, and you can see its class...
Is that like a Palm Beach? What we used to call a Palm Beach?
Barker - II-48

Yeah, but it's finer than a Palm Beach. It's a Bangkok. My Dad had one. A Palm Beach is just white, white straw like. But this is a silk straw, like shiny. Very small! Very-very-very-very small. I gave (?) a Panama. So... Well, you get what you want.

So when you're playing music, you wait your time. You know, you say, well, you bide your time. Because here in New Orleans they had bands, and it was impossible for you to get in one of them bands. It was a family band. Piron's band, I mentioned that before -- it was impossible for you to get in that band. And you want to advance when you're playing music.

So they had Fate's band. Everybody looked at Fate Marable with awe, because he played that calliope on that boat, and he had a helluva band. That's the band that Louis Armstrong got his finishing touches [tetches], under the tutelage of David Jones. David Jones was a great reading musician. He helped Louis with his parts. He spent hours with Louis.
What did he play? Trumpet, too?
Saxophone. He played [C-melody] saxophone, trumpet, cornet. He played mellophone. He was a great mellophone player.
David Jones, huh?
Barker - II-49

David Jones, yeah. A fantastic musician. He's the man that when he went to New York with the Missourians... He went to St. Louis, he joined R.Q. Dixon and them in Missouri, and he went to New York. And he was a terrific tenor saxophone player. He played legato. See, Hawk and them people in New York was playing staccato and slap tonguing. That would have been ...(?)... And they heard David Jones, and they all come to play legato.
Yeah. Flowing style.
Flowing style.
Yeah. That's wild. That's interesting.
Lee told me. He said, 'You see, when David Jones was in New York, he changed all them saxophone players.'
So Lee Collins told you that, huh?

Yeah. See, he knows. He said they was slap-tonguing, [DOP-DAP-DOP-DAP-DOP-DAP-DOPPA/DOP-DAP] After David Jones was up there, he had them playing 'High Society' or something, and flowing with all those notes, leading (?) into one (?). Everybody changed their style, and went to C... So he mentioned that. Now, you say that and they all look like... They say they're always taking credit for something. I ain't takin' credit for nothin'. I'm just telling it what it was.
Barker - II-50

What's the way it was. I just want to say we're sitting here with your friend and your bass player, Smitty. He's sitting here with us. He's from New Orleans, too, so he understands this whole thing... [ETC.] So what did you tell us about David Jones?

So David Jones was a fantastic musician. David Jones was a showman. He played mellophone also. Everybody respected David Jones. And he played this mellophone, so all trumpet players looked at him with respect, and all saxophone players, none of them had the nerve to even challenge him, not at that time, in 1930. But he never claimed nothin' or never thought about nothin'. He was more of a teacher. Everybody in this town, you'd say David Jones... David Jones was like, when I was in New York, Benny Carter.
Oh yeah?
Everybody respected Benny Carter -- trumpet players and saxophone players and arrangers. The same thing was here with David Jones. They'd say, 'Well, that's David Jones and...' So don't...
[POURING] Have a little coffee there, Danny, while you're talking. You don't have to stop a thing. Here, Smitty.
Barker - II-51
Thank you. In New Orleans a man have to have his little coffee every now and then.
Yeah. At one time he would have had whiskey.
Yup!

Or we would have had a bottle. But when you get up to a certain age, you have to watch your diet. That diet business, huh? If they had had a diet in the early Thirties, King Oliver and all of them people probably would have been living. But they didn't have the proper diet.
That's right. Well, we kept working nights on that whiskey, Danny, for a long time.
I'm telling you. That whiskey lots of times kept you going, too.
It sure did. Sure did.
Because you didn't give a damn. You'd say, 'Okay, well, this is rough, but we're going to make this.'
Yeah. We had enough youth and strength in our body to accept that shock ...(?)... Ah, I'll take me a little taste of the grape every now and then.
Yeah, you can?

I don't want to leave it completely. I'm trying to think about the times that you and I would sit up with a few good whiskeys, and it would last us about an hour. And in ...(?)... before we'd go to the theatre, you'd
Barker - II-52
sit there drinking, and you'd have to have another one to take to the hotel that night.
Boy, if we would have been thinking, the way things have changed, we could have documented damn near every musician in this country.
That's right.
We just wouldn't have thought about it. I got the first idea when that cat (?) took Big-Eye Louis' picture. He was the ...(?). giving hell. Who was the cat who used to write for Esquire? Miller?
Miller, yeah. Oh, that was Miller. Paul...
I accused the wrong man!

It's a great experience to sit with a man like Danny Barker.
Yeah, yeah.
Isn't it (?), Smitty.
He can think about the past.
He's so logical.
He can think so much.

Well, he's so...not so narrative, but he knows it all. And I'm just glad to have been in Cab Calloway's band for five or six years with him, and I saw this happen. He's telling me, "I saw him write these," "I saw him sit
Barker - II-53
there," and play songs....
You were with him for five years in the band, huh?
Yeah, I'm sure. Danny, how long were you in Cab's band?
Eight years.
Eight years!
How about that.
Eight years.
How about that. That's...
So the band was real popular then.

'39 to '47. Oh, it was a great band. Really a great band. The band was greater than we ever got credit for, because Cab was a superstar, and people more or less came to hear Cab. But the musicians were conscientious enough to want to take care of it themselves, you know, to be good musicians and make the arrangements and everything.
Cab is still around, too, isn't he.
Yes, he's in very good shape. [THEN OFFERS SOME MORE REFRESHMENTS]...
You want to tell them about the fish bar, Danny? Your experiences in them fish bars? (?) those piano players?
Barker - II-54
We didn't have too many piano players playing fish bars, Smitty.
Yeah, they did.
In my time, of course, the piano players had all the gigs. Even in a lot of the speakeasies they had a lot of the gigs. Just piano players alone. And they'd open ...(?)... what they called suppers.
Oh, yeah. Well, when they got to Chicago, there was house rent parties and things.
Same thing, they just called it different, you know. People supplement the rent. If they have a little trouble or the money is short, they'd give a party and invite all their friends.

The most personable ones became landladies. And they had enough charisma to attract attention, and they were very popular -- served some good booze and kept some nice ladies around in their apartments. Somebody could come by...
It was (?). No humbug, but...

Yeah. My favorite was Jabbo Smith then in Chicago. When Louis left, he took his band. I was trying to play at 1:30 or 2, and Jabbo came in. And we would take out tips that we had made from the night, call up some lady that had a nice apartment or flat, and when we got off we'd
Barker - II-55
all go up there, and she'd have the chicken and whiskey, and we'd sit right up there all evening, you know, until daylight, havin' us a ball.
I went to Europe with Jabbo.
Did you?

Mmm-hmm. And Ron Elliott(?)...See, Jabbo didn't know me. So I went on to tell him, give him some courage, because he was kind of down, see. [CHEWING, INAUDIBLE SENTENCE] And I went on to tell them how important Jabbo was and what a great trumpet player he was, and he was a rival of Louis. Because at this (?) his lip was done, and he stayed off to himself, which he ....(?). But this guy can play, man. When his lip got up, that band went to Europe, he was something else. But Ron Elliott(?) looked at him like Jabbo, Jabbo wasn't... But none of them could understand....
He was fabulous, Danny.
...how fantastic that man was.
He was fantastic. When I played with him back in the Thirties, I had never heard anything like that. It was like listening to Charlie Shavers and somebody who had that...
He had a thing of his own, and a rivalry with Louis. He had nerve enough to challenge Louis.
Barker - II-56
Yeah.
How about that.
I don't know about the ballad. But this man was fantastic.
He was really fantastic.

And In New York... He cut everybody in New York. Everybody who thought they could play a trumpet ain't messin'... Him and Jimmy Harrison, they were the two, trombone and trumpet... They were in Charlie Johnson's band, and they're speaking(?) to him, and then Sidney DeParis, and them three... Fletcher Henderson's band didn't have nothin' on Charlie Johnson's band. But Charlie Johnson was working at Small's Paradise, and the difference was that Fletcher was down at the Roseland Ballroom. But them people was out of sight. Jimmy Harrison started all that first position trombone playing.
Yeah, I heard about it. I missed him. I didn't get to hear him. What about Big Green, too? Because I hear so much about him. Did you hear him?
Yes. Great trombone player. Pretty trombone player. There was about ten trombone players. Little Shorty, Little Stump...
Stump, yeah. I remember Stump.
Not the saxophone player. [STUMP EVANS]
Barker - II-57
No, the trombone player.
He was with Andy Kirk, and he ended up being a messenger around...
Working for Manny's yes. The cat ...(?)...
He was cheeky. The little son-of-a-bitch could play.
I heard Keg Johnson always talk about how good he was.
Exactly.
Yeah, if Keg said it, it had to be so!
Yeah. Well, all of them was in the Brickwood(?).
The hotel?

No. That was where I saw Jabbo. All these people was in a gin mill on Seventh Avenue down in a basement, and I'm in there. And Big Green is in there, and he's drunk, and he'd lost his weight, and he said ain't nobody would hire him after Fletcher, and Chick Webb hired him for a while but he couldn't depend on him...
Big Green the trombone player, yeah..

Yes. And he was this big, tall cat, almost seven feet. But he had once but robust, but his clothes is hangin' on him; you could almost lop his pants from him. And he was foolin' with that smoke, that shit that they used
Barker - II-58

to drink. Nasty alcohol. Cheap. 25 cents for a little jar they had made like a little cow, and you'd get one of them. I drank some of that, spat it on a wall and messed the paint up. That's how bad this shit was. So all them trombone players was playin', Big Green was sittin' at the bar and listening. And then when Budd... And they were swingin' down there, man! Trombones burnin'. Higgenbotham and all of them.
So they asked Green to play. They said, "Man, play something, man." The bartender said, "Man, why don't you play something?" He had a funny eye...
He had a funny eye, didn't he.
One of his eyes looking this way. So they give him a trombone, and that big, tall son-of-a-bitch got up with his trombone and said, "What you gonna play?" "Play a waltz." [SINGS REFRAIN]...
"My Buddy."

Yeah. A waltz... They was playing that waltz, and the cat was improvising on it... [SINGS REFRAIN] He played that (?). When they got through, them sumbitches give him a standing ovation. Sure. Well, who all was on that? Who was in there that morning?

Yeah...

No, Herb Flemming was in Europe. He hadn't come back. He came back later. This is around 1932. Sandy Williams.
Oh yeah. Trombone...

"I've got something new, something that nobody has ever heard before." And it would be "Margie" in another key. Well, that was the challenge like of New York. You
Barker - II-60
can go in there for hours about that, who was on first and who was on second...
Yeah, who was at the plate.
Because there was a man who was a helluva saxophone player, and he never got a chance. That was Fields(?). Fields(?) was a virtuoso. He played like this cat, Rudy Wiedoft.

Fields(?).

Leonard Fields. He come out of Ohio. I think he came with a helluva band out of Ohio. This band came to New York and went to the Savoy and broke up. And Leonard Fields(?) had one of them...a little bit of a small moustache...
Like Sammy Stewart used to wear?

Yeah. One of them kind. A wax moustache. He was sharp, and a helluva musician, but somehow Fletcher and all of them big bands never hired him. And I had a chance to play with him, and heard him play, and he was a virtuoso on that saxophone. He could play all of Rudy Wiedoft's solos, "Soliloquy" and all these kind of things. There was a whole thing, a bag of classic saxophone. And he would play them things, and the people had to look at him,
Barker - II-61

the way he played so beautiful, man. They never heard that kind of music in a saxophone. You know, you hear Johnny Hodges, you hear Benny Carter, you hear Earl Bostic, you hear Tab Smith, and you hear just about everybody. But you've never heard nothing in the classical veins like Leonard Fields.
There was a good saxophone player around New York that I happened to play with years ago named Jerome Pasquall. Did you ever hear him?
Yeah.
He was good.
Jerome Pasquall was one of the masters. He had been with Fletcher, he had been with King Oliver, he had been with that big...that great...Cooke's band... Charlie Cooke.
Charlie Cooke, that's right.
That famous band he had at that White...
White City.
White City. I got a picture of that.
White City. Is that so?

63rd Street in Chicago.

Oh, Garland on t the West Coast. Ninety-year-old Eddie Garland, worked with that band...
Ed Garland.
He just died.
Yeah, he died.
Did he?
Yeah, he did.
Oh, I'm sorry to hear that.
He was on the West Coast. He was with Kid Ory's band. That's that group of New Orleans cats who went
Barker - II-63
to...
That's the one I saw in Nice. Yeah, I saw him in Nice. Gee, I'm sorry to hear that.

Those are the ones that migrated to Chicago, migrated from New Orleans around 1915, '16 and '17, and migrated from Chicago to Frisco and Oakland and San Diego. Jelly Roll and all of them went out there, when Watts was... They speak of Watts as a cowboy place, a country...you know, Western town.
That almost makes me the oldest one now standing. After you get past Garland and Pops Foster. I guess you ...(?)... and your day will come. There it is. You have to look at Bill Johnson...
Mmm-hmm.
When the (?), you never know. But go tell me about that, Danny.
What's that?

who were known, like...
Boy, he was really... He was in this band with Jabbo Smith, that they tried to come in after Louis Armstrong left, to make a tour in Chicago, and Cassino Simpson took over the band.

Yes.
Yeah. What a fantastic musician he was.
A fabulous musician.

Way ahead of his time. I just want to tell you about that band, then we can go on with this.
Yes.

...and he was up in Milwaukee. So they sent for Jabbo to come in from Milwaukee to take the job, and

they organized a band in Chicago. So they had Cassino Simpson...

Yeah, an all-star band. Cassino Simpson on piano... Almost, because I was in it, and I sure was no star!
Well...

Mmm-hmm.

A lot of personality. Very dark, good-looking man.
Yeah.
A very good looking man. He was something else. Well-dressed, always smiling, he had... [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE]

He had a nice voice, too. So Floyd Campbell on drums. Othello Tinsley, Paducah Tinsley from Paducah, Kentucky, who was on banjo. And I was on bass. And I tell you, that was (?)some band(?). And Cassino Simpson was

making arrangements.
And this is where I really heard Jabbo, man. He came in there, and man, I tell you, he took that place... Gangsters owned the place. He was so sharp, it hurt, man. He wore them black ascot ties, and all of the ladies in town were after him, and he loved it.

And I remember, he had to be living... Now, we were Downtown, at State and Lake Street, over there some place, and he was the South Side, down on 46th Street or 47th Street. So the next season, they just gave up on him and hired Cassino Simpson to be the leader, and then Jabbo went on some place else, and we stayed there with Cassino, and we finally played the Regal and got to make some pictures, and
Barker - II-67
then a (?) have some pictures made, and then made some appearances.

And Cassino was a nut. Everything he wrote, every tune he wrote had something about food. Pig feet and pig ears, mustard greens and pig knuckles... Every tune of his, black-eyed peas, red beans and rice... Every song we had, everything we had in the book was about that.
[CHUCKLES]

Well, I just wanted to bring that in. Then I want to go back to New York, where you are. Because I want to ask you about a friend of yours, a guy I used to see who was a very neat man, named Steele(?).
Louis Steele(?)?
Yeah.
Steele(?) was a drummer... He'd been a waiter until he finally started playing drums. And he was from Florida, and he had migrated to New York as a kid. He was...
A very neat man.

Yeah. Well, he was sharp. And he was into things. He wanted to be into things. He had a very quick temper. And he wanted to play drums, and he played drums; you know, New York swing drumming, they called it, in which you throw your whole body into motion when you play with
Barker - II-68
brushes.
Yeah. [LAUGHS HEARTILY]
And if you were setting a tempo, you had to... Because once he gets that little sassy swish he did on his seat, you had to say somewhat with him.
Aha.
You understand?
I got you.
Or whatever he did, he did it in the whole body. You'd almost throw your whole body into it.
I would give about a dollar for a videotape of this with you.
He and I became friends because he was a friend of... See, Paul had a way of getting to people -- my uncle.
Paul Barbarin.
Yeah. 'How you doin', buddy? How's everything?' A smile for everybody.
Yeah. He was a nice man.
And he'd move in on you, and said 'Hello,' and he would help you. He was good. He was good people. He went to... Nearly everybody in New York knows PB, Old Paul...
That's right.
Barker - II-69

Steele(?) had him called Big Brother. Even the racketeers, like Bob Ewing and them...Blue and all of them, he said, "Hey, big brother." He'd call him and give himself protection gettin' in with them hoodlums. That's my big brother. "How you doin, big brother?" "Talkin' to Blue." Blue was one of the baddest hoodlums that ever lived. He'd say, "Hey, Blue, Mister Blue, how you doin', Blue." He'd get with everybody. Everybody. "Hello, Brother, Cousin, Bub." He'd give you a name so he would remember." Where did this man come from? Is this man(?) that I call (?) brother gonna accept me? Is he as well-dressed as me? You know, it's a psychological thing...

So everywhere Paul went... So they called me "Little Peewee" or "Little Barbarin." Most of the musicians when I first went there called "Little Barbarin." So I meet Steele(?). Paul would say, "Steele(?), look out for him, because he's just come from down there. He don't know much. He thinks he knows, you know." Steele(?) said, "I'll pull his coat." So Steele(?) would tell me everything...always... I've never forgotten. He always kept explaining me things until I left New York.
That's far out.
He'd see people, and he'd see... He'd tell me who they was. How much weight they carried. Who was what.
Barker - II-70

Who was who. He was working in Barron Wilkins' joint as a waiter when Charleston killed Barron Wilkins. Barron Wilkins had the big nightclub where Ethel Waters and them went, on 135th Street. And his brother had Wilkins' on the other side of the street, that was one of the greatest nightclubs in New York -- but he didn't allow no White folks in this club. The White folks would go up to Barron Wilkins' club and say, "Let's go... Why can't we go to the other place where they're swingin' over there?" He'd say, "No, my brother don't have no White folks comin' in." No, you come to the door and ask permission, want to pay money to come in. He said, "No, I can't go to your club; don't you set foot in mine."
Mmm-hmm.

That's the Wilkins that you hear some (?) people talk about of that particular time. Well, Steele(?) worked there, and he tells me that. So he was in the... what's it's name seat... The Hot Seat? No, not the Hot Seat. I'll get the name of the club. He was in a club when Jack "Legs" Diamond killed another gangster. He was on the stand. And the last thing they saw when the guy was going out, they saw Steele(?) lookin' at 'em. When they shot the gangster and they were going out, the gangsters looked around and they saw Steele(?) lookin' at 'em. So they
Barker - II-71

watched the papers. And Steele(?) said he went in... So they closed the pub down and left these drums in there. The police made him get out after the killing, see. So he goes home. Kid Kemp?

No. One of them kind of names. So he'd tell me all...you know, who was (?). And he'd see old performers, old musicians. He'd say "Do you see that woman? That woman..." I'm trying to think of this woman's name. He said, "That woman performed for the Tsar of Russia." She was a little dark woman. She was what you call... She did a whole lot of tumbling.
A juggler?
Some kind of... I can't think of that name. But he'd tell me... And he'd tell me who was who. And he'd
Barker - II-72

say "Lovie Joe. That's the great Lovie Joe." Lovie Joe was the star of the song that got(?) "Stop It, Joe." It's an old risqué tune that all the performers used to do. And Lovie Joe was supposed to have been an old-time Mack Man, an old-time pimp. Now, this is an old man, dark, with real keen features, and he looked like he's got blue eyes. Strange looking. And he's always on 135th Street, going into one bar, into another one, always dressed immaculate. He was about as big as me, slim, and... He said, "That's Lovie Joe." "What about him? What about him?" He said, "That's Lovie Joe." He said, "Now, they got Lovie Joe and they got Rat Lovie Joe." That's the way he talked. He said, "I'm gonna show you Rat Lovie Joe." So later on he showed me another cat, said...later on... He said, "That's Lovie Joe." He said, "He's been in and out of jail. But this man's has been classed(?). He's just livin' on his old reputation now."
That's the kind of cat Steele(?) was. He knew everybody, he'd get gigs, and call me on a gig, and we'd always meet and...
He was always... I always remember him because of you, and I was always around wherever I could find you, and he would be there, and he sort of accepted me and treated me very nicely.
Barker - II-73

Yeah, he respected musicians. He would respect everybody. I used to bug... I bugged him once. I said... He was crazy about Hawk. "Who was the greatest?" And he'd talk about the greatness... He was his idol. He worshipped...idol...idolized...
Idolized people.

And they'd say, "Hawk is in Europe." I said, "I heard Hawk is in town." He went around to the Rhythm Club, because he didn't think I'd lie, man, tellin' everybody he'd heard Hawk's in town. He didn't say who it was. But Hawk wasn't in town. That's how he was. He was an idol of the musicians. And he was nice.
He was really a nice cat, man. I really...
He's around there now. I went to New York twice and saw him a little bit.
Is still alive?

Mmm-hmm.
Do you know Don Kirkpatrick? The piano player that worked with Don Redman and Chick Webb? A tall old guy...
No, I can't place him.

Unassuming. He was a hell of a musician and a hell of an arranger.
No, I can't place him.
Well, he was fantastic. He died. You remember Lloyd Phillips?
Oh yeah. Lloyd was a very good piano player.

Well, them two was together. They'd stand on the corner, man, until daybreak every morning when they was working, and talk about arranging. They this old... What's this old, quiet man who used to teach everybody arranging? He looked like a little White man. He'd come to your house and he'd teach. What's that new arranger they had?
Sheridan(?)?

Yeah. This little old colored man. Everybody in Harlem went to him. He was supposed to be the mostly highly rated mathematician of music, the calculation of what resolved into this and what resolved into that, how you can resolve this -- and they'd sit up there and talk with him until the morning.

Well, when you get back there, check about this guy in Harlem who used to teach. Like that boy Gene and them probably could tell you.
