Lloyd was a fabulous piano player.

Well, I worked with Lloyd in the Nest Club, see, with Big Dave Nelson's band. And I went to his wife's funeral, which was a sad thing. I was the only... Me and her brother was the only two people at the funeral.
Whose funeral was this, now?

Lloyd Phillips' first wife. She died with TB. And we were working together. He said, 'I've got to go to the hospital. My wife ain't gonna make it.' That's what he told me. So then I went to her funeral. It was me, him and her brother. We went out to Woodlawn Cemetery, the first time I saw that, when you go to the grave and they put the body in the ground. It was snowing and there was ice on the ground. Cold, cold out. Since I'd come to New York... I'd been in New York, what, about three or four months. And in the Woodlawn Cemetery. Because I remember... In passing where they buried her, I saw Bert Williams' tomb.
Barker - II-76
The great comedian? Yeah, sure.
It was up there. It was fantastic.
The Woodlawn Cemetery, huh.

Yes. And they buried and left... They left the body on this thing, this sort of platform that they wheeled out. And they left the body. And I thought to myself, 'Is any undertaker going to take that casket?' -- you know, your superstitious thing. They should put it in the ground and dirty the casket and cover it up. A lot of people believe that if you leave that casket out there, later on that night, around midnight, they come and look in the (?) box ...(?)...(?)...

So Lloyd Phillips, and... He's the one that told me about Mozart. I said, 'I don't know nothin' about no Mozart.' He said, 'This is a movement from Mozart, Danny.' He played them big, beautiful chords. He said, 'This is a resolution of Mozart.' And I'd give him attention, if he wanted to talk. I'd meet him up in the Clubhouse(?), a (?) until around two o'clock in the morning. And he would play this, and he said, 'Now, this is Liszt. Liszt has this dynamics.' And I'd listen. I'd listen to Liszt. Brahms, [SINGS CHORDS], kinda... And he analyzed Brahms, Mozart, and quite a few of them big Classical composers. And that's

what he was interested in.
Him and Don Kirkpatrick used to talk about that.
Because Don Kirkpatrick worked with Don Redman's band, and

Don Redman?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah. That whole-tone scale, yeah.
Well, ain't nobody had heard that.
He had the ...(? )...

Beautiful. That was a new sound. Then the
next time I heard a new sound was Clarence Profit. Clarence

and [SINGS REFRAIN]...
"Lullaby In Rhythm."
Yeah. [CONTINUES REFRAIN]
Clarence who?

Clarence Profit. You want to get his
records. There's a classic... Him and Jimmy Sherman.

Mmm-hmm.

Clarence Profit was doing that basically on the piano. You see, all that stuff was in the air, you know. It was just (?)a question(?) of the time of who would get that bug to do it... Charlie had it out West, Dizzy had it here, and it's something that they come together and they fell right in.

Yeah, the Jungle. All of them come out that Jungle, see. Partly West Indian and partly Carolinas.

I'm not being different. Because I'd heard Clarence Profit makin' them progressions. Because Edgar Sampson had taken "Stompin' at The Savoy" from Clarence Profit. But Clarence Profit was a little cat, didn't say nothin'.

Yeah, that was Clarence Profit's idea, that composition. Mark that down. When you see Jimmy Sherman, ask him where can you get Clarence Profit's records. He must have made about a couple of dozen records. Fantastic piano player.
I sure will.
See, he's the one that...

Ask Thelonious Monk about it. Thelonious Monk tried to play like him. See, because Thelonious Monk is tricky.
Barker - II-80

See, when you sit next to piano players and you get to analyzing who is great and who ain't, Thelonious Monk is counting like crazy, but he's trying to throw you, because his purpose was to get popular with the new things that was supposed to have been unorthodox. So of course, in the turnaround, where you make the turnaround, he's gonna play all through the turnaround. And when you get in the middle where you want to get the guts of the tune, it's open. That's where he starts counting. So you get in the meditation, and he's gonna trick you; have the whole world in a trick bag who's listening. And that's the basic of his style of playing, is to hit when you don't expect it -- to catch you off-guard. To trick you. Like, if you're gonna play with him... He runs a bass player crazy when you first go with him.
Right.

Because you've got to keep playing, and he comes up with some things... You think you've reached the turnaround, but he's playing that, then when you're supposed to relax, he breaks all the rules that ever was broken on top of piano playing.
That rhythmic feel that he gets.
He breaks all the rules, purposely.
So what about the Lion?
Barker - II-81

Well, Clarence Profit... When they used to have the sessions, Clarence Profit would come around the Rhythm Club, and they asked him, "Play something, Clarence." When Clarence played, everybody listened, the Lion and Jelly Roll -- everybody listened at this little crippled boy. He had a funny foot, he was sick. And he was from the West Indies Islands, he was a West Indian. And his father was a neat West Indian man who played piano, and he would come and play something around -- nobody paid him no mind. And they'd say, "That's Clarence Profit's father." He'd get at the piano and play, just playin', just the ordinary piano, you know. But he loved to hear 'em talk about "That's Clarence Profit's father." Then you'd see Clarence Profit comin', and everybody put their pool sticks down and everything, and listen to Clarence Profit. Clarence Profit was...
Where was this, Danny?
In the Rhythm Club.
In the Rhythm Club.
Because everybody would be waitin' around him.
Explain the Rhythm Club, Danny.
The Rhythm Club was a club... They had one called the Band Box first. It was a little small club which

had two pool tables on the side, and a gambling house where they played poker -- two or three tables hidden behind a door. It was just a...a third-rate, run-of-the-mill dive, in other words. But that was the musicians' headquarters.
Now, they've got two pool tables in the Rhythm Club and...
These are Black musicians, of course.
Black musicians.
Because we wasn't mixing then.
Well, some Whites would come around. It's the first time I saw John Hammond, around the Rhythm Club. Young White boy with the crew-cut haircut.
Barker - II-83
The Rhythm Club was owned by Bert Hall. Bert Hall had been a...
He had come from Chicago, hadn't he?
Yeah. A successful musician in Chicago. And he and his boy, he was a gambler... He came to his funeral when he died. He was a big man in the Chicago union. He was a bass player.
Harry Graves.
Yeah... No, not Harry Graves. Not the President. It was another little cat who was a gambler out there. A man...
Joe Jordan.
No, not Joe Jordan. There's another one.
A gambler? Walter Hite? He was a bass player. Walter Hite.
Yeah, I think it was.
Walter Hite.
And they was buddies. He gambled.
Yeah, he was a big gambler. Yeah, Walter Hite. Big, big...

No.
Yeah, Walter Hite. He camped at Bert Hall's, too. Well, Bert Hall opened up this gambling hall because

he was a gambling musician, a musician who gambled, and... That was part of their life, too. They could, you know, sit down. You've got that kind of patience, you know, to sit down for hours and gamble. And they would gamble, because they... They was gamblers!

Yeah. That piano player you know. What's his name? He was kinda gay.
Jerome Pratt? Jerome...
He worked... He had kind of bushy hair. He was a legend.

Yeah.

No, it's not Jerome Carrington. No, it's another one. This was another cat, a great, great musician. He's supposed to have been a Classical genius -- from Chicago he came.
Zinky Cohn?
No, not Zinky.
A little red guy?
He was kind of tall, and he smiled all the time. But he had a strange name. He would be in there. And James P. Johnson would come through there. Fats Waller come through there.

Jelly Roll stood on the corner. They didn't understand Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll would be talkin' like he talked to night people, who understand Jelly Roll... Jelly Roll would stand out in front of the club and talk to all these defeated musicians; half of them couldn't play, including me. We'd stand around there waiting for a gig and looking up at Jelly Roll. Well, Jelly Roll is from home. But Jelly Roll, he loves an audience. I noticed Jelly Roll had two little things on the end of his jaw that he could establish in ...(?)... When he wasn't talkin', these little muscles would be moving. Bill Robinson had the same thing. Yeah-yeah-yeah... See, look.
Oh yeah, I see.

No, just of those, at the corner of their mouth.

Tell you...
[CHUCKLES] That's weird.

That's a whole act with this mouth, see. My old folks said a mouth can get you in a whole lot of trouble. You see? And he'd have his mouth propped up, Jelly Roll.
Okay, that's beautiful.

And he's waiting. And his lips is juicy, not dry at all. Bill Robinson had the same kind of mouth. He would do the same thing. He was waiting. He wanted to be the leader and wanted to support the talk -- get the last word in there. If he didn't get the last one, he was liable to start to pull his pistols out. [LAUGHS]
And actually, when you mentioned Jelly Roll standing on the corner, that's where I saw him. Of course, that had to be the Depression, it had to be summertime. And

they had them candy-striped silk shirts.
Yeah. High-powered shirts.
Yeah.
Them shirts cost maybe twenty or thirty dollars.
Candy-striped silk shirts.

Yeah. See, they was perfect for him, but he was a little older and they was a little big, you know. And Hart, Schaffner and Marx suits. He had trunks full of them at his house, four or five trunks of clothes. And he had them two big Lincolns around the corner in a garage. When he played a gig, he'd take one of them out and put seven cats in it, and go play his gig. Any entertainer... When the Ford Company gave Fats Waller a Lincoln... He mesmerized somebody up in Detroit, apparently, and they just gave him a Lincoln. He come to New York with a Lincoln and said, 'Folks, go and see Fats Waller's Lincoln. Everybody's makin' (?).' So Jelly Roll said, 'You want to see an original, genuine Lincoln? That's a jive Lincoln. Go over there and look in there, and ask the man to let you see my Lincoln.' That's...
He was truly fabulous. There was a fabulous man.
Fantastic. You see, but Jelly Roll was night

people. And you see, you talk different from night people than you talk day people. Night people, they don't plant nothin'. They don't like no sunshine. They want to get up in the evening and have ham-and-eggs, just like cats, and they start business around five or six in the evening.. When everybody's getting ready to have supper, there come the night people first, waiting for the day people -- the fools, you know; waiting for the suckers to come in. Night people don't want to hear nothin'. "Let's get this table set over here. And let's open this door. Open that door and see that the door is... Treat them people nice. That's your bread-and-butter." And here come the people who wants to slum, and they're waitin'... The night people are waitin' for the day people.

So you have to know the difference between night people and day people. Day people, you talk to them different than you talk to night people. Night people don't want to hear nothin' about no wheat and no corn, no production line or no assembly line. He don't want to hear nothin' about that. He wants to know how you get the fast buck.
Mmm-hmm.
See, and the things that are tragic, a little girl who got raped... Well, the night people, they'd say, "Well, she's a young woman; it's about time that she's goin'
Barker - II-89

and get herself straight. That ain't gonna hurt her. It's just rape." You know, they got a whole different attitude than what you think. There's things that would shock day people don't even faze night people.

Well, Jelly Roll could talk about all that, and people would be laughin'! Jelly Roll would walk in the joints, like...you know, and say, "Let's see the cat." Most joints have a cat around. "Give that cat a quart of milk." Just signifying. "Look at that mange. Get that dog a steak." Signify. Walk in, and people say, "A man come in town, Jelly Roll Morton. He used that word, "Civilized world." [LAUGHS HEARTILY] You know, "I'm the greatest so-and-so in the Civilized world." And the people are...all them squares around the Rhythm Club lookin' at Jelly Roll. Then he opens his mouth; he got a diamond in his mouth. "Yeah, he's got a diamond." Wait til he open his jaws, make him mad so he can open his mouth. "What you say?!" And when you really looks, you see [LAUGHS] he got a big diamond -- about a 10-carat diamond.
Yeah, in them days he had all that stuff.

Some cat stole it when he went to California. He died, and the cat sneaked up ...(?)... one of these little hearses, took a chisel...
And stole that diamond.
He raised his neck and chiseled that diamond out.
Mmm-hmm.
And sneaked that(?) undertaker for a (?).
Hey, Danny, is it true he had a dog, and he put it down there, and the dog... A bulldog? Somebody told me that he had a bulldog.
[LAUGHING...]
He was just fabulous.
How'd he come by all that money in them days?
Oh, he was a Mack-Man. He had women. He had...
Yeah, he didn't need money.
A good-looking guy, then.

He was a composer. He wrote some of the best music yet. He's the first Black man to walk in the control room and say, 'Wait a while. You all ain't doin' that right there. That's bad... How do you get more... Whyn't you raise up the body? Here, where do you get it to?' 'Well, we'll open this up.' 'Okay.' And he'd go out. Because I

think the people had told him, "You know, go and make the records." But his records... He made some records called The Red Hot Pepper records, some of the best records recorded at that time.
That's right.
Because they're full and they're big.
And he orchestrated, too. He was the first guy that orchestrated.
Yeah, you know, orchestrated...
He was great.
And he's the first one that started to give you a part and give somebody... Well, I won't say he was the first...
But he was practically around the first.
So I think Duke got some ideas from him. They said Duke's first band sounded something like what Jelly Roll had done already. I don't know if that's true.

Well, he certainly did... I don't have any recollection of anybody doing too much writing of the parts. He used to tell his men, "Just play them black notes. Just play what I put out on the paper for you."
How about that.
And he did all the solo work. But he wanted you to play his background. You were background for him. I
Barker - II-92
mean, he really wrote it.
He had good musical training.
Oh, well, gee, yeah, you should know about him. He came out of... He was Classically trained. Well, Ferdinand, he come from kind of a first-class family, now, and...

Well, it was a respectable family. It had a whole lot of poor people, but highly respectable. They didn't have nothin' much. His mother chased him out... His grandmother chased him out because he was coming in late, and he was a bad influence for his sister. Once you went in that District... The District was a fascinating place to be. Because nobody done shit in the District. See, you went in the District and there were.... Nobody picked up nothin' heavier than a slice of bread.
Right.

That was an old saying. "Don't put your hands ...(?)..." Now I'm talking about night people and... In the District, that's strictly night people. It was quiet as a mouse, two o'clock in the evening in the District. You might see some stragglers out. By four or five o'clock, then you'd see 'em coming out. Well-groomed, the women all... Waitin' for the night. That's the difference between night people and day people.

Jelly Roll knew...talked night talk. You talk the night talk, and they got four West Indians, they got two from Trinidad, one from Barbados, two from Cuba -- they're comin' around. You've got some Negroes from Georgia and Alabama; they stand there and they look, 'cause they want to get in there. You see somebody standing up, talking on the street. You know, they don't do that in the small towns. And here's Jelly Roll standing with them...
Dressed to kill!
Mmm-hmm.
Yeah, see. And he's talkin', and he's talkin' loud enough so you can hear. And there was always somebody like... "Why did so-and-so...?" "Well, I'll tell you why."
Mmm-hmm. Mmm-hmm.

"I'll tell you why. 'Cause it went like this. Me... Wasn't nothin' happenin' til I started playing. All the things you hear comes around me." You can say that to night people and they laugh. They take it with a grain of salt.
Sure.
But you get some idiots around here that say, "Well, he said he started this and he started that." Well, Jelly Roll also had confidence in himself. Like, see them
Barker - II-94
(?)s... You know, like you travel. And if you're a piano player, you have to prove it. Prove it. Prove the talk.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah.

See, the Lion said Jelly Roll couldn't play no piano, you know. Like, the Lion is fantastic. The Lion's playing eight-beat, trick you. The Lion paid me a compliment I'll never forget. Yeah.
"Well, you're cool. You don't be runnin' through there. I'd know I can(?) lift my hand." And they'd respect you for that.
Sure.

He's moving.

He's in A and he's in E, you know, and they want to get you out, see. He'd play, and he'd hit a definite [HUMS EXTENDED NOTE], and you'd play in that key -- and it's somewhere else.
Yeah. You're lucky if you understand it. But Jelly had a thing, you know.

Well, Jelly Roll, you know, played stomp. He slowed down rag, and he called it stomps -- stomp-down. You see, everybody, Eubie Blake, everybody...Joe Jordan... Foot-tapping music, yeah.
Yeah. See? So he'd say, 'Well, that's Swing, that's Jazz. I did it. I started it.' He said he

invented it. He believed that his music was the only music. The rest of it was garbage. He'd say, "Now, Chick Webb and them? Too fast. That ain't supposed to be played like that." Mmm-hmm. Mmm-hmm.

But if you had been around and seen how Underworld, Nightlife people kid and joke, and they talk about... The women, they'd talk about other women. Nobody got mad. Talk about her clothes, you know, what she was doin', who's she shackin' up with. And they're playing the dozens and they talk.

You can't do that around Day People, though -- polite people. You can't come in somebody's house and... I've had cats, night people come in my house, and I have to tell them "Shh. Watch how you talk." Because there's a looseness.
Sure. You can't talk that way in the daytime.

Yeah. Well, that's the difference with Night people. If you know that, you know how to act. If you walk in a joint, and it's some sleazy joint, and you go in, you know you act cautious when you go in there. You act different than when you walk into a church.
Barker - II-97
That's right.
Look at the dives we've been in in different towns. You have to know...watch where the windows are at when you go in ...(?)...
Sure. Did you ever get to see Luckey Roberts around there, Danny?
Yeah, I played with Luckey Roberts. I played with Lucky Roberts, me and Luckey Roberts and Sonny Thompson.
What did Sonny play?

Sonny Thompson played drums. He was a friend of Steel(?). He had a vaudeville act, a quartet -- a trio, and his wife sang. And he did comedy behind the drums. And he got killed in Steel's car. They was drunk, comin' in from Saratoga, and they ran over a bridge, and Sonny Thompson, and I forget who else was in the car, got killed. They went over the bridge and went into the creek. It was winter-time, and the creek...the water was running fast, and it got up to the car, Sonny and the other guy was drunk in the car, and they drowned. And Steel was jammed in the car, and just his nose was up. And the lights was on in the car, and some people who was coming behind them ran down there, a man and his wife, and saw the car down there. And they forced that door open, and there was...Steel was in there,
and they got him out. But it was too late when they got... When the sheriff come to get the other two out, and they were dead.
Oh, that's too bad.
And Sonny used to call me New Boy. "Hey, New Boy, how you doin'?"
[LAUGHS] What kind of... I have this... Luckey Roberts was in Society. He wrote some beautiful songs.

Oh, Luckey Roberts, you can't imagine. Luckey Roberts has never been given the credit. Luckey Roberts had the longest span on two hands. He's the one that cut this thing between these little fingers so he could make some kind of an octaves.
Great player.
Yeah. And Luckey Roberts had been an acrobat in vaudeville, in circuses from a kid.
Little short guy.
One of them little pups(?). And he was one of the strongest men. He had been trained for that. You know, he had been an iron-man or something.
I heard that. He was always at the YMCA.
Yeah. I got a list of things that Luckey Roberts made of his compositions and his shows. He had been

on Off-Broadway... They had Off-Broadway shows long before it was called Off-Broadway. And Luckey Roberts used to take shows and do, like, this White guy... He'd have a show, and he went around for years, playing auditoriums and thaatres around the country. I can't think of his name, but he was a big... But Luckey Roberts used to do that, play all over the country in all kinds of different, and have the... He had the score of all the tunes in each one of them shows, and it must have been about ten shows he had.
He had one song that was a very popular song. Nobody credits him to it. I can't think of the title.
"Midnight..." "Midnight..."
[SINGS REFRAIN]
Yeah, "Midnight Cocktail."
Yes.
[SINGS REFRAIN]
Yes.

I used to hear Luckey Roberts. He'd be around the Rhythm Club. You'd see Luckey Roberts come up and pick up two musicians, and there would be a chauffeured car that would take him. He wore a tuxedo (?).
He had all the high-class work.
Yeah.
He had high-class jobs.
Barker - II-100
Him and Ford Dabney. They played for...
What did Ford play? Was he a piano player?

Ford played piano; he was a piano player. I never saw him... I think I saw him once. He always lived high-class, up on Sugar Hill. And Ford Dabney was a big-time player for these millionaires. And Luckey Roberts played for them, too -- for Roosevelt and all of the Tuxedo Park(?) stratum above New York. And out on Long Island, you got Southampton, and he knew of places where they played... A lot of musicians. Fats Waller. He played for their grandchildren and met you, and he played for their mother...from way back -- and he made that good money.

If you worked with Luckey Roberts, you never got your money til later. I played a gig with him, it was six months; I had to bring him to the union to get paid. When I get to the union, he's there, and he's been ...(?)... it all before (?) like that. And he's there, and you go before the board for a hearing. "Mr. Roberts, I just come here to get my money. Everybody played with him there a week.

You see, when he gives you... When he'd tell you to come to his house, he'd give you the wrong address. Because he was keeping three women at all times, in different apartments. A maniac.
He was a little short guy, wide as he was tall almost.
Yeah, he looked like a little crocodile.
Yeah! [LAUGHS]

But he was well-loved with those people, and he played... And all ...(?)... that thing, they don't stop playing. The last one I did, the one I played with, that's where them other people got there -- them big-band leaders, society band leaders.
Yeah. They got that for real, boy.
Yeah.
Continuously.

Continuously. I played with Wiley(?), Hugh Wiley(?). Hugh Wiley. I played the last one with him. That's the first time I played one. After the first set of about an hour,

Hugh Wiley(?).
I had seen him ...(?)... But (?) Hugh Wiley(?) played for the Society people, too. There was about a half-a-dozen of them that played for the Society...
Yes. What's his name was the top one. Luckey was...
Yeah, Luckey was...
Hugh Wiley(?).
Ford Dabney. And what's that brother's name? There's about seven of them brothers around there.
Played piano?
They played piano and they played violin, and they was always in the union.
Oh, Fenner(?).
Not (?) Fenner. That other big tall one, with the little hat, wore glasses.
I can't think of his name.
Sterling Conway. The Conway Brothers. They played there. And (?) Fenner(?), he was in that, too. See, all that happened around the Twenties.

Fenner(?) was a violin player.
Yeah, and his father before him. Them people entertained Whites. And it was the Clef Club. The Clef Club would send you fifty banjos.
Yeah. Mr. Pope was there. That old man named Pope was head of the Clef Club. He later opened up a hotel up in Erie, Pennsylvania, the Pope Hotel. He was a big man in the Clef Club. Banjo player.

Yes. Well, there was a great thing with banjos, and they got pictures of the Clef Club. Well, them people, they didn't hang around the Rhythm Club. They would hang around the Amsterdam Club. Because that was the old New York club. And the Amsterdam Club resented the Rhythm Club, because the Rhythm Club catered to newcomers.
The Amsterdam Club, I think, is still going.

Yeah. Your membership, you're supposed to... The (?) come on when you get a piece of the billing. When they ever divide the money, you get your share. Steel tried to get me for years to come and join in it. But there was nothing it but a whole lot of decadent old musicians who don't play, and they worked with the Elks band the Moose band and the Sanitation Department -- all the Have Mercy Musicians, I call them. They ain't out there. And they resent any son-of-a-bitch comes to New York. Now, them,
Barker - II-104
some of them come from somewhere themselves. But they're old. All of them got...a lot of them got their homes. I'm sorry, but I'm...
No, that's all right. That's all right.

See, and then you go, "I don't want to fool around with no Amsterdam Club. It's dark, they've got a little small light in there, and they don't want to have enough light in the goddamn place." You go down there, you know, they say "Come on down." "Well, no, man. I don't know..." The last time I went there, I went there and made a rehearsal, and the guy from Europe was there. John... From Switzerland.
John Simmen.

John Simmen. He was there. First time I met him. They had brought him in there (I was making a rehearsal) for somebody, to make some record. That was the Band Box...no, not the Band Box, the Amsterdam Club. Then Bert... I can't think of this guy's name. He was a trumpet player, and he owned the Band Box. He was a West Indian. And he got smart. He went up and got up on an electric light post, and hooked up some gimmick on there for stealing electricity from Edison, and lit up his place, had it all lit up, you know, and get the people come in and see (?) with all that power. Something to do with them boxes up
Barker - II-105
there. Then they sued him, and almost...I think they sent him to jail or something. But he was taking...
Where was the Band Box?
The Band Box was on 130th Street, right around Connie's Inn.
Oh yeah.

Right around the corner from Connie's Inn. In the back of the (?) was started(?) the last year or something. All the (?)s were right on that corner. The Tree of Hope, (?) went crazy there for years. Connie's Inn. (?) be at the Alley Way outside...
Sure. Right in front of Connie's Inn.
Yeah.
Did you know Sam Wooding?
No. Sam Wooding had been in Europe.
Oh yeah. He went there and left here, didn't he.
Yeah, he went to Europe and he... He was ambitious. He went to Europe. He was the toast of Europe after Jim Europe.
Yeah. I heard he said he couldn't take it to call Paul Whiteman "The King Of Jazz," and he took his band and went to Europe. He was in Russia in 1923. [sic: 1925]
About that time. Bushell...
Barker - II-106
Yeah. Garvin Bushell. Gene Sedric. And even in 19...later on there, the ...(?). . .went over there on soprano saxophone...
Bechet.

Bechet. [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE] I've got some recordings they made in Spain in 1924 [sic: 1929], and they're fabulous. Fabulous records. Unbelievable. Tuba player, I don't believe this guy, he was so great. They did a "Tiger Rag" and...
That's the guy who was with Fletcher, and left Fletcher to go with him. I can't think of his name. He was around New York. A fabulous bass player.
Oh, he was fabulous. So you didn't know him.

Well, no. You don't get to know them more than you'd see them. Like, you'd see Sissle. But you don't run up in Sissle's face. Not me.. Other people run up there and introduced theirselves. I know ...(?). . . "Oh, that's Sissle. He's (?) in the business." So you see him. There's Sissle. There's Claude Hopkins. You see Sam Wooding, and you understand he's coming back, and he came back to America, and everybody's glad to see Sedric and all them. But when they came back, nothin' happened. So what's his name, the clarinet player, Willie Lewis, he ends up being a bartender, and the trombone player ends up being his
Barker - II-107
assistant up there on Amsterdam, or on St. Nicholas, and...
Al Wynn was a trombone player with him, too.
That was one. But he came back.
Yeah. He went right to Chicago after that gig.
Yeah. Al Wynn was from here.
Was he from New York?
Yeah...

To me, Charles Elgar was a very high-class man. He was one of Eddie South's teachers, a great violinist -- Charles Elgar was a violin player. And he had an orchestra, a very good orchestra. Not a Jazz orchestra, from what I can understand, but a dance orchestra that played nightclubs and played parties. From what I can hear of it, it was... I wasn't old enough to play with him, but I saw him, you know.

I did reach the age where I did play with him. Because when Eddie South came back from Europe, which was in 1931, I believe, he was supposed to organize a big band to play at one of the hotels downtown. It was decided... Jules Stein, the booking agent for MCA, who had been the President, had
Barker - II-108

decided... He had heard Eddie South playing for the Rockefellers in Europe, and he was playing all them high-class gigs. And he thought it was time to put Eddie in one of them high-class hotels in Chicago. So they told him they'd organize a big band like Charles Elgar had, because now Eddie was the big violin player, was the star violin player -- and he was going to have a band like Charles Elgar. So Eddie wanted Charles Elgar to organize the band for him. And ever since he was a teacher, he organized this band. And he got really the best musicians available around Chicago at the time. Bob Shoffner was on trumpet, Ed Burke was on trombone, I think Jimmy Bertrand was the drummer, a drummer who had been with Erskine Tate's band, and Wright Smith was one of the violin players, who had been at the Regal Theatre. And Charles Elgar was the assistant director.

Well, we rehearsed... Eddie South is still in Europe, and this band is going to rehearse and get the gig together, so when Eddie comes back he can put the nucleus... He had Cliff King, and a guy named Wilson, Stanley Wilson on guitar, and a piano player named Antonia [Joe] Spaulding from Louisville, Kentucky. They were...
That's who I was talking about. Spaulding.
Spaulding, yeah..
Barker - II-109
Helluva piano player.
Oh, fabulous.
Yeah, that's who I was telling you about. A sort of tall guy, kind of (?).
Yeah. He was gay. Yeah, you're right.
Yes.
Oh yeah, he was fabulous.
Yeah, Spaulding would come around the Rhythm Club, smile all night and (?), because he's talking about how great Spaulding was. And the man is this...you know, this...wings clipped, you know...
Right.
You know, his suits need to be pressed... Just a decadent thing. This is nothin' for people...

You're absolutely right. Anyway, the three of them were in Europe with Eddie South, and they were going to come back and augment this band that we were rehearsing with. And so, we rehearsed about three or four weeks. And they had one of those managers in Chicago, whose name was Sam Scaldi(?), that was putting the band together. And he was so sure of the job that he signed us all to contracts. So we were supposed to work forty-five weeks a year and get seventy-five dollars a week. Well, in 1931 that was a big...
Barker - II-110
Yeah.

That was a biggie. And we all signed the contracts. And the band rehearsed. And Eddie South came back and put the band together, joined us.

And they decided that the time wasn't right to put no big band like that, a Black orchestra like that....

[PAUSE]

Yeah, they decided the time wasn't right to put a big orchestra like that together...
You know, that happened in many, many cities. The same thing. They'd build you up to this big thing, and then they'd tell you the time ain't right.

Now, what they did... Now, Charles Elgar had rehearsed this band for Eddie South, and now Eddie obligated to hire all of these men. And he had to take whatever money he made in Europe and buy those contracts back from the musicians. Because now he has no work for them. And they had signed the contract with them, he and his manager, Scaldi(?). So they took all the money that poor Eddie had made in Europe, and he bought the contracts back from each musician for three hundred dollars a piece.
Ain't that somethin'.
I remember, I got $300. And when they got to me, this guy told me, "Look, you're going to need a bass
Barker - II-111

player if you're going to be playing in town here." And he's got this these three guys, Spaulding, Cliff King and Stanley Wilson, and then Eddie South -- so you need a bass player, the fifth man. So he said, "Don't give him no three hundred dollars; give him the job." So I got the job!

And we went in the Club Rubaiyat, and worked in the Club Rubaiyat on the North Side, which was a gangster-run place. That's where I got to meet Dick Stabile who is here in New Orleans, a bandleader. His father was a violin player, and Dick Stabile was a saxophone player, sensational, with Ben Bernie's band -- and he used to bring his father over to hear Eddie South.

Now, what I was going to...what I wanted to bring this to here was about Charles Elgar. Now, after this, Charles Elgar didn't get much work. He began to get around to where he didn't get much work. I didn't see him playing any place any more. Now the violins... This is, of course, 1927. The violins are all out of the business. All the Black violin players have lost their jobs because Jolson has made the movie, The Sound Of Jazz [sic] or something, and no more pit bands in the Regal. In Chicago, where you'd have everybody at the Regal, everybody at the Metropolitan Theatre, all these musicians, all of our Black violin players are out of week.
Barker - II-112
It was sad around New York. They were all hanging around the Amsterdam Club. You'd see them with their fiddles, and they're still rehearsing and everything, but nothing's happening.
Yeah. Well, that's the same thing that happened in Chicago.
Mmm-hmm.

So now I'm seeing guys like Mister Elgar and a couple of these guys from New Orleans, and they always was doing very good, and looked like they'd be... They'd be out to the union, but they didn't look like they was really hurting for anything. And I asked you, I said, 'Well, how are these making it?' And you told me that these guys were... Do you remember what you told me?
[LAUGHING] No.
They were cigar-makers.
Yes.
And they could sit at home, and they'd roll those cigars, and sell it to those big men like Mister Marshall Field or whoever owned those stores Downtown.
They were very good cigars, yes.
And they made those cigars, and that kept them in business.. While the rest of the poor guys were starving(?). Do you remember telling me this?
Barker - II-113
Manuel Perez was a cigar-maker, a very good cigar-maker. [Omar] Simeon's people were cigar-makers.

Yeah. And I'd wonder how they were doing, because I know they weren't gettin' no gigs. Now, I was beginning to get gigs now, because I'm a bass player. And bass players... I'm working at them...what they called roadhouses and whatever I can pick up.
You got the ambition.
Yeah.
You'd take the big ones and the small ones.
Yeah.
A lot of musicians wouldn't take the small ones. They wanted the big ones.
Well, the violin players couldn't take it. There was one guy named Charlie Levy that would try to take it, you know...
That name sounds familiar.
Songwriter.
Very good cigar-makers down there, a lot of them.
Is that so?
Yeah. They knew how to make a good cigar.
Yeah. Well, that's what they were doing...
People couldn't buy, see? So they made them.
Barker - II-114
And that's what they were doing in Chicago. They were making these cigars, and they would make them at home on their back porch.
Yeah..
Charlie Levy. I know a piano player named Levy, a helluva piano player.
Well, that was the tragic thing about this whole thing that movies....
I didn't even know they had that many Colored violin players.
Man, Chicago was loaded with them.
Yeah, loaded with them. I mean, excellent ones, too.
How about that.
Excellent ones.
How about that.

Yes, indeed. Well, Eddie South had a lot... I mean, Erskine Tate had them down at the Vendome. We had three big... In Chicago, we had in the Twenties and up to the Thirties... We had the Goddard and the Vendome Theatre on 31st, and across the street, where Dave Peyton was, the Grand Theatre... Dave Peyton was like our Eubie Blake. He was a big, Classical-type piano player. They didn't play Jazz. In fact, he was kind of anti-jazz. You know, some of
Barker - II-115
those guys were anti-Jazz...
Well, they had come from the Classical world.
You know, they had their thing...

And it made 'em mo' mad when they had some of these raggedy sumbitches from all over the country, out of St. Louis, playing this funky music in them dives and tonks, and they become celebrated. Because the mass of the people dug that kind of music. See, and they all...
And they went out of business, yeah.
They're all sophisticated... I mean, this went on...

Yeah. I remember Dave Peyton was... He lived right near me, and he was very indignant... He lived with his sister. And he was very indignant, because he was very classy, you know, and... And he wrote in The Chicago Defender, and he always put down Jazz.
He wrote... He had fantastic penmanship for his arrangements. It looked like print. Paul had arranged some tunes for him, you know....
Paul Barbarin.
Yes.
Your uncle.
Yes. And I saw that printed music.
Oh, he was very learned. Very learned.
Barker - II-116
Yeah, that was a fantastic time.
Sure.

But it was tragic, what you had to go with this discrimination. And you had to be tough, because discrimination, in a sneaky sort of way, killed a whole lot of musicians -- because they couldn't understand to cope. You see, you finally had to do something else. Yeah, you had more than one thing you could do. But some of them wanted to just play 90 percent music; you know, all music. You can't. Because there would be slumps sometimes. And in a city like New York, you've got to cut the mustard and produce. People want their rent, and they want things to do. Now, if you're going to sit around and lag around, you're going to be dispossessed.

It's a hard thing for a man to sit around and play in a smoke-filled room, in the cellar, and play his heart out, and have some White guy come in there and listen to him play, and go out there and half play what he's played, and become famous.
Yeah.

And you're still in that hole, and can't ever get there. And this guy, he wasn't even a good copyist, in many cases. In this (?) it took a lot of strongness for a man to survive that. That's the reason you've got to give a
Barker - II-117
guy like Louis Armstrong so much credit. You've got to have a really tough skin to...
What he must have went through...
To last so long.
Imagine what he went through.
Somebody's copying and claiming everything. He was just about fifty when he started making some money.
That's right.
Chased him out the country. He had to get away...you know, stay in Europe for a long time.
Down here at the Suburban Gardens. He played for all of...you know, the better people. All we could do was listen at the radio.
They treated him like a dog, you know. They threatened him and everything. They didn't want him there.
Who's that?
Louis Armstrong when he came here.
Oh yeah.
Man, he tore New Orleans up with that music.
Well, you saw what the niggers did out there. Did you see what them niggers did?
No.
Ain't nobody said nothin'....
Barker - II-118
Yeah, you the only one that spoke to let him...
Now, you should have had a dozen people out there talking about Louis Armstrong, the opening of his statue...
That's right.

And people come up and talk about it disrupted the neighborhood when you put this man here. You all can celebrate Louis Armstrong's statue, but there was people living here. And you move these...displace these people and put them somewhere else.
It was the greatest thing that could ever happen when they put that statue there.

Disrupt a man's (?). Well, I know something about Louis, but I wouldn't actually qualify to do that. You dig? They should have had one of them people from Dillard, one of the men that knows just what to say, that knows the right words to say, to give this man... You know, like a good helluva preacher to talk about this man and to put the proper words. For me, I forget what I'm saying trying to keep from saying...using the wrong English.
Mmm-hmm.
You dig?
Mmm-hmm.
Barker - II-119
Well, the best thing I found I could say about him, I said, 'You should have heard Jazz before Louis Armstrong started making records. It was nothing like it is today.
That's right.

Because Jazz wasn't shit. I mean, it was all right. But when Louis started makin' them records, they changed the whole new concept of (?), about scat singing, and they got the popular singers... Before that, you had to have a...if you'd look on a record, you'd see it had to be a soprano or a baritone, and it specified what you were. When Louis come on, after he started singing "Heebie Jeebies" and doing all that shit, everybody was... They'd come up with the word "song stylist." Is that right? People like Hoagy Carmichael, he had no voice, but he was a stylist. Johnny Mercer. It's a unique thing about their voice that you like. Maybe not the whole public. But it's a style. It's his interpretation of a sound.
So that's the best compliment I could pay him. And I told about how he kept that roll in his pocket, just for people who don't have nothin'. He would ask you...
You sure did. You sure did.
Then he'd ask you, 'How you doing?
I remember he did that. Around in here, too.
Barker - II-120
He had a special roll for all them cats, like Foster -- John M. Foster.
John Foster.
A fine(?) comedian.
Stump crouch.
Yeah, he had a whole... Stump Crouch.
He sure did. I was with him when he did it.
He was a wonderful man. Now, Stump Crouch, the cat that you see with Redd Foxx... It looked like Stump Crouch. Was that him?
No. It was another cat.
Not the one that they give a (?) to and he couldn't keep it. It's a light cat. Looked like Stump Crouch.
I don't know.
Looked like a lot of people right here in New Orleans.

Excuse me. I can remember when I was working with Louis, little old ladies would come backstage to see him, you know. They were sixty-five and he didn't know them when he was a young man, and they would just stop back by the stage to see him. And he would scream, and he would call Mona, my wife, and he'd give her a hundred dollars and say, "Honey, take her out and buy her something nice for
Barker - II-121

me." He'd really do that, man. He'd say, you know, "Great to see you." And his wife could do it, you know. But my wife... He always had great respect for Mona. In fact, he used to call her "Mrs. Hinton." He would never call her Mona. "Miz Hinton, would you take this lady, take this [it's a couple of hundred dollars], take her out and buy some nice things" -- because they would look a little shabby, you know.

There's nothing... I can't possibly, in any way... The most amazing man I ever worked with in my life was Louis Armstrong. To see him... To see the dedication. I don't know of anybody that was dedicated to music, to entertaining people as this man was. His whole being was to entertain and serve the public.

You always saw him smile, and he'd laugh... He gave you a full laugh. Now, people get annoyed about that. He laughed, and his face, his muscles in his face... His whole face gave you a laugh. It wasn't a half-laugh, a jive laugh or a make-believe laugh. "How ya doin', Daddy." It was a whole, full laugh. Now, maybe it was different if you worked with him. But he'd give them people, everybody when he smiled... When he went out on stage and they'd give him the ovation, he leaned his head back with his handkerchief and his horn, and laughed.
And he was friendly. When he walked on that stage, it was for them people.
Yeah. Mmm-hmm.

I was with him when he went to Japan, and he had probably been every place in the world except Japan. And everybody went with him. Joe Glaser, Doc Schiff, the whole entourage. This was his first trip to Japan, and the people were all prepared for him. Man, when you want to see him, see him play some place where he's never been before. Because he's really... Now, he was gettin' to be a old man and a little tired. Man, he rose to such an occasion, playin' for them people, that I found myself standing with the bass in my hand, not playing, listening -- and I'm supposed to be playing! It was so amazing, because here I'd been working with him every night around the country, and we're playing the same thing, "Give Me A Kiss To Build A Dream On" and "Back Home In Indiana," and he's doing his thing. But here tonight, these people that had never heard him before, a whole carton(?) of people who had never heard him, and man, he was like three feet off the ground! It was just amazing to me. And he did it every night, man -- every night.
In the Madison Square Garden, in the bottom, and they've got all these bands. And all them trumpet
Barker - II-123

players warming up. Harry James. Feedback(?). All the famous... Ziggy Elman. All of them cats were down there in different... Tommy Dorsey, all them bands was there. And all of a sudden, you say, "What ...(?)... is this?" You could hear horns -- saxophones, clarinets. Everybody's blowing. In (?) everybody's trying to... You just hear all this... And all of a sudden, you hear, [SINGS ARMSTRONG PHRASE AND SUSTAINED NOTE AT ITS END]
Yeah. He had a sound.
And every horn in the place [SOTTO VOCE] stopped. [LAUGHS] Every horn! Man, there's nothing except ...(?)., he's still noodling, because he's playing obbligato(?). But [SINGS ARMSTRONG'S PHRASE]
Yes, he had a way with that horn.
Oh, and then you could hear a pin drop. "Pops is here, man. Pops is here!" Then you see the mad rush to his dressing room.
Yeah.
All them big, first-class trumpet players in the big time, with a lot of money, they're all in there first. You'd see 'em kowtowing to...
Yeah, it was amazing to see him.
But to hear that, boy. He could just... He did something with that horn different..
Barker - II-124
Yeah. He did somethin' with that horn.
Oh, there's no question.
But the people who went through that disappointment, like you said, Charles Elgar and them people, they... I guess they had seen a lot. And he was a high-class man.

Yeah, he was a high-class man. Yeah, he did... Mister Elgar did a great deal for Chicago, the Black musicians of Chicago until he died. He almost lived... He quite a life -- past ninety. And he got involved with the union, with those bands, with the union trust fund. And he was always for helping young ones, a couple of young cello players... Guys like Richard Davis came out from under Mister Elgar.
Is that right?
Yeah.
The bass player?
Yeah. Richard Davis' folks are from New Orleans, too, you know.
Yeah, I heard that.

His family was from New Orleans. And Mister Elgar... That was the next batch of young people after us that came up, you know, after we had come out of Chicago. The next batch would be, like, Richard Davis, in the Fifties
Barker - II-125

or something like that. And of course, we were gone or out then, and Mister Elgar would get to be Vice President and get to be an official in the Union, because he was one of the most knowledgeable men... You know, there was no room for violin players, so he just... He could give young people advice. And I used to come back through there, and I'd have a chance to sit down and talk to him, and he would tell me about the young violin players and the young cello players. He was trying to form a little chamber music thing and get some place for them to play in those trust fund monies.
How about that. He was a high class... Good-looking man, too.

Yes, a very handsome man. A very weird thing happened. For some reason, his wife lived in New York for years, in Long Island, and he stayed in Chicago. And he used to come like once every few years and visit.
The same thing with Simmons, him and his wife. He'd send his money home just as dutiful(?) as to keep his alliance. And his wife had another man, and he had a kid...
Yeah... Russell Smith was the same. It happened to Russell Smith the same way.
Yeah. And Wheeler.
Right, DePriest Wheeler.
Barker - II-126

The woman would raise some hell if he didn't send that money. We got paid around four o'clock, and if that money wasn't somewhere at five, the phone would ring. Cats were talking(?), because I think that's(?) what happened.
Russell Smith had one of the most beautiful stories that he (?) on your life(?), that you were in band... You would have been possibly in the band.
Yeah, sure.
He said that... Did you hear Russell Smith couldn't...? He was the first trumpet player, and he couldn't write. He couldn't write. But he could read anything you put up in front of him music-wise.
How about that.
I used to write the letters to his wife. And he'd send his money to California to her...
And she bought the house.
She bought a house. And when he was sixty-six years old, he quit the band to go to California to live, and she was all set, and she told him she didn't want him, and she had a guy -- and put him out.
How about that.
But Russell Smith was a member... This is one thing that America stands for which is beautiful. Russell

Smith was a member...was in Jim Europe's band in the First World War. And he went down to the Veterans Association and told them that his wife was putting him out. And they sent...the Veterans Association sent lawyers, got lawyers for him, sent them out there, and told that lady that she had to sell that house and give him half of it. And she wanted to keep the house. They said, "Well, okay, if you want to keep the house, then give him half the value of it." And they took it to court, and they gave her... Then the judge decided, "Well, he's a musician; he needs a car." They gave him a car. He said, "He's a musician; he needs a radio and the hi-fi." And they gave him portions of the furniture and everything that he would need...
He probably bought it all anyhow.

The Veterans Department did it. Then they took the money that they got, the half of the house (and the value had gone up), and they bought him a condominium, one of those little condominiums out there, with four units to it, so he could live in one, and they managed it for him. They took the rest of the money from the three to pay the mortgage and keep the upkeep. And he lived there until he died. That's one of the most beautiful stories I know about what can happen in a bad situation. And the American Government did that; I mean the Veterans Association.
Barker - II-128

He and I were kind of tight. He always kept his little bottle with him. Always sharp. Always got a good word. Always clean. Helluva trumpet player. He played that horn til the ....(?)., right with them young cats that's blowin'. And it was a pleasure; a pleasure to know the man.
His brother was a great trumpet player, Joe Smith. I didn't know if you knew him.

Joe Smith... Well, I didn't know him either. I saw him once. He went to Kansas City with the Cotton-Pickers, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, and he met a woman out there and he stayed out there for six months. Some big sportin' woman. 'Cause he was a cat could mesmerize you with that trumpet. Joe Smith, yeah.
Yeah. He was in Kelly's Hot Chocolates and those shows. I remember Andy Smith used to talk about him, and another guy named Pike Davis. Did you know Pike?

Yeah, Pike Davis. Yeah, I used see Pike all the time. Pike Davis was a trumpet player who was a rival of Johnny Dunn. He used to be the first trumpet player in the branch of them Broadway shows. They know how to play with that dead tone. They don't use no vibrato in those shows, in that pit.
Yeah, straight...

Straight tone, in there with that... And I used to see... I saw Joe Smith a couple of times, when the Cotton Pickers came to town. He went to Kansas City and met that woman and died out there. [JOE SMITH MOVED TO K.C. IN 1931, BUT LEFT WITH FLETCHER HENDERSON CIRCA 1936(?), AND DIED IN NYC IN DECEMBER 1937]

Then there was Luke Smith, the other brother. He played trumpet, but he was a gambler and stayed inn the Rhythm Club all the time. He looked like Joe and Russell. But he was a hustler and a gambler, well-dressed all the time. Luke.
And at one time, Fletcher had the three brothers in the band.
Is that so?
Because Fletcher married Russell's... Miss... what's her name...? Miss Hamilton, she was a trumpet player.
Oh yeah?
Fletcher Henderson's wife, Miss Leora was her name. She was like the mother of so many musicians. That was Russell Smith's first wife, and she fell for Fletcher and left Russell.
Oh, is that the way it was?
And they still played together.
Barker - II-130
Uh-huh!
Because she was in the band with that woman...you know, that woman who played a helluva trumpet, had a daughter who played -- Doll.
Oh, Doll. Yeah.
Doll. Well, they had this woman band at one time, it was a helluva band, in vaudeville. And Fletcher's wife...
Doll Hutcherson was her name.

Yeah. She had this little daughter. I used to hit on all of them, and she'd say, 'Leave me alone. You're not my type of man.' 'I like you.' Hit on her (?). 'Why don't you leave me alone?' I'd annoyed her. She went to Philadelphia, got pregnant, and started making a whole lot of babies. Mmm! Little Doll. She could play.
She sure could.
That little girl, the daughter.
I don't remember her daughter too well.
You don't remember the daughter?
I remember she was married to a guy named Hutch who was a tenor saxophone player around Chicago. Hutcherson, a little short guy.
Another (?).
Barker - II-131
Did you know a guy named Jimmy Strong, who was a saxophone player from Chicago?
I heard of him, but no... Jimmy Strong was a terrific... Jimmy Strong...
These are names out of the past, and they just were fabulous musicians that really supported, were responsible for our being here now...
Yes.
...that didn't have the break... And sometimes in history, somebody's got to know that they were there.
It's tragic. That's right.
Hobson, a trumpet player named Hobson.
A cat who looked like Freddie Keppard in Chicago, who was such a terrific trumpet player. Great, big fat guy. They called him Fatso...
Mmm-hmm, that was Reuben Reeves. Which of course, everybody knows about him.
This was an old-time trumpet player. He was fat. He would look like Freddie Keppard. Big, fat guy.
I can't place him.

Well, he was playing when I was out there. Oh, man, Chicago was a... Oh, man, this was... There was a cat who played the saxophone, he'd come around New York -- he'd been around Chicago. Played a whole lot of saxophone,
Barker - II-132
slobbered when he played, but that son-of-a-bitch could...
Oh...
Drank a lot -- later on. He was so dark...
There was a great clarinet player named Blue. Do you remember Blue?
Oh, Thornton Blue.
Thornton Blue, with the big teeth.
Yeah. Thornton Blue came out of St. Louis in the wake of ...(?)...
Fabulous clarinet player!
...and he asked for Buster. And he hounded Buster for every (?) second(?).
Buster Bailey?

So Buster said finally, "Go get your horn," and they went in the joint and they blew it all night. And Blue was a virtuoso. He'd come out of St. Louis. His father had the Imperial Band. I hung out with him a while. He told me a lot...
[PAUSE]
His father had the Imperial Band, huh? They hung out in St. Louis.
Yeah. Well, he had the Imperial Band and the Elks Band. They had that thing going in St. Louis, too, this marching band. But I don't think they had the funky
Barker - II-133
bass drum beat that we had here.
Oh, you've got to be here.
Yeah. Well, I don't think they had that. Because it would have been similar... I think Jazz would have been similar if it had had that beat. But that beat is something that you only hear here.
And I hung out, you know, with Blue. So my Uncle Paul said, "What you hangin' out with that guy? What's up there? He's notorious.." He didn't want me to be ...(?)...
He was a wild cat. I remember him...
Oh yeah!

I remember playing with him at this Pope's Hotel that I told you about in Erie, Pennsylvania. Some guy, a rich man's son, like young guys who do get hung up with the musicians, fell in love with being around Jazz musicians...
Mmm-hmm.

And he took a batch of us to his home. His father was a rich man in Erie, Pennsylvania. And he took Ed Burke, Blue, Jerome Pasquall, put a bunch of us...come through Chicago from Milwaukee, picking up musicians, and taking them up to Erie, Pennsylvania, so as to organize a band. And we were kids, all young, and we went. And this old man Polk, that owned that hotel, who used to be at the
Barker - II-134

Clef Club in New York, he had a big, old, rambling hotel there, and this boy paid for the hotel, and we all stayed there, and we could eat there, too, and we rehearsed every day. Blue... Oh, we had a wonderful time.

And evidently, this boy's father was in Europe somewhere, and we come back and found out that he was up there feeding us. And the boy would get... All the guys were going down, and bought brand-new clarinets at the music store (this boy was paying for it), brand-new cymbals for the drums... [LAUGHS] So his father come up there, and he broke the whole thing up, and gave everybody their fare back to wherever they were going. And of course, Ed Burke and I went back to Chicago, and Blue and Jerome Pasquall and them came back to New York.
In those days... Yeah, that Blue went around and asked for everybody. He was in Cab's band, and he quit Cab's band.
Yeah, but that was before me, though.
Yeah. Well, he was in the Missourians band.
Oh, I see.

Sure. And him and Cab couldn't make it, because... I don't know. He just I guess didn't look at Cab right. So you know, you had a thing where if you wasn't a musician, some musicians don't respect you. You know, he
Barker - II-135
was ...(?)... and all that. Yeah, he rubbed Cab wrong, so Cab... He left, and who they got in his place...?
Dunbar(?) Brown, wasn't it?
Well, Brown was the original man.
Brownie, a little-bitty short guy. Wasn't Brownie a little short guy?
Brownie? Yeah, it was something else, though...
There was two brothers.
Yeah. I think it was... Oh, I don't know, I can't hardly remember who came, because that was before I came in the band. That band went to Europe before I got in there.
Yeah.
Well, I'm going to wind this one up for right now, Danny, and we'll get back to...
[ETC.]

Well, we want to talk about your genealogy. We've got to get into that. And I really want to get... On this next thing, we've got to get to your marriage, when you married Lu, and about your composing. We haven't spoke about the Cab Calloway era...
Danny Barker (Milt Hinton, 4/80) - (Tape 4):

I found when I got to New York... I looked around and saw all the virtuoso guitar players (there wasn't many [?] banjo players, and they weren't doing much. They were with tramp bands, or they were working in dives and... I saw Banjo Bernie come through, and I saw Speed, Speedy... Speedy worked with Luckey Roberts and them. And I looked in the big bands, and in Charlie Johnson's band was Bobby Johnson, who was neat, cool, clean, didn't have too much to say, tended to business -- a banjo player. There was guys greater than him, but he was in Charlie Johnson's band.
There was [John] Truehart in Chick Webb's band, who was the master and the boss of rhythm. Everybody remarked how great he was.
Truehart.
Yeah. He didn't...
I remember him.
Yeah. He was (?), the poor boy died of TB. But he was a master. He would never take a solo, maybe a little break here.
And there was Clarence Holiday with Fletcher Henderson's band.
That was Billie Holiday's father.
Yes, Billie Holiday's father. He was immaculate, wore them hundred and some suits, at that time
Barker - III-2

them Coleman Hawkins suits with the hand-stitched lapels, and immaculate hats and shirts, and neat and cool. And he was no virtuoso, but he was the pivot in the band; he was the solid foundation in the band.

And I found all them other virtuosos, Banjo Bernie and all them kind of people who played, you know, all kind of fantastic banjo, and they was out there scufflin', you know? So I found out that you keep appearance and watch the clock and be on time. And that was my success, not that I was actually...you know... Because at that time you had to try and play a rhythm and try to work with a section. See, now, you can be a virtuoso... You wouldn't be no virtuoso, not in them bands, because you'd get fired. So you sat down with the bass player, the piano player and the drummer, you got together and you had a machine going there. And they had what you call very famous, popular rhythm sections. They would say, "Who is in the rhythm section?" Who was in McKinney's Cotton Pickers' rhythm section? Or who was in the rhythm section with Fletcher? And who was in the trumpet section with Charlie Johnson? You know, you had sections.
Yeah.
Who was in the trombone section...?
Oh yeah. You had to get into them cliques.
Barker - III-3

Yeah. See, but you had to be competent and you had not to be an obnoxious character. They'd put up with you, but after a while you'd head down with that. You'd find out... If you worked with Noble Sissle, there was Jack Carter on the drums, big diamonds on his finger. He wasn't no Chick Webb, but he had rhythm and he had personality. He was brash.
He wound up with a bar on Seventh Avenue didn't he?
He had a bar, and a whole lot of money at all times.
Is that right?
Always immaculate...
He loved this bar.
He had a whole...about five of them brothers. And all them were into things. They were all Night People. Three of the brothers had gin-mills in Harlem, three different brothers had barrooms.
How do you like that.
Another little brother...
Were they musicians?
No, just Jack Carter. Jack Carter...him and Valaida Snow and them went to China with Albert Nicholas.
Valaida Snow was... Did you know her?
Barker - III-4
Yeah.
She played trumpet and sang, didn't she.
She played trumpet, and she sang, played a little piano...
Yeah.
She could sing...
Good-looking woman, too.

Yes. She was everything. She was a master showman. She directed the band; she directed Blackbirds. She got up on the stage and did her thing. She was a star, almost a superstar. For nothing but personality. I was with her one time... Jack was her old man. They had a fight in China, a mix-up. She got to the pistol...
Who was her old man?
Jack Carter.
Oh, Jack was? Yeah?

They went to China together. And she got... They was always arguin', and it's who could get to the pistol and make the other one shut up. And if he got to the pistol, he told her to shut up or he'd blow her brains out. And if she got to the pistol, she told him to shut up.
So one day he must have smacked her or something, next thing you heard is a bullet shot. POW-POW! So we ran up there, and there was... Valaida had shot at Jack Carter.
Barker - III-5

Jack Carter went out; he probably fainted. They revived him, and that was the thing of... A man said they have fabulous ...(?)... in China. And he could tell you some stories about them people. But this woman was super.

And I found out that if you go on and be cool, don't get into things, things you can't change... They got a saying... What's that vow you make? "I want to do this, because if I can't change things, I want to go with things... It's some kind of classical scene. And leave things the way they are if I can't help them.
Oh, yeah. I know...
Yeah, some kind of vow. Do the best you can, and if you can't do that, don't turn the boat over. Don't ...(?)... life...
Yeah, I got a sampling on that...
Yeah. You remember that saying?
[LAUGHS] I like yours better, Danny!
Yeah. It's a lamb. You want to make a lamb out of (?). If you just sit back, you don't do nothin' but starve to death.
Mmm-hmm.
[LAUGHING] So I found out...
...(?)... day-by-day.
Barker - III-6

I found out you can be sharp... See, you be sharp, mind your business, be friendly with certain people, and try to play the best you can. Because when I started, there wasn't nobody around who could teach me nothin'! Because I mean, it wasn't like music. I took lessons about a year with George Augustin, all he could show me. He showed me them little notes and everything. I'd ask him, "Well, show me this chord." He'd show me this chord. "What is this chord?" When I got enough of them from chords him, he wouldn't even show me nothin' no more. See, because that's all they wanted you to play.
That's right.

So then, we tried to get along with people and tried, you know, to do the best you can. That's how I come to jump the ladders to go from all them bands to Cab. When I get to Cab Calloway's band and get in the dressing room, man, then you start pulling out them books -- all them books, look out...
Well, you was in the band before Milt?
No, I found Milt there. He welcomed me. He was nice.
Milt was in the band. Yeah, I see.
You see, you had to make a name for yourself in New York. See, and I jumped from like Baron Lee's
Barker - III-7

band... From Baron Lee's band to Lucky Millinder's band. From Lucky Millinder's band to Jimmy Johnson's band. Then back to Lucky Millinder's band, then to Benny Carter's band. When you get into Benny Carter's band... Benny Carter organized a band like every two years. You see, he'd sit down and he'd write six arrangements. Then he'd get a new band. So he'd rehearse his arrangements, see how his arrangements are. Then he'd get two or three books of bookings, then he'd break up the band. Then he takes all his arrangements, he brings them to Benny Goodman and sells him some, and Tommy Dorsey and sell him some -- all them bands. And he'd sell them over and over. Everybody had a saying, "This is a Benny Carter arrangement," just like you see...
Yeah, you see him around right now.
Yes. So that's what he would do . And after a while, the cats said, "Man, Benny's just got a band to try his arranging."
He used it like a little laboratory in that sense. He really did.
He'd experiment all the time.
That's what he did, see. Well, right away, when you'd make Benny Carter's band, it was a status for you.
Barker - III-8
Everybody... That's right.
Well, who's in the rhythm section? Danny Barker, Johnny Williams, O'Neil Spencer, and who else... Who was on piano...? Eddie Heywood on piano.
Wow. What a rhythm section!
Then Eddie Heywood became a star.
Yeah, I got a recording of his.
Johnny Williams was a wonderful bass player; you know, played real, real good. Myself -- I'm trying to play a bass-like chord.
Beautiful!

So there's Benny Carter smiling at you his approval... If Benny Carter gives you the stamp, and you stay with Benny Carter, you could play with anybody. Because Fletcher and all of them... They'd get scared, see. Because they're going to have a battle of music up at the Savoy or somewhere, and Erskine Hawkins and all them bands are waiting...
Yeah.
Benny Carter's gonna blow your ass out. He's gonna blow that saxophone, he's gonna scare all the saxophone players.
Yeah, he got his stuff together.
Barker - III-9
He's just like that. He's gonna blow all the saxophone... He's gonna play... [SINGS REFRAIN OF "BLUES IN MY HEART"] "Blues In The Night." No, no....
"Blues In My Heart."

Yeah. When he wrote that, all of Harlem was singing it. See, that how close... Big a city as (?), that's how small New York is. Benny Carter's got a new song out, and if he's playing at the Savoy, well, everybody stops, and they'd go on, listen to that. Listen to him play it on the saxophone, then he'd pick that trumpet up and play. And the band is cookin', because the band is well-rehearsed. The arrangements is all continuity of good music. It's not a sad... Sometimes you can play an arrangement and it's raggedy, or it ain't got the thing -- it kills the spirit. But Benny Carter's music was a whole solid thing of... Each chart, each one of them was a masterpiece.
Sure.

So when you got that, you'd been in his band, everybody would look at you. All the guitar players from all over, in every band, looking at you. Well, you're playing just about the same chords they're playing until Charlie Christian came on the scene. Jimmy Shirley upset everybody, playing a whole new context, you know.
Barker - III-10

You know, you're so very much right about the Benny Carter laboratory. I don't know whether it was official or not, but you must put John Hammond in there, who always liked Benny Carter, and he was the one who... Remember in 1932, he was the one that John Hammond recommended... He'd heard Teddy Wilson in Chicago, and told Benny Carter "Why don't you send for Teddy Wilson?" So Teddy Wilson came into New York to play with Benny Carter's band on the suggestion of John Hammond. And of course, when he got there, he'd been playing in Chicago with Keg Johnson and Budd Johnson and those fellows. And when Benny Carter was looking for a trombone player...
Teddy recommended Keg.

Teddy recommended Keg Johnson. They had all been living in the same house together, Miss Artis(?), in Chicago, see -- you know, old buddies -- and had been working on the same gig. So they sent for Keg Johnson. Now, Keg was my biggest friend. So my heart was broken because nobody had sent for me. You see? Then Keg Johnson gets in Benny Carter's band, as you say. And when you get in there, as Danny said, this is where everybody's looking. You're in the laboratory now. Anybody who is looking to get some musicians is looking to get it out of Benny Carter's band, because you've got to be pretty good to be in Benny
Barker - III-11
Carter's band, to play this music, and you'd be showing off at your best.

So consequently, Keg gets in there, and then he gets recommended to Cab Calloway, and Cab takes Keg out of Benny Carter's band. Teddy Wilson goes to Benny Goodman. And Al Morgan, who is from New Orleans, went to California to make a movie with Cab Calloway, The Singing Kid, and he was so photogenic out there, every time Cab looked up, the camera was on Morgan, and Cab didn't like that, and they got into little altercations. And then people told Al Morgan "If you were in California, everybody they make a picture with a Black man in it, you'd be in it." So Al Morgan quit and stayed in California; he was with Les Hite's band, see.

Then Cab was without a bass player, and he's coming back east. And Keg Johnson, it's now his turn to say, "Well, if you're coming back east, you've got to go through Chicago. Get Milt Hinton." And that's who... I was with Zutty Singleton at the Three Deuces -- with Lee Collins and Zutty Singleton. That's where I came in, through that same kind of avenue; you know, whatever the next steps were.
Well, maybe they got it today. Well, now I'm not involved with them youngsters. But I imagine it is. They know who is who, and who is on second first, and who is on and who ain't.
Barker - III-12
This kind of Jazz (?).

But that's what it was. And after that, well, you'd walk the streets and they'd say, "Hey, you're with Benny, huh? Man, you sound good, man. The band is great, man. Now you're with Benny, you've made it, man. That's great, man. Benny's a great guy, man." And you'd get all that yak, you know. And Benny's smiling at you, and your status is even higher. And he's trying to make it, and he's frustrated, because he's got a band that can go...he should be going into Roseland or the... What's that other ballroom on Broadway?
The Arcadia?
Yeah, the Arcadia, and the Rosemont in Brooklyn. They were places we could go, but they.... We had to play one-nighters.
He worked with Duke Ellington, didn't he, Benny Carter?
No, I don't think so.
No?
I don't remember him working with Duke. I don't think he ever did. I don't remember, anyway.
He had a sound on that saxophone. A sound on everything. And such a nice guy!
That echoing sound. He's got his picture on it.
Barker - III-13
Yeah, you went through that scene, man.
But you came in... That's when you came... So that way you were stepping through...
Yeah, when you went with Benny Carter, it was an opening. You'd get an opening. Musicians who wouldn't speak to you before speak to you now.
Well, we had some fun sitting in Cab's band together, Danny, in that rhythm section. Let's see, it was Bennie Payne and you and Cozy -- it was Cozy there, wasn't it.
Yeah, Cozy...
Was Maxey there when you came?
Maxey had left now.
Maxey had left and Cozy had come in.
Yeah. I was after them, in the shake-up. No, Maxey was fired, and then that guitar player...
Fruits. Morris White.
...he decided to leave...
Morris White.
I couldn't understand it.
He went back to St. Louis. I hear from him... He's got a brother who lives in New York, and he's still around.
Barker - III-14
Yeah. He was having trouble with his wife, and his daughter... She died. His kid died. He married (?) behind his daughter.
That's right!
He married, and was supposed to have given the money to that pretty girl.
You're right. I forgot about that. Well, he's got some kind of decent business in St. Louis...
Yeah. Well, him and that boy, Maxey, they went... Maxey went... Well, he did all right. I've seen him come back, and he's sharp as a tack, like he wasn't...
Yeah. He's in California now. Bennie Payne told me that he lives somewhere near him -- Leroy Maxey.
He was a nice guy...
Yeah.
Personality and everything... Man, shit, when they pull the rug from under you...
That's so.
And I've seen many cats leave Cab's band crying.
Yes!
When they'd get a notice in Cab's band, I'd see them cry. I've seen Greeley Walton cry.
That's right.
Barker - III-15
I've seen Brown, Walter(?) Brown cry.
Bushell.

Yeah. They had tears coming out. It's a shock. You know, you were with Cab... Because it's a stigma on your career. You'all been fired. But he didn't fire me. I just left. Because I was late and missed a show. And he damn near cried when I left, I don't know for what reason. He said, "Why are you leaving me?" Well, I guess it was a stigma on him, to have a fourth-rate guitar player quit on him. He never had that shit before.

I just quit, man. I said, "Give me my money." Because they had fined twenty dollars for being late. I missed a show. Now, nine cats missed the show. You all went on a stroll(?) with a seven-piece band. They come in sneaking one at a time, in the Paramount Theatre on a Sunday morning. You been away, man, you know, like six months and you come home. And shit, it's Saturday night, you're gonna play almost the midnight show -- you did five shows at the Paramount.
Mmm-hmm.

And Sunday morning shit, you in bed, and you've been out all night, and you get up and look at the clock, and it's 10:30, and shit, the first show is at 11:55 or something, and how are you gonna get downtown. So you
Barker - III-16

say just 'Fuck it, I'll take my time to get up.' And when I get down there, the band's on stage. He said, 'Well, who's late?' Bob Dorsett's(?) late, Ike Quebec's late. And it's a bitch when you open up a stage, and then you got a half a band and all them empty seats. And man, he was furious behind that shit. When payday comes, it's right there. Boom, Cab fined you when you were late, twenty dollars. I said, 'Well, I'm gonna put it in my nose.'
But I wanted to do something with Lu, my wife. I wanted to stay there. I figured this is a chance for her career, you know. She had been interested in Jazz...
And you had been sitting there in the band, writing songs and writing plays...
Mmm-hmm.
Because you would write a play, write a sheet and give me the thing to read. I'd sit there and read it, like, while some comedian was on or something.
Trying to get my English together -- trying.
Mmm-hmm.

But you did something in the band, because the band was encouraging. There wasn't no apes in that band. Everybody was on their toes. They don't get in no argument in there about something wrong, because they go to
Barker - III-17

the library. Like you'd say, "How long is a pool stick?" "What kind? A billiard stick or a pool stick?" They said, "Both of them." "It's the same size." Then an argument would start." Then somebody who knows something about pool said, "Well, no. A billiard stick is made out of oak; the other one is made out of pine." And they said, "Well, we'll find out. Put up or shut up." Somebody would go to the library and come back. The dictionary says a pool stick is made out of so-and-so." Now, you can't beat Webster.

And they'd do that on you. They had the argument about piano players with different sounds. One of them said, "All pianos sound the same." Somebody said, "No. Different pianos have different sounds..." No, different players. No two people play alike, to get the same sound out of a piano. They said, "Well, it's the same instrument." And there was some kind of technical argument. So they went to the library, and they come back and find out that that's right. Some scientist said that a piano, everybody plays different, that's when they... So I said, "Well, I'm there(?)." Now, he's got all these books, he's got some music -- I never seen nothin' like that. Looked like a diamond. Have you ever seen that? It's a diamond. Notes like that? I ain't seen... I said, "What kind of music is this?" I see him reading this stuff! [LAUGHS] He said, "Go get your guitar,
Barker - III-18
man. It's time." I don't let him know I can't read it.
For those certain notes.
You understand?
Yeah-yeah-yeah.
I'm not ...(?)..., man. I'm tired. So instead of me getting to him... If I'd listened to him, I'd have been a virtuoso.
That's right.
Then he could have showed me how to make those chord changes, the intervals and all those things, you know.

But you had something that didn't nobody have, Danny. You knew how to get it. Like, you walked out... You were the only man I know that had enough nerve to quit that band. At that time, that was the highest-paid band in the country. Duke wasn't paying no more money than Cab was paying.
No.
And for a man to just quit it... And we worked fifty weeks a year. And for a man to quit it, you got to be either crazy or you just got the strong fortitude of your convictions.
Yeah-yeah...
Barker - III-19

Which is, of course, what Danny had. He knew that he could make it regardless. Like, he just said here the other night, just give him a slice of bread and he'll make it. So if he didn't agree to whatever the principle was at that particular place, he would abdicate it -- he would leave it. Because I stayed there until the thing went right down. I didn't quit Cab's band.
Uh-huh.
