The band broke up around me.
Is that right?
There was no more band.
Uh-huh.

And there I was out there floundering around, and there Danny Barker was in New York, and he said, "What you doin'?" And I said "Nothing." And he said, "Well, come with me." And then what do you do? I took my bass and he took his guitar, and we got on the subway, and I wound up in Hoboken, New Jersey, with Danny Barker, and he says, "Come on with me..." Tell him about it, Danny.
We did the big ones and the small ones. We'd go out there... I just want to say this. You see, what...
So Mister Wright says, "You know, Cab Calloway fined you." I asked him, said, "Give me a loan," so he gives me, I think, thirty dollars. So I am getting a hundred and a

quarter. He said, "Now, you know you're fined, so don't (?) yourself." I said, "Fined? Did you fine anybody else?" He said, "No, he didn't fine nobody else." But payday comes, and I got my money, and I was twenty dollars out. I said, "Cab, why did you fine me and you didn't fine the rest of them guys that was late?" He said, "Well, you know better." I said, "I know better? Well, okay. I'm gonna quit the band." He says, "Oh, man. Go on and ...(??)... Go and work. Don't come at me with that kind of shit, that talk."

So I walked out and I went and wrote a notice, and I give it to Mister Wright." So Cab calls me, and says, "Man, why did you quit? What did I do to you?" I said, "You fined me." He said, "Well, you know better." I said, "Well, just give me my twenty dollars." Because if they fine you, they got to pay you. They can't take your money. If you stay, you're subject to the...

So that's that. I had wrote some songs, and people was telling me, "Why don't you promote your wife?" So I said, "Well, I'll stay in New York." Then you're staying away from home." See, my old lady don't come on the road with me, see, and then we'd get into arguments when I'd come home: "Where you been?", etcetera. "Have you got women out on the road?" -- which I did have. [LAUGHTER]
Who didn't?
Barker - III-21
All kinds, all shapes...
Who didn't, man? How could you survive out there?
That's right. So you're out there...
When you're away... I don't know anybody out there on that road who was in that band that didn't send that money home, though. Did you?
That's right. They all provided.

They all provided. I mean, there isn't a man out there that lost his wife or his family because they religiously didn't send that money home. Because everybody knew you worked with Cab, you got to get paid, he's got a reputation. He never mis-paid nobody who ever worked for him. They'd never say that he missed a payment. Did they, Danny?
No-no. He don't know nothin' about that.

You got paid. So everybody, regardless of what you did or whatever developments you got into, including getting drunk... And Lord knows I did. And I could borrow money. I was three weeks behind in my salary sometimes. Because if I threw that money away, I'd better get some money to send home. And you could get some more. He'd give it to you.
Yeah. You can go ahead.
Barker - III-22
Yeah, it the thing with security there, man.
So where did we go, Danny, when you...?
So I'm there... So the bands, all the big bands broke up. All the bands, man...
What year was that?

What year? It was around '50. From '40, it started falling to pieces. When Louis Jordan come out with the Tympany Five, with them little bands, down to five... He could play them big old ballrooms with the Tympany Five...
King Cole and all of 'em come out with them trios, too...
He'd (?) them and put up the five mikes. When Louis Jordan came out with "Do You Call That A Party".
Yeah, it sounded like a big band.
No, it was a small band...
Yeah, I know...

...but it was the amplification. All them mikes. So the people didn't need twenty cats sitting on the bandstand. Then you go around again, and then the Rock stars come in -- not Rock, but Rhythm-and-Blues...
Yeah, yeah.
And you get all them little bands from the West Coast. Pee-Wee Crayton, seven piece band. Joe Liggins, The Honey Drippers. There was another little band
Barker - III-23
out there that had that big old (?).
Were those bands around New York? I don't know about them guys.
All of them come played the Apollo. And what's what chick, Camille something, from the West, from Los Angeles...
Camille Anderson?

No, she worked with a band. And boy, it was a swingin' little band. Little cat looked like Baby Dodds. She had a swingin' little band, one of them rhythm-and-blues bands in California. The Honey Drippers. Then they had what... Then Earl Bostic got a band, a small band.
Brown. What's that guy's name? Brown. Buddy...
Buddy Johnson.
Buddy Johnson.
Buddy Johnson. He had a big band, but he started with a little band. But all them little bands went around. It was a whole new concept of Black music.
Yeah, I remember that.
Now, Cab had a repertoire playing sophisticated...
Clean.
...clean music.
Barker - III-24
Bright.
Mmm-hmm.
Flashy.
Yeah, dress a little.
...(?)... they're looking at. And later on, they started selling sweat. See? Sweat. Who sweat the most got the most people.

Yeah. And Race records now begin to get on the air. There's a lot of contributing factors. Race records, which used to just be for the home consumption, were now being played on the air. So all through the South, people were hearing about "I'm gonna cut yo' nappy head [haid]. I'm gonna kill you." But Cab Calloway's comin' and trying to tell 'em about "Copper Colored Gal Of Mine" and "Don't Worry About Me, I'll Get Along," and they don't want to... And all they're hearing all day long is these Blues where "I'm killing you; I'm gon' cut yo' head." And so they don't weren't going for our classy things, the fellas with the zoot suits on and the Cotton Club boys dancing on the boat. That was one contributing thing.

The other one, television came in. Now you can see all these people from New York. You don't have to wait until they come to your home town to see them. The airplane travel came in, which became expensive, but it gets you
Barker - III-25

places faster. I remember we went to Philadelphia when they started using them planes to travel. And all these things were what you'd say contributed to big bands... You couldn't pay for a big band to fly them guys all over, at the prices they were getting in those days, you know, in the theatres.
Money wasn't (?).
It wasn't like it... And the video just destroyed us.
Yeah, it was a thing, man...
Yeah.

So I just left. So I'm around there. So I hit Broadway now. Now I'm hustling, hustling songs, see. And I'm a rhythm guitar player; I'm not a fast fly guitar player leading in order to be up front. You know, they got them cats got them groups and they're playin'. So I figured I'd do a little thing with my old lady.

So I tried, and we got a little group together, and we couldn't get nobody to cooperate 'cause she's singin' blues -- and they look at you after a while. You know, I had two or three cats, and one of them told me... I booked them, and we played the first night -- and he was one of them Muslims, I can't think of his name. A piano player... And we washed him, washed his clothes, fed him, gave him some money and everything. And we're going to Montreal. We
Barker - III-26

go to Montreal, to Ciro's, and when we get there, it's good, he's playing, she's goin' over great. The second night we hit, and after we played the second note, he said, "Man, I ain't playin' no more Blues." No, we started off; I hit the introduction...
Who was that?
A little piano player. He works with Hawkins' little brother... What's that boy's name, a tenor player from Kansas City who got hurt...
Arnett Cobb?
He used to work with Basie.
Arnett Cobb?
Good-looking, big fellow.
Arnett Cobb...
Cat that took Lester's place.
Buddy Tate.
Buddy Tate. This piano player played later with Buddy Tate on 125th Street. They worked on that gig for years -- between Lenox and Fifth. Remember that club down there?
Yeah.
He said, "Man, I ain't playin' no more Blues." Percy, that Percy that we saw... Percy Gamble...
Is that right?
Barker - III-27
Yeah.
Is that a bass player?

Yeah, from Detroit. He was out at this... Well, he was with me. He said, 'Man, what are you talkin' about? You gotta play this music.' He said, 'I ain't playin' no more Blues.' He said, 'Well, lay out.' So he sat there. And he started hanging out. He'd met some musicians from New York that was there, Louis Metcalf and them, and they wanted him, because he was playing modern -- he was a bopper. But he was starving to death, you know, in New York, because the Boppers weren't working too much. There was a few of the superstars. But a lot of them was on the bandwagon, considered Boppers, when they was wearin' the dungarees and the goatees, and they was changin' their names. They had joined this Muslim society. This guy in Newark... It was Mohammed. There was another society they had.
Yeah, Mosque Clubs they called them.
Anyway, it was some guy in Newark who was brainwashing them. Musa(?) Kaleem, who was Rudy Powell...
Rudy Powell, yeah.
They believed that if you changed your name, that you wasn't black. When they'd get through talkin' to you and they would wash your brain, you thought you was an
Barker - III-28
Arab. You was Arab! You was ...[INAUDIBLE NAME]...
They had an identification card that read... I remember Rudy Powell's card that read "I am a descendant of the Father Abraham..."
Ibrahim.
"...Ibrahim and the Mother Hagar" -- which is a Biblical thing, you know. We are descendants of that. "And the son of Ishmael." It was on the card.

I remember that. They'd go to Newark, and this man would straighten your head out. They was defiant with that. Like that time we walked into that hotel in Springfield. The man said "no rooms in here" when he saw us.
Omaha.
It was Springfield.
It wasn't Omaha?
No.
What Mushid(?) went and got the rooms?

When we all walked in, the manager said "Wait. I have no rooms. Mushid(?) said, "Wait a while, let me explain to you." And he kept walking... He was always crippled; he had a gimpy leg. He walked to the manager and said, "We are Muslims." And he told that man something else(?). "Well, I didn't know that, fellas. Come right
Barker - III-29
in." And Shad Collins and all of us signed at the register and got rooms and went in there. The man, "When you showed that card..." He was defiant with that. And then we come down...
He said, "Call the State Department." And it scared the man to death.
And we all went to the theatre, and the man... Somebody went and told that man that we was the band in town...
The colored band in town.

And the man finally asked us... We had to move. By that time we had got rooms. They didn't charge us nothing for staying there that day, but "just get out of this hotel." Because it was a White hotel.
Yeah, you all had to get out of there and go somewhere else.
Yeah. Well, Mushid(?) was so defiant. Looked that man right straight in the eye, and the man reads that, says, "Son of Abraham..."
Yeah, he had a beard... They wore a goatee and beard.
Yeah, just like them Arabs.
He had a fez, he wore a fez! [LAUGHS]
Barker - III-30
He was somethin' else. But what a musician he was.
He sure was, Danny.
He's the first one that told me about Benny Goodman. He said, "Man..."
[END OF TAPE 4, SIDE A]
When did you record "Don't You Feel My Leg"?
Yeah. Well, I went....
Well, when did you write that "Save The Bones From Henry Jones"?
Yeah?
Yeah, in '49.
Because I didn't hear about "Feel My Leg" until afterwards a little bit.
Well, they banned it, see.
Oh, that's why.
See, I go to Decca. Now, you got this thing where you got Guy Lombardo on Decca, you've got the King's Men(?) on Decca, you've got the Boswell Sisters, all of
Barker - III-31

them... Dave Kapp was a liberal sort of a man, and Jack Kapp had been around Chicago, around Paramount Records and all that... They come to New York and they opened Decca, Decca Records, and they picked up all the artists of Victor and Columbia. They were particular who they'd record, see. And Decca, they come on with their thing.. So they got a guy named Mel Williams, who is a bandit. He robbed you. He wouldn't give no royalties.
Was he a Black man?

Yes, Mel Williams. He was an All-American. Him and Fritz Pollard were on the same team, one of them teams that ran over everybody in the Eastern League...what do you call that league...? The Ivy League.
In Track?
No. Football. All-American football players.
Oh, yeah? Is that so?

Mel Williams. He was... You get them people who make their big reputation in national and international sports, they always can get good jobs, because the White boys that go to school with them... They keep the positions hereditary, and they always can get a job. So Fritz Pollard (I saw him on the air the other night; he's a very old man), he was a young cat who weighed about 175 pounds, but he was
Barker - III-32
swift as lightning on the football field, and he made All-American -- him and Mel Williams.

So Mel Williams has got the Black repertoire of Decca. He records everybody, Joe McCord, all them people out of Chicago. He lived in Chicago. And he even started the Race Records which they call on the catalogue, in the Decca catalogue. So they're looking for talent.
[BRIEF PAUSE]
So what happened?

So they're looking for talent. So they tell, 'Well, Decca...Mel Williams is in town, and they're looking for talent, so why don't you go down there?' So I bring Lu down there, and she's singin' the Blues. So Mel Williams says, 'Ain't you got somethin' a little raunchy?' Yeah, yeah, a little under-the-table stuff. Somethin' funky. He didn't say it like that, though. Something like...you know, like a cathouse song or something. Because in the Black market you could do that, because the records weren't played... About this race record business. They weren't played on radio, because they didn't have that many disk jockeys at the time, and they were very highly sensitive to what was put on the air. You know, you couldn't even swear. But there was a big market that the same jukeboxes... The Black jukeboxes, they would have a whole different
Barker - III-33

repertoire than White jukeboxes.
One of the first artists to play on White jukeboxes, in White joints, was Louis Jordan. After Louis Jordan, then came King Cole. When he made "Nature Boy," you found him in every hotel in the country. You would hear... He's the one that revolutionized this thing where you can hear Black artists on White... Because some jukebox owners didn't have a record... I knew some of them, because I approached them with my record. They had never had a Black record in the store. Everything was for hotels and...you know... So you had all that to go against you.

All right. So I go to Mel Williams. So he said, "Well, would you..." He looked at Lu and said, "Yes, you can sing, but we need something more." So he said, "Think of something raunchy, and come back." So I get back home, and I think "What was that thing that my mother used to sing, 'When you feel my leg'..." "When you feel my leg..." I said, "What else?" She used to sing, "When you feel my leg, when you feel my thighs..." I don't know where my mother got that from. It's (?) original, because I never heard nobody else sing it...
No.
Because they would come out and tell you if it got taken from them.

Now, the music has got a thing whereby... [SINGS] "I'm Alabama bound, Alabama bound, [HUMS 2 BARS], Leave a dime(?) for beer(?)..." Now, Perry Bradford jumped up and said he wrote that. But you see, Perry Bradford...Mamie Smith... He's the one that introduced Mamie Smith to Columbia...
Was it Victor?

Columbia. He went to Victor first. Victor laughed at him. He made a fool(?) of Victor ...(?)... So he went to Columbia, this man understood, and let him make a record. They did "The Crazy Blues," and it swept the country, and that's when they started looking for Blues singers like crazy. There was Mamie Smith, then there was Bessie Smith, there was Clara Smith, there was Trixie Smith, there was Sara Smith, Emma Smith, Beulah Smith, Saponia Smith -- as long as you had a Smith. And that big old Smith name in vaudeville. You put that on a marquee: "Smith: Blues Singer." And they don't look at the name in front. They say, "Well, it's one of them Smith sisters." You know how Black people are? Well, all them Smith sisters could sing regardless of who it is.

Well, how many Smiths have you got in the Baptist Church? It would be two million of 'em. So you'd get all the chicks could sing, I could understand why Whites sometimes were leery about how many Blacks they let through.
Barker - III-35

Because if you go in the Baptist Church I belong to, they got at least fifty chicks in there who can sing...sing meters and beats and never have recorded. And they would really explain something about them tempos, which I researched (which I didn't know; it was new to me) in the Baptist Church. That's the source of it all. All of that Jazz, everything that happened come right out of that Church. I hear them people doing that, and they don't know nothin' about Louis Armstrong, Coleman Hawkins, Dizzy Gillespie. But I hear them people do these sounds and these passing tones in the church...
Yeah, the passing tones!
The music that comes out of that Church is out them people. And it's primitive, it's natural -- fantastic.

Okay. So I can see why these people had...you know, kept... Don't let too many of them. Because if you let all the Negroes with talent out there, there would be nothing for them other people to do. I mean, (?) all them millions of Chinamens out there. They got some Negroes who can do some strange things. Like that boy who dance them on vibraphones and make music. Isn't that something? What was his name? Had a whole keyboard, he did that tap dance, would sing that song.
Barker - III-36
Yeah, sure! I can't think of his...

Made the news. There were ...(?)... people like that. They tell me they had a hoop act one time, a cat made six hoops, and they told me he'd stand by the wings and he'd throw these hoops out, and them hoops did all kinds of things on the stage. And they almost bumped into one another, and they moved out. They said, "How do you control them hoops and made 'em do that?" There was a guy who would take a chicken on the stage and talk to the chicken, and the chicken followed. He says, "Count me to five," the chicken says, "CLUCK-CLUCK-CLUCK-CLUCK-CLUCK," and the chicken count... All kinds of fantastic acts.
See, if you let them... If people would let everybody who could do something... That's why so many of us had to die... By being so innovative, we had to die on the vine.
Out by the wayside.
What was that guy's name who used to be able to dance on them skates, who was so great?
Yeah, yeah...! He was strange, too. He used to do some things that would entertain you off the stage and on the stage. So many of them.
Yeah, he was a champ.
Yeah, well, that scene was something, man, that New York scene. And then you'd go away and you travel,
Barker - III-37

and you... You go to Detroit. There's a whole bunch of musicians there that's got a cult going, and they're playing up there. You'd go to Minneapolis, there are some musicians there, them Pettiford Brothers, the Pettiford family. Adolphus...
Yeah, Adolphus Allsbrook.
Big-talkin' Adolphus. He knows everything.
He played trombone and bass -- unlimited bass. Adolphus Allsbrook was hugely respected.
Incredibly respected...
I respected him. Did you know he wound up writing for Lawrence Welk?
Yeah! You told me that. Adolphus was a big heavy-set boy who looked something like Mingus, and he carried himself... He'd come around and look at us like....
Judo expert. Judo expert. He had a black belt in Judo.
Yeah, all of them respected him. Pettiford would run around him like a little poor dog. He'd take him to dinner; that's his home(?).
That's right.
He come around there, learning something, hang around him like a little puppy dog...
Barker - III-38

Adolphus knew about Judo, and we didn't know anything about it. He said, "Come on, I'll show you something." And he threw up against the wall. I thought the building was gonna... VROOM! He would get up...
Strange, though.
Yes. Very strange guy.
And he got this book, The Thirteen Families That Run America...
That's right.
...and he talked about that. Do you remember that?
Yeah.
Yeah, he was annoyed by that shit. The thirteen, fifteen first families of America. The Firestones, the Rockefellers, he knew their names...
He knew some families in Japan. He had it all together.
The people with all the money..
Yeah, the people that run the country. You do what they say.

The first time I saw Adolphus Allsbrook was in Chicago. He came to.... He was a Golden Glove fighter. He was boxing. And he was a converted gambler, just insane for gambling. And he won he Golden Glove contest out there, and
Barker - III-39

he brought his bass along with him -- he'd tuck his bass under his arm like it was a matchbox, he was so big. And I was playing with Erskine Tate at the Savoy Ballroom, and he came and stood and listened, and he stood right in front of the bandstand, looking up there at me all night, you know. And I look at this cat. So he said, "Man, you're wonderful," you know. I said, "Thank you." So he said, "I'd like to study with you." I said, "Well, if you want to come by my house... I'm living with my mother, and if you want to come by my house, it's cool," you know. So the next thing, he comes by my house and brings his bass, and I open my book to show him -- and he ran through that book like it was a no-sense(?) quote(?) (?) or something.

So I asked him out of my house. I told him that nobody comes in my house and insults me like that! He says, "No, you do some things I really like." I said, "Yeah? You do some things I really like, so let's study with each other."

And he went out that night gambling, and the guys in Chicago, they... He won some money, and he wanted to leave. And he had to come through one of the alleys, and the cats tried to waylay him in the alley, but they didn't know he was a Golden Glove boxer -- and he left about a half-a-dozen of them laying out there in that alley when he left. He was that kind of guy. And he went home, back to Minneapolis;
Barker - III-40

and the next time we saw him was in Minneapolis.
But Danny, what about that scene...? I know, like, Perry Bradford is from Atlanta, Georgia, and he was always talking about what was happening in Atlanta. Also, Eddie Heywood's father was from Atlanta, and they had some things going on down there in Atlanta...

Well, there was a junction. There was the Eight-One Theatre. It was a theatre that was one of the pivots of the TOBA Circuit, the Eighty-One Theatre. They had three theatres of vaudeville in Atlanta. And Atlanta was like the metropolis of the Black South, more so than New Orleans. They had three or four big insurance companies there.
Mmm-hmm, that's right.
They had a whole lot of money there in Atlanta, Georgia...
A school, too. Some schools.
Well, about six schools. Spellman, and they've got schools...Atlanta University...
Caladaga(?) or something...?
Yeah, there's nothin' but schools. It's the height of education for Black people around there.
So there was this market for Black vaudeville. And you played the Eighty-One Theatre, the Crawford... His daddy was
Barker - III-41
the piano player in that theatre for years -- Eddie Heywood's daddy. [EDDIE HEYWOOD, SR.]
Yeah. I hear he was a pretty good piano player, too.

Well, you can hear him on some of them records. When you went there, there was a school... When you played vaudeville, you had all these little performances. The Whitman Sisters, which was a family. The Gibson Family. These people were into vaudeville, and they were dedicated vaudeville people -- old people. Sidney De Paris' and Wilbur De Paris' daddy and their mother was in vaudeville. And there was whole families that went around...
Sidney De Paris the trumpet player and the Wilbur De Paris the trombone player.

Yeah. They come out of Indiana. And their mother and father had a show that used to be on side shows. They called that the midway, the show that you'd... The (?) little tab show. But they kept this little show together. And that's where... Jelly Roll's old lady, Mabel, was on the show. And the old man was Diamond Toot Willie... Diamond Toot Willie Arnkey(?)... Jimmy Arnkey(?)... Jimmy Arnkey was an actor and dancer that had a big diamond in his tooth, and when he went to Chicago with Mabel, Jelly Roll took Mabel
Barker - III-42
from him, and they were supposed to gonna have a shootout in back of one of them theatres, one of them cabarets. And that's how Jelly took Jimmy Arnkey's(?) old lady. Sidney said he used to see...
Sidney De Paris.

Yeah, he said he seen Mabel and how pretty she was (because for quite a few years she was on the show), and how Jimmy Arnkey(?) used to mistreat her, you know, slap her around. Then she met Jelly Roll in Chicago...
What did Jimmy Arnkey(?) play?

Jimmy Arnkey was... I got a picture of him. I'll get it, I have the photograph, and I'll show it to you. Jimmy Arnkey(?) was a little short, dark cat who was a dancer and an MC, a straight man... He was a straight man or a comedian; he could be either one. But he was a showman. I saw him in Selma, Alabama. He came by and gave me his card. He told he was in vaudeville. And I didn't realize who the hell he was... No, Columbia, South Carolina. You know that big guy who looked like white we used to stay at his little hotel, and that school right across the street?
Right.
Well, Jimmy Arnkey(?) came in there and introduced himself, and nobody paid him no mind, so he talked to me. And he told me who he was, and he gave me his
Barker - III-43

card. And he was on there, and it said, "Diamond Tooth Jimmy Arnkey(?)." And De Paris was telling me, talking about Jelly Roll, he said, "Yeah, Jelly Roll took Jimmy Arnkey's(?) old lady, Mabel." Mabel had a diamond in her tooth. And Ma Rainey had a whole gang of diamonds in her tooth.
Really?
Yeah. You look at the picture with Dave Nelson and...who else was in that picture... Out of Chicago? She got on diamonds. That was the current thing, you know what I mean?

So when you played the Eighty-One Theatre, man, you had to be, like, you know, good, or you didn't make more than one show. So the Eighty-One Theatre and the theatre in Baltimore, and there was one in Memphis... Man, there must have been about fifteen cities. Birmingham, Alabama. Mobile...
Mobile, yeah.

Pensacola. Dallas. Houston. Little Rock, Arkansas. Memphis. Going up... Memphis, Chicago... There was something in between. But you could play that Black circuit. And they had their stars. Some of the stars graduated and went on to the Orpheum circuit. And then ones played on the Pantages circuit and went from New York...from
Barker - III-44
Chicago to the West.
Yeah, the Whitman Sisters were out in Chicago.

The Whitman Sisters were out in Chicago, and they had Princess Weewee(?), and a little girl called Shorty. And she had kids. So after a couple of acts they had this little cat called Groundhog, who was supposed to have been the greatest dancer of all times. He come to New York and run Honeycomb and all of 'em out. Groundhog was (?). Then he disappeared and went to Boston. You never heard of him?
No.
Check on Groundhog when you get to New York.
Okay.

Baby Lawrence... He run 'em all out. But he'd been with the Whitman Sisters, and they didn't believe in paying you, so he disappeared. That's how they come in (?). He was a partner of Pops, and that's why they got Louis Williams from there...
Pops and Louis, yeah.

Pops Whitman, yeah. Because Groundhog would disappear. But Groundhog was a fantastic dancer. He's got a funny little eye. But in the dance world, everybody, Honi Coles, all of them, when they'd see Groundhog...
Barker - III-45
He's from the Gibson family, isn't he. His folks were...
His little brother got killed.
Is that so?

He had an act. He appeared in New Haven. On the train, during the War... He got in an altercation with some soldiers on the train. And his sister was a great performer. But she ended up being a maid in one of them hotels on Broadway. And she'd come and sit in Beefsteak... not Beefsteak Charlie's, a little joint next door...
Oh, C&B(?), yeah.

Yeah. And nobody don't know who she is. But Gibson introduced me to her. I'd go in and buy her a drink. I'd say, 'Why don't you go back in show business?' A little dark, brown-skinned woman, you know.
That's wild. And then, Wilbur De Paris, I didn't know their parents were in show business. They used to have a great band, though. He got up to Duke's...he played in Duke's band, didn't he?

Yeah. Well, he was... You see, like Dave... I worked with them for about three months, then I quit. Wilbur De Paris and Sidney De Paris... Wilbur De Paris was sophisticated; Sidney stayed with the people. And they had an argument in the Savoy at a rehearsal, and they had an
Barker - III-46

argument, and Wilbur went on... They almost come to blows. And then after that, everybody stopped. Simeon, myself, Don Kirkpatrick, Freddie Moore, we all sit there and listened. And they went through the whole thing. "Well, you left Mama when we needed you. We was on the road, and you left us and went to school." On and on like that.
They took you all through that, huh.

Yeah. And then he said, "Well, Mother wanted me to have an education. You was more devoted to Papa than I was. You was Mama's boy and I was Papa's boy." "But you didn't treat us right." You know, just a... They told all their business. So the mother used to... Wilbur was her first-born, I guess. I don't know, I think they have a sister, a sister in Baltimore. Cripple Slim used to go down there with Sidney (they were buddies), and spend a couple of weeks in the summer. Wilbur...
Trombone player.

His mother used to send him to schools, like go get a semester of education here or a semester there if she saved a little money. But Sidney stayed close to his Daddy, being a trumpet player, and he played the baritone and he played the bass -- he played the whole things, he used to tell me. But Wilbur would go and then come back. And Wilbur would be the well-adjusted one, and Sidney would

never get the sophisticated education that Wilbur had. So Wilbur started traveling different tracks than Sidney. Wilbur went with...what's the helluva band out of Detroit, supposed to be the best band there...
McKinney's?
No, it was before that. Leroy Smith.
Leroy Smith. He was a violin player. A little guy who leaned over...he was kind bent over with arthritis. A violin player.

Yeah, Leroy Smith. Had what was supposed to have been the greatest band out of Detroit. Before Fletcher. At one time they spoke... I got a picture here of that band. Well, Wilbur was in that band, and that was one of them bands like Chicago, the Vendome, what's his name...?
Erskine Tate.

Them kind of things, but out of Detroit. So Wilbur was that type of musician, you know, laying the parts. Sidney was more gutbucket. He ended up with Charlie Johnson and made a big name around here. Sidney DeParis, Jimmy Harrison, and June Clark that used to be with Louis...
Yeah, a trumpet player.
All of them were in that band. June lost his lip and contracted TB. So he's...you know, he talked. But Wilbur was a musician that believed no other musician should
Barker - III-48

have no money. He was the first musician that I know who said the tips belonged to him. See, the people would come to the bandstand and say, "Ten dollars, play a 'Saints' or play so-and-so." And he'd put his (?) and say, "We've got some tips." So I'd say, "Well, where is the tips money, man?" He said, "Well, I need this money for our... If we're going to get anywhere, we need this money for promotion. I've got to write people. I've got to write letters. I need this money." I said, "You know, man, no musician I've worked with them have ever taken tips." So Simeon and them allowed it... Then he didn't want you to drink. But when you play Jazz, you're with Jazz people, and they're drinking, and they're offering you a drink. See? So you have a drink. So I take a drink. So he says, "All this drinkin'; this band will never go anywhere with drunkards." So he's hitting at me, you know.

So we go to Boston, and we worked there a week. When we get paid...I can't think of the guy... Steve, who was the head of the Savoy; he runs the management. When we get paid, it's supposed to be... Payday is Sunday night, but you have to go there Monday. He gets the check, and he goes there to cash the check. So the first thing... He's just got the band and he's successful, so he's got to get a serial number from the government -- you know, the Social
Barker - III-49

Security takeout. So he went and got that, and when he come back... No... He'd taken out a hundred and a quarter. He took twenty five dollars out my money. I said, "Man, I ain't paid this much Social Security tax since I've been around." He said, "Well, Danny, I don't want to (?). I'm just keeping this in case the tax comes to that." I said, "You pay... I've got three dependents, me, my wife... And it don't come to no twenty-five dollars." So Steve came through. So I'm mad, man. He took twenty-five dollars. And I'm (?) supporting myself already. I've already sent money home, and I'm planning on maybe taking out $12, $9...
Yeah.

So I said, "Steve, how much money do you pay for two or three dependents? How much money?" He said, "Wait, I'll tell you." So he went and got that chart there. He said "Eleven dollars." I said, "Man, give me my money."
You told him to give you your money, huh, Danny?

So he paid me. He said, "Well, I don't like this. This is my band, and I don't know what the tax is." I said, "You heard what the man said." The rest of them is lookin' at me. And I said, "I quit." I look around, I couldn't find no pictures -- because you've got to write a written notice. I went in the toilet, got some toilet
Barker - III-50
paper, and I write: "As of now, here's two weeks notice. Danny Barker to Wilbur DeParis."
On toilet paper, huh?

On toilet paper. And just walked out the rehearsal, man. So you have all them kind of people... So he did a whole lot of things with... He was planning to record. So he recorded Doc Cheatham, and I made about six albums with the promise that he was going to pay them as he sold the records. And he took that money, and he gets that money... I said, "When are you going to pay us, Wilbur?" That went on for about three years. So finally, I had to bring it to the union. Because he didn't believe nobody should have no money at all. And no sense in going to him and ask him to let you have ten dollars. Like, he argued with me once(?) (?) the bandleader. "I don't have no cash."
That's wild.

So I didn't have no respect for him at all. The only bandleader in the existence of music that didn't believe a musician should have nothin'. When he takes the tips, and they allowed him to do that -- he wasn't gonna take mine.
That's unbelievable.
To be continued...
Danny Barker & Milt Hinton, May 30 1980) - (Part 4):
[BEGINS CLOSE TO THE END OF TAPE 4, SIDE B]
It's May 30, 1980, and I'm sitting here in my room in the Hyatt Hotel in New Orleans, Louisiana, continuing our chat with my dear friend, Danny Barker.
Hey, Danny, we just got through talking about one band that you played with in New York there. Who else did you play with around there?
I played with a multitude of bands.
You were with Lucky there for a while.
Yeah. With Lucky for about three years.
Lucky Millinder, that is.

Lucky Millinder. When I went to New York, which is 1930, it wasn't exactly the Depression; it really hadn't hit New York. And there was a multitude of musicians around from all over the country who congregated around the Rhythm Club. And my uncle right away said, 'Well, come around the Rhythm Club...'
[PAUSE]
So all of these musicians were around the Rhythm Club, you say.

Yes. So you went there, and you had to start from scratch. Unless you were a sensation on your instrument who could be what you call a super-duper, you just were another run-of-the-mill musician, and you had to
Barker - IV-2

start from scratch in a new town. And that is New York City, because the great musicians came from all over. There were musicians from Chicago, from St. Louis, from the Islands, and from the South, from Florida -- they were all there. There was a new pool of musicians who had come from depressed areas to New York.

So I became one of the many who came to the big city, and had to start from scratch. And at that time, you'd start playing gigs. The top gig you could get in New Orleans at that time was twenty-five dollars, and maybe thirty-five. The idea of making super money hadn't... I hadn't had a taste of that yet. The record industry was still in its virgin era of expanding, and Victor and the record companies... Columbia and Victor recorded very few people. Unless you had arrived, they didn't record you.
Now, what year was it? 1930, you said.

1930. So everything was new. Vaudeville was sort of in a rut, but there still was star musicians and performers who made the circuits, the Paramount circuit and the Loews circuit, and were going out on shows. There were some shows going to Europe. Well, there was this mad bunch of musicians, a whole lot of guys who came from various areas of the country with their bands, and the bands fizzled out in New York. King Oliver, it happened to him. It
Barker - IV-3
happened to Jelly Roll. It was happening to Fess Williams. And it was happening to the band from Detroit I called...
Leroy Smith.
Leroy Smith, he was around there, in and out. And there was... Elmer Snowden had come from Washington with Duke, and he...
He was a banjo player, wasn't he.
Yeah. For some reason, he'd left Duke. And he was around there trying. There was Danny Logan, who was trying to do something.
What did Danny Logan play?

He played trombone. He had a band, and every week he would rehearse, week after week after week, and you made the rehearsals, you went around rehearsals, and you made yourself active. And being young, you had this energy and you can do that.
The second week I was in New York, a guy approached me who had been...my Uncle Paul had introduced me to. His name was Harry White.
Your uncle was Paul Barbarin.

Yes, Paul Barbarin. This guy's name was Harry White. He had been one of the original trombone players with Duke Ellington. He'd come out of Washington. He was a member of the White Brothers Band. Eddie and three
Barker - IV-4
other brothers...
And they called him Father White, didn't they.
Yeah, Father White. So he came to me and said, 'Are you working?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Do you want to go with me to the Nest Club? I've got a job.' I said, 'Yeah.' He said, 'Okay.'

So I started two weeks after I got to New York with Harry White in the Nest Club. A six-piece band. We go to work at ten o'clock. You might tune up until eleven, or fool around, because it was somewhat of an after-hour joint. It was a famous...
[END OF TAPE 4, SIDE B]
An after-hours spot, huh?

An after-hour club. It wasn't exactly an after-hours spot. It didn't have a license. The bosses were Mal Frazier and Johnny Carey, and they were all, um, sweetie-pies... Because all they did was, a whole lot of women came through there. It must have been an assignation joint, where you send out chicks to hustle. Because they had these all these glamour, supposedly glamour women coming to...
Barker - IV-5

We were going into Fall. It was the month of October, and it's cold, beginning to get cold. I had never actually been in snow. I saw it from a train going from Chicago to New Orleans. I saw it, but I had never been in snow. I was waiting for the snow. I had bought my overcoat. It wasn't a lead sheet, because there was a difference between an overcoat and a lead sheet. They would tell you if you had one of those little flimsy coats in New York, "Hey, you'd better get rid of that... Hawk is comin' through here. You'd better get rid of that lead sheet and get you a full orchestration."
[HEARTY LAUGH]

All right. So I worked at night at the Nest Club. And you go to work at ten, you sit on the bandstand, and you look. You don't say much, because the action starts maybe around two. You went in there with the specifications and the agreement that you stayed until the last customer went out. Then you could make money. It was noted that you got tips and you could expect tips, and the entertainer split with you. It was a hustle for everybody, so you agreed to stay in there maybe until eight o'clock in the morning -- as long as they had people. That was the (?).
Do you remember any of the guys that was in that band?
Barker - IV-6
Yeah. It was...
It was probably Harry White's band.
Harry White's band. There was Cripple Smitty.
What did he play?
Glyn Pagve
He played drums. There was Glen Pack, who played alto sax, who went to Europe...
Yeah, I've heard of him.

He was disgusted in New York, he said, 'I'm going to Europe,' and he went to Europe. He never did come back. He died in Switzerland. The trumpet player was named Ted...Ted something. He had been with Leroy Smith's band. He was a legitimate trumpet player who played a little Jazz. But he was a linguist, spoke six or seven languages. He worked for the State Department. He was a very polished man, and I sat next to him... Glen Pack, him and Harry White was the three horns. Lloyd Phillips, who later played with...
Glyn Pagve
Oh yeah. He last played with Pearl Bailey.
Mmm-hmm, he was on piano.
He was with Pearl Bailey for something like twenty years, until he died.
Mmm-hmm. He was on piano. I played the banjo, and Cripple Smitty was on drums.
Barker - IV-7
Now, I had just played... Sidney De Paris used to come in and jam. Quite a few trumpet players used to come in there and jam. Bobby Stark came through there a couple of times.
He was a trumpet player, too, wasn't he.

Yeah, he was with Chick Webb. They wanted somewhere to jam and play, so Harry would put them on. Sometimes we'd go to work at ten o'clock, and see half-a-dozen musicians there with their horns. They wanted to play, and also at the same time make auditions.

Harry was a wonderful musician. He was an arranger. He arranged some things that Duke used. And he and I... He just liked me. So later on he asked me... Albert Morgan had come through and made a splash on the bass, and Pops Foster was with Luis Russell, and everybody was taking lessons from him. They couldn't get to Braud, because Braud was doubling with Duke, playing theatres and the Cotton Club. And he asked me, said, "Man, that's a helluva bass. Have they got any more down there like that?" I said, "Yeah." I said, "The boss is down there. Simon Marrero." That was Billy Marrero's son. He said, "Do you think you could get him to come up here?" I said, "Yeah, he ain't doin' nothin'." So I told Paul about it, and he and Paul got together, and they got Simon's address and sent for Simon.
Barker - IV-8
That's Paul Barbarin, your uncle.
Yeah, my uncle. So here comes Simon, with his bass. The man on the train said "New-Ark!" Simon got off and thought it was "New Yawk!"
Oh, he got off in Newark! [LAUGHING]

So we went to the railroad station, but Simon... That was a long joke for a long time around this town. Instead of him, you know, waiting... He didn't know... So he had to get another train, a local to come to New York, and it would be... He was missing. So when he got into Pennsylvania Station he called us, and we had to go down there and get him.
Yeah.

So he joined the band. It was a whole new concept. It was like me and him were swinging, and Smitty fell right in. The band was swinging like crazy with Simon. Because these people would usually use the bass drum, and here this man's playing these big, heavy notes, man, big, fat notes, and didn't say nothin'... The first day Simon come there, he said he didn't like the city, he said, "'cause all the buildings looks like hospitals."
That was the only big buildings down here, I guess.
Barker - IV-9

So... Yeah, that's right. So we fooled together... I mean, we were close together, now, and he comes to the house. He goes around to the Rhythm Club every day, because everything was centered around there. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers are in town playing some New England dates. So they got him involved in a rhythm section cutting contest. All the bass players. And Harry would have got (?) to the gig with (?). And Simon went on to play to the amazement of the people in there, because they ain't used to hearing nobody play...
That kind of bass.

....that kind of bass. There was an old man, Harry Hall, who played bass. And Tizol, Juan Tizol's uncle,, who played bass with the Latin people. And there were two or three other Latin bass players from Cuba who played a three-string bass. But there was nobody played finger bass, you know what I mean; they played the bass with the bow in their hand...
Yes.

But Simon upset the Rhythm Club. So he came back, he said... He told Paul in the evening, he said, "There's a guy who spoke to me today, whose name is McKinney. He asked me if I want to join his band and go on to Detroit." Paul said, "Do you know who McKinney is?"
Barker - IV-10
"No, I never heard of him." You know, he's down in New Orleans...
Sure!

So Paul said, "That's McKinney of McKinney's Cotton Pickers. He wants you to join the band. It would be a great thing for you to join." He said, "I don't know if I want to go to Detroit." See, his old lady was Goldie, and Goldie was a fine Creole woman, and Simon wanted to go back to Goldie. So to keep him from going back, they sent for Goldie to keep him up there. They were interested in trying to help(?) him. So he stayed.
Then we closed the joint. Harry White closed because the money was slick. And Dave Nelson, who had been rehearsing, he...
Trumpet player, right?
King Oliver's nephew.
Yeah, he's the one, King Oliver's nephew, Dave Nelson...
He wrote the "Mule Face Blues" and some other things. He was a good arranger. He was out of Chicago. And he and Jones, Richard M. Jones...
Oh, the piano player?
Yeah. All them were here...
He wrote a lot of songs.
Barker - IV-11
Yeah, he was...
He used to live right across the hall from me in Chicago.
You told me that. He was a nice, nice gentleman.
Yeah, he wound up with one leg. Did you ever ...(?)...?
I don't know, maybe diabetes or one of them things. But he was a nice fellow.
He sure was a nice man.

Richard, but they called him Mynee(?) Jones. He was one of the pioneer producers of records, and writer, and he should have had his own publishing company. But them days it was... Handy just was about the only one, Handy and...
I don't want to ...(?)..., but I think he had kind of eyes for my Mom. He lived right across the hall from me. And that made him take an interest in me. He gave me my first harmony book, man.
Yeah?
Richard M. Jones. So go on. So he was the piano player in this group?
Yeah. Well, all of them migrated from New Orleans to Chicago. Clarence Williams, Spencer Williams,
Barker - IV-12
Jelly Roll Morton, Willie Hightower...
Oh, Mr. Hightower. There was a couple of them, wasn't it?
Hmm?
Was there a couple of them Hightower brothers.
Yeah... Well, I knew of one. Him and his wife.
Right, that's right, his wife, Mrs. Hightower. They were very big in the union in Chicago, Local 208.
Yeah. They were pioneers in helping... getting into things.
Mmm-hmm.
So Simon, he plays around, and gets everybody snatching at Simon, and Simon ain't going with nobody. I have Vernon Andrade wanting him on the Renaissance.
What did Vernon Andrade play?
Vernon Andrade was a banjo player, had a great band at the Renaissance Ballroom. That was the hall where they had the great basketball games, the Renaissance basketball team.
They were like the Globetrotters.
Yeah, the Globetrotters came out of that. Abe Saperstein got his idea from their super-foolishness. Because them guys used to make fools out of legitimate
Barker - IV-13

basketball players with their all unorthodox playing.
Well, Simon is around, I'm around -- and the next thing you know, Goldie's there, and the soldiers get a bonus. And they look again... Simon's gone to New Orleans. He came back to New Orleans and died.

Well, that was Harry White. Then I lay off a couple of weeks out of the Nest Club, and Dave Nelson, he goes in there. Now, when I got in there with him... His wife is Miss Olive Burgorne(?), who had been a dancer and a singer ways years ago, had toured Russia with a Black group, she was high in show business, and yet she was relegated now to doing maid work, like a lot of old Black woman performers became maids to White stars who knew them -- and they knew show business. So they hired these women, because women knew how to keep their mouths closed and knew all the intrigue of how to keep...how to answer the phone and how to keep one Stage-Door Johnny from bumping into the husband, or... It's an intrigue thing. So they kept all these slick Black women as maids.
Maids, yeah.

And they was part of the theatre, and they kept in the background -- but they loved the Theatre. Just to be there in the footlights. That's a science to be explained in itself, about how these women, dedicated stage-
Barker - IV-14

door people, who handled show people and who were showmen, who are telling you, you know, "Don't be afraid; this is your opening night," encourage the young performers. "Just go on out there and kill 'em and slay 'em, look 'em in the eye" -- give you all that kind of encouragement. So they kept them...

Miss Olive Burgorne(?) was one of these type of women. Her and Trixie Smith, they both worked for Mae West. Mae West opened a show called A Constant Sinner with George Gavotte(?). It was a story, a racial thing, where George Gavotte played Money Johnson, a Black hustler and a pimp uptown. Mae West went up there, and there was some kind of rubbing elbows or something. But there was an implication that there was a mixture there. And the show lasted about six weeks. And Dave Nelson got the job... Well, Dave Nelson got the job to play in a cabaret scene...
[PAUSE]
Go ahead, Danny.

Dave Nelson got the job in a cabaret scene, and using a five-piece band. So we... I'm on Broadway! I didn't know nothin' about legitimate theatre. I'd say, "I'm on stage on Broadway." "Yeah, that's the legitimate theatre." That's the way they spoke of it.
You was in that? You played in that?
Barker - IV-15
Yeah. We played on the stage.
Did you ever see this guy Nicodemus, a comedian?
Yeah. He was around there.
Yeah. He finally wound up being kind of close to Mae West, didn't he.

Well, she... Nico... Yeah. Well, she...she respected performers, and she loved prizefighters, she loved wrestlers. She loved the big He-Men, those big, muscular guys. She always kept two or three bodyguards with her.
Yeah.

Well, Nicodemus, he was supposed to have been a great comedian. but he... I never seen him perform because he didn't want to talk. And I couldn't... It was a mystery to me how he survived, how he made money to live.
Well, he was on the type of...the Stepin' Fetchit type of thing.
Yeah, one of them things. Yeah, a slow-talking, drawlin', Southern...
Yes.
...lazy, indifferent Black.
Mmm!
And he portrayed that. Well, they were getting out the market from that, of portraying these things
Barker - IV-16
in a way. And even though he was considered... He made a movie, and that gave him his acclaim. But after that, he never done too much.
So what happened with that? So you got in this show What was the name of that show?

The Constant Sinner. So we had a rehearsal in the day, and after the first week we go to the Brighton Theatre in Brighton Beach -- that's near Coney Island. That's where the show opened for the tryout, and then we go to Atlantic City for a week.
And at the rehearsal in...in the dress rehearsal in Atlantic City, we're all on the stage after the rehearsal, and the...
[PAUSE]
On stage after the rehearsal, and the stage manager did what?
The stage director.
Oh, I see.
He was an old Southerner, a middle-aged man -- to me he looked old. He had made a remark. He told somebody 'Get all the darkies together.'
A White guy.
Yeah. He was the stage manager. And Olive Burgorne(?) heard him. And she was a woman that, you know,
Barker - IV-17

she don't go for nothin'. So she told Mae West, Olive said, "Well, I ain't gonna call 'em and I ain't gonna do nothin' until he apologizes." That's what she told Mae West. And Mae West came out of her dressing room and called him, and explained to him that his remarks about the Darkies... "There are no darkies here." Well, he laughed and he said, "Well, I didn't mean no harm." I thought it was a familiar thing that you say. Black people don't get angry about them kinds of things." She said, "Well, we do get angry up here, and don't use that remark no more." And she said, "You owe these people an apology." So he said, "I'll apologize. I'm very sorry." And he apologized.
All right. So she looked around at me. She said, "You stay after the show. I want to see you." So Rudy Toone(?) was on the show, and he was a sharpie. Mae West told me that...
What did Rudy do?
Rudy was an actor, and he was the go-between between...Mae West's connection from Uptown-Downtown. He was a dandy, in other words.
Yeah.
In the play, he was the contact man for Mae West.
He was Black?
Barker - IV-18

Yeah, he was handsome. You know Rudy Toone(?). He wrote...what's that thing..."One Mint Julep." You'd see him down on Broadway. They killed him, they busted his brains out where Minton's place is. He lived on that block.
Oh, I never...
Well, Rudy Toone(?). You'd know him if you ever see him, see a picture of him.

So Rudy Toones, he said, "Man, you got it made, boy." Mae West done went for you like a ton of bricks." So I waited and I went to her dressing room after, when she got through. So Miss Burgorne(?) said, "Miss West is ready to speak to you." So I went in the room. She said, "I've never noticed you on the show before." I said, "Well, I've been here, Miss West." She said, "Yeah. Well, I've got an extra part for you in the show. I wish you would consider it." I said, "Doing what?" She said, "Have you ever done any acting?" I said, "No." She said, "It's very simple." I want a punch line for my show. I want to get a wonderful laugh."

She said, "You know the scene where everybody..." It's a prize-fighting scene. It's in the front of an arena, the opening gate, where people pay to go to the ticket box and go in. And it's happy. Everybody is going to the
Barker - IV-19
championship fight. She makes her entrance, and she goes in there with Money Johnson on her arm.

So this scene, how they did that, everybody rotated. They'd go on stage, run back, put on another hat, kept coming around, and it looked like a whole lot of people going in, see. So she said, "For the last scene, I want you... When you come on, you do this." Just like a...
Like a fairy.
Yeah.
Like a gay guy.

DANNY BARKER: Yeah, like a fairy. "See, when you go in there and close that scene, that will be a terrific laugh." I said, "Well, I don't know about doing that." "You see, I'll show you. Hold your hand like this. Now, snap your fingers, see." [SNAPS] I said, "I'll think about it." She said, "Think about it."

So I had to go back there, and the cats was waitin'? Said, "What did she say?" I said, "She wants me to act like a morphodyte." I said "Morphodyte." That's the word... In New Orleans, we said "Morphodyte." "Morphodice."
For a gay, for a gay guy.
DANNY BARKER: Yeah. So they said, "Go on, man, that's a good chance. You'll get maybe a hundred dollars more, man. You'll be an actor." Slick Jones said... I mean, Smitty
Barker - IV-20
said, 'Man, I wouldn't play no part like that.'
Smitty? Now, who's Smitty?
The drummer.
Oh yeah.

He said, 'Man, I wouldn't play no part like that. In case your people come up to see you on the stage and you're out there swishin' like some woman, man.' He said, 'Man, I wouldn't do that.' He says, 'Suppose your relatives come.' They said, 'Oh, man, relatives. This is the stage.' They had a big argument. 'This is the stage. He's just an actor. You're just portraying a character. You ain't...' Smitty said, 'I wouldn't care what it is.' He said, 'I'd be a lover, but I ain't gonna be no goddamn morphodyte on the stage.'

So Miss Burgorne(?) said, 'Did you come to the decision, Danny?' I said, 'No, Miss Burgorne(?), I ain't gonna play that part.' She said, 'Oh, that was the chance for you. You don't get a chance but once in a lifetime. You could be in the Theatre.' So that killed that.

So the show lasted what, two weeks on the road and two weeks on Broadway. Then it closed, because they had bad reviews. That was one of the first racial... And Mae West had been on Broadway two or three times before. All her shows were way ahead of their time, controversial. And one
Barker - IV-21
time they raided the whole show, took all the actors to jail, because they were doing something on the stage... We have to check that out.

All right, in six months, I had been in the Nest Club, the Rhythm Club, I'd been on Broadway -- and I'm back in the Nest Club again. And up over the Nest Club, Smitty... No, Slick Jones is now working there....
Slick Jones was a drummer, too.
A drummer who worked with Fats Waller. And Slick Jones wife was a nice performer. Can't think of her name now. Well, we're in this band, Dave Nelson's band. Lawrence Phillips is in this band, too.
Pianist.
Yeah. So we get to be tight, and I'm beginning to understand what great piano playing is all about.
So upstairs of the Nest Club on the street level... The Nest Club later became Dickie Wells' club.
Where is that? Give me the location.
That's 133rd near Seventh Avenue, between Seventh and Lenox, but it's near Seventh Avenue. That's the Nest Club.
It was in the basement, huh.
Barker - IV-22

It was in the basement. Later it was Dickie Wells' club. On the ground floor, there was another club overhead called The Mad House. That's the first place I saw Billie Holiday. And opposite the Nest, facing the Nest was Pa's(?) and Jerry's, which is the club where Willie Smith, the Lion, worked for many years.
The pianist.

Yeah. Next door to that was Tillie's Chicken Shack, where they had the fried chicken and the candied yams and the cornbread -- that was a big thing in New York during that period. Tillie's Chicken Shack. A couple of doors from there was a joint called Mexico's, served like Mexican food, tamales and tacos and.... It was a guy who was half-Black and half-Mexican. I met him -- Mexico. He was a hustler and he... All them people who owned them places were night people.

And down the street were about three or four five joints, what they called juice joints. You'd go down in the basement, knock on the door, the guy would see you (or the woman), and they'd bring you in. And when you go in there, after the smoke clears, you can see maybe two dozen people sitting there, drinkin', smokin', tellin' ghost stories or something, telling lies and just sitting around.
All these joints, you went from one to another....
Barker - IV-23
On 133rd Street.

133rd Street. That was like the beginning of... 52nd Street happened right after that. The other thing, on 33rd Street they did not have no marquee outside. It was strictly you know the joint and you went in. On 52nd Street there was...
It was like brownstones, old brownstones, right?
That's right. Old brownstones.
Buildings.

Yeah. And the Nest Club was a regular little building. It looked like it had been a store or something. I mean, the Mad House overhead, because it was... Or maybe it was ripped out. I can't actually figure the construction now.

But that was a wild street. Smitty and I used to come upstairs some mornings... We'd go in the Nest Club. When we'd have a break, then we'd come upstairs and go in the Mad House, and we would buy Chicken Cock Whiskey, which was whiskey that came in a can.
Really?
Yeah. You'd get a pint of whiskey, a regular pint bottle...
In a can.
Barker - IV-24

It came in a can. And it came in quart cans, too. Like an olive can, like an oblong, square, tall... Just like you'd pack whiskey, but with a can. Now, the reason for that was they used to make this Chicken Cock Whiskey in Canada, and when the rum-runners would chase the guys... Owney Madden and them people that used to run whiskey. They talk about it now, if you mention his name...
Sure.

They made their money, the racketeers, running whiskey across the Hudson River or some bay up there which connected the United States with Canada. And when the Coast Guard would overtake them, they would have these cans, not in cases, but in a big old thing like a net. And they just would throw it overboard, and the whiskey wouldn't sink. And later on, while the Coast Guard was chasing that boat, this other boat comes behind it to pick up the whiskey. Because they wouldn't worry about the whiskey so much as to catch the guys who were pushing it. So that was the reason why the cans...

Ross told me that, Ross who was a great ballplayer with the Black Elite Giants, which preceded the Black Yankees. One of the great Black ballplayers. He was a great ballplayer. He never did make the Big Leagues, because there was no Blacks in the Big Leagues. And he was the
Barker - IV-25
doorman, see, so he...
The doorman where?

At the Nest Club. See, he would stand up outside, and... I saw him for quite a few years out there, rain or snow. In the wintertime he had this big, long coat like them doormen have in front of the Waldorf Astoria and in them other clubs. He would just stand out there, and lead the people in.

Now, they had a secret. In the Nest Club, nobody would be down there. We'd be just sitting down and waiting for a live one to come. Johnny Carey and Mal Frazier would have some women, they'd be talkin' to some hustlers, all sleazy looking people, lookin' real wise -- night people. And Ross would be upstairs. And they had a bell up there. So when somebody got out of a cab or a live one would come in a party of two or four, Ross would press the button. When he pressed that button, ZING-ZING-ZING-ZING, that means that some live one's coming. And the band would strike up. Right away the piano player, whoever's got a horn... They ain't waitin' for the whole band. Just start playing. That means you run and you'd get something, somebody would be coming out of the men's room, we're sitting down talking -- you know, you're relaxed. But you jump up and you start this music.
Barker - IV-26

And they had about five or six entertainers all the time. One time when I was there with Harry White, they had Mamie Smith, Clara Smith... They weren't sisters, because they mentioned it, both of them. "She ain't no sister of mine," Clara said, and Mamie said, "God, she ain't no sister of mine." That's all the Smith sisters. There was Mamie Smith, Clara Smith, and later, in about two or three weeks, Trixie Smith, who worked with Miss Bargorne for Mae West. All those were Blues singers. There was Margie Sith(?). Mattie Hite later, who was... Mattie Hite was considered the greatest entertainer, Black entertainer, cabaret entertainer of all of them.
Who was this?

Mattie Hite. Everybody went to see Mattie Hite. She sang a song, "Stop It Joe." It was a fast thing. [SNAPS FINGERS] "Stop it, Joe." [SINGS, SNAPS] "Stop it, Joe." It was a fast thing she did. And she went from table to table, see. And she'd pick up the money, you know. They'd put it on the edge of the table with the bottle, you know, the Coca-Cola bottle. But she wouldn't do that. She said, "Give me that money. I ain't puttin' an act for nobody." And she was a dynamic woman, and highly respected. They'd say, "Mattie Hite's coming to work, Mattie Hite's coming to work." All them other big-time entertainers for
Barker - IV-27
some reason acknowledged that Mattie Hite was the greatest. Now, you should check on some more performers later about Mattie Hite.
All right. Now, there was Margie Sith(?). Later on there was Mary Stafford. You'll see her name on some records. She made a few records during that time.
Margie Sith(?) was a great big woman, looked something Lizzie (?), a big buxom woman, like you see them opera singers, with a little waist and... And at that time I was...
Big breasts, yeah.

Yeah. Double-breasted chick. Heh. Well, they had what you call ups. Now, they had this little cat, Jazzbo. You'll see a picture in magazine...in a book of a cabaret scene. I think Tiny Parham is in it in a magazine, one of them history books, of a revue in either the Grand Terrace or the Royal Garden. And there's a little-bitty guy there, Jazzbo, a great entertainer. He could equally sing with two voices, a soprano like a woman, then turn and sing like a baritone, like a man.
Oh yes, yes. I remember that.
There was two. There was another one called Jerry Hall. They were little stunted guys, but they had this great talent.
Barker - IV-28

Well, they had what you'd call ups, one after another one, once the people could get a corps of people in there, maybe ten or fifteen people, they'd put on a show. And there would be one after another. They'd come up, and they'd do... They'd make the rounds with the hustle. They went from table to table. They lingered if the people encouraged them. If they didn't, if the people acted indifferent to them, then they went on to the next table. And you could tell if they could hold an audience. Because when Mattie Hite or Clara Smith hit the floor...

Clara Smith was a defiant little dark woman. She sang the low-down Blues. There was Clara, and Mamie and Bessie, that trio. Trixie... There was just a whole slew of Smith sisters. As long as you had name Smith, you could put that on the marquee... I don't know if I mentioned it before. They just put that big name of Smith, and people took it for granted that it was...
Old Perry Bradford handled them for a while, didn't he.
Perry Bradford recorded the first Blues singer, which was Mamie...
The first Black woman on record.
Yeah. He went from record company to record company (there wasn't but four of them then), and nobody
Barker - IV-29

would accept it. Finally, one of the guys broke through and let him record, and they recorded his tune, "The Crazy Blues." And that swept the country.. And he was a smart... He was a relentless little man. I mean, there was no such thing as trying to tell him "That can't be done."
Yeah, he stayed right with it.
Up until the last.
Right to the end. I was with him when he died, Danny. He was that way when he died!
I understood you was responsible for burying him. You don't mention that...
Yeah, that's true. Well, we got him a place and kept our eye on it. But he was...
[END OF TAPE 5, SIDE A]
...overshadowed the rest of them. Mamie, the last I seen her, she was a tired old lady around New York.
Didn't we do something with this girl Victoria Spivey? Didn't you and I do something with her once?
Yes.
We did a record date with her...
No, I wasn't on that one. But Victoria Spivey was down in Arkansas and Texas, and she did a thing
Barker - IV-30

called "Mean Black Snake Blues." "Mean black snake's been sucking my (?) down." And that was a terrific hit, and that just threw her up to the top. But she didn't follow up. And she had a sister called Honey...Honey...Honey Somethin'... Sweet Pea Spivey.
Oh yeah?

Yeah. Victoria Spivey and Sweet Pea Spivey, two sisters. They came out of Arkansas, or maybe St. Louis. And they made quite a name for themselves -- moreso Victoria. And she came around New York, came around New York in her later years. Her and Leonard Kunstadt(?), they had a joint record company together, tried to promote their own records. But time had marched on.
While we're talking about, let's digress a little bit. We were talking about this club where you worked, the Nest, and how you had what you call ups.
Yes.
But just to name a few of them singers that was around during that time. Do you remember May Alix out of Chicago?
Yes.
Good-lookin'...
Well, at that time May Alix was starring in the Cotton Club. They brought May Alix... That's why she
Barker - IV-31
was such a star, she had a beautiful body...
Yes, she sure did!
And she looked like a White girl.
She sure did.
And they starred her in the Cotton Club.
She had pretty legs...
Yes. She made the thing, "Everybody Loves My Baby" or "I Want a Big Butter and Egg Man." She sang that with Louis Armstrong on that record. That was her theme. "I want a butter-and-egg man."
She did? She sang that on the record?
Yeah. That's May Alix. And she hit...she... At the Regal. She starred at the Regal Theatre with Louis Armstrong. She was a superstar in Chicago.
Mmm-hmm.

Her father was a waiter down at the Sherman, a little Black and a little Italian. I used to ask him how was May. "She's doing pretty good." She was a barmaid up at one of them popular bars in Chicago on the South Side. There's two guys that had a club; I can't think of their names.
They had a club?
Yes. It wasn't a big-name club. It was a little like a lounge. Dave...
Barker - IV-32
Simmons Lounge at DuSable and Oakley Avenue?
No, no. It was before that. About that time. A little earlier than that.
Squares? Squares over on 63rd Street?
Yeah.
That's where it was, Squares, down on 63rd Street.

Yes. It was the type of bar where the barmaid made a whole lot of tips, just being there. The people would go there to see her, to talk to her. Because that's the way they idolized her. Chicago was a town where you still could live on your reputation. People still accepted... It's a notoriety town, word-of-mouth. "So-and-so is at such-and-such a place," and you went there, and you paid homage to whoever it was.

Well, I was out at the Nest Club. And upstairs over the Nest Club was the Mad House. And Roscoe, who was a hustler, a young, handsome hustler, he owned this joint. That was the first time I saw Billie Holiday. We went in there, me and Smitty, and we sat down. A girl come out the back, this fine-looking, brownskin girl, very defiant, and she starts bitchin' with some guys to give her some money. It seemed like she had served some love or something in there... You know, we don't want to mention the ..(?).., we
Barker - IV-33

don't want to talk about people. But she wanted her money. And they were trying to (?) her because she's a woman. And she said she wouldn't leave there until they gave her all her money. And they gave her her money, and as she passed she said some cuss-words and she went out.

Well, the door was open. I seen she went across the street to... You had to look at her twice because she was such a fine young girl, and to see that... You know, to hear her involved in something like that... So later on I go across to Pa and Jerry's, because they was tellin' me about the Lion, and I went over there and I seen her in there. And she was waiting tables, and later on she sang. So there was... Tommy Dorsey, Jimmy Dorsey, Bert Lom, Paul Whiteman, everybody, all the White musicians used to go to Pa and Jerry's in the morning to get that chicken that they served, just like at Tillie's next door.

And they had this upstairs, too, but it was a little crowded place, and it would get real smoky quick. And there was Willie Smith, the Lion, playing piano, playing his versions that was ahead of time. Like his things, "Morning Air" and all them pretty things he'd play at intermission, was constructed in a manner that it's not the run-of-the-mill Irving Berlin song. This thing is all intricate, and you don't even sit down with him if you don't know what
Barker - IV-34
you're doing. I mean, this man is a fantastic musician.
He was very hip.
Yeah. And people don't know... As of today he's done things. He's got about five or six albums out. And if you get them albums, you can dig the inventions he was doing, playing the piano...
Duke Ellington worshipped him.
Oh, they all went there to get their lessons. And they'd sing ...[SINGS REFRAIN]...
The modulations, yeah.

Yeah, that turnaround you hear. Tommy Dorsey used it in a lot of his records. Dig it, that's Willie Smith, the Lion. For a time, a lot of arrangers were using that quick...the quick turnaround. [SINGS REFRAIN] It will strike you. Your ears got to... Because you've got to know whether you're pressing all the right ones!...chords...

Well, the Lion's in there. My Uncle Paul had introduced me to Willie Smith, the Lion -- Paul Barbarin. He introduced me to him. He said, "This is the mighty Lion." There was the Lion on the corner; there was Jelly Roll looking at the Lion like he was a lamb. Jelly said, "Ah, he's a good piano player, but he's Classical. He ain't playing no Jazz." It was one of the things.
Barker - IV-35

So I was at the Mad House. I told you about that Chicken Cock whiskey... So there I saw Billie for the first time. I never got to know Billie personally, because I had been involved with young ladies who knew Billie and I'd hear about Billie, and...um, from then on, she went on. But Billie always knew the right people. In fact, she knew too many right people. She knew the right people, the wrong people, and she always had a group of people with her, because she was a fascinating young lady.

You'd see Billie with maybe three Mexicans one night. Tomorrow you'd see her with some Chinese. Some cat from Georgia somewhere. You'd see her with some... Always with some people with them dark glasses. Later on you wouldn't see her with a man. You'd always see her with a dog. The last dog she had, his name was Mister. Yeah, Mister. She used to go to Creole Pete's Restaurant with Mister, and sit with Mister at a table, and if you were half-drunk and you looked over there, you would think it was some little midget or something sitting over there.
Creole Pete just passed recently, didn't he.
Yeah.
Yeah, I'm sorry to hear that. He was such a nice man.
Yeah. His boy gave him a hard time.
Barker - IV-36
Yeah, too bad.
He was a Globetrotter, his son.
Yeah...

Billie used to go into Creole Pete's and eat, and she'd order ham-and-eggs, and she'd order hash-brown potatoes for her dog. And the dog would sit there, and she'd eat and feed the dog, and both of them eating out of spoons. Because she loved that dog. People would come in there and they'd give Pete hell. They'd say, "Well, goddamn, we're not eating that food off them plates, and no way we're eatin' behind no dog." But that was a ritual to see Billie, you know. Because the dog would be sitting up there... You know how a boxer dog is. He's sitting down, and if you look, it looks like...
A little fellow sitting over there or something.

[LAUGHS] Yeah. So they made her stop or get paper plates to feed that dog in. "I don't care who it is, Billie or... Man, I ain't gonna in here no more." A lot of people said that. Because she'd sit there feeding him, "All right, Mister, come on now, Mister, open your mouth." [LAUGHS]
That's sure unusual. So let's go ahead and try to get to some of the bands that you worked with.
Barker - IV-37

Yeah, all right. So there's bands all around. There was a whole lot of dancing school bands. New York must have had about fifteen dancing schools. There was three of them on 125th Street, there was about four of them on 57th Street, and along Eighth Avenue between 56th down to around 14th Street, was dancing schools. And you had all these dancing schools, and they had bands in them. The bands had been in there, like the Orchid, on Broadway and...where Father Duffy's at. Is that 46th Street?
48th Street...
46th Street.
Yeah. Tango Palace is still there, right across from the Cotton Club. It's still there. That's over McGuinness's. You know where McGuinness was, at 48th and Broadway?
Yeah.
Well, the Tango Palace. That's an old one.
Yeah, but two blocks down.
Oh, 46th Street. That's the Gaiety(?) Building now.

I think it was then. They had this guy who had been there so long... Well, he couldn't play piano no more, and his boss just kept him, and he directed -- and he couldn't sit down no more, some kind of... But he had been a
Barker - IV-38

legend there. He's been there about thirty-some years. But I used to play with him. And in the morning you'd see all these musicians getting on the subway coming uptown, going from dancing schools and nightclubs and cabarets.
You remember a great trumpet player named Gus Aikens used to work in one of them.

Yeah, I remember Gus Aikens. Well, Gus Aikens came out of Jenkins Orphanage with Jabbo. He was a good player. But he lost his lip. I gave him what I think was probably his last job, a little job I had on 110th Street. He came in and he couldn't get his lip up. But then he'd take a drink, and then nothing happened. Then he'd stand on the bandstand all night and apologize. The boss came up to me and said, 'He's a nice guy. He can't play?'
He was a good player at one time.
Oh yeah, he one of the tops, you know. And his brother, the trombone player...
Was that his brother...
Yeah. He was Juice Aikens or something. Well, you'd see all these people. You'd see legends around. Now, at the Amsterdam Club, you'd see all them guys that worked the theatre. Pike Davis...
Trumpet player.
Barker - IV-39
Yeah. And I was fortunate enough to see Johnny Dunn just before he went to Europe.
Trumpet player.
Yeah. Saw him. He was a tall man. Didn't have much to say, only that he was... He would make this great announcement: "I am the King." He was the King trumpet player....
Well, you had to sell yourself in those days. Everybody did. Bill Robinson. Jelly Roll.
Well, that was it. They didn't have no press agents. You had to be your own press agent. That's what people don't understand about Night People. They'll accept with that Night People.
You've got to live up to it!
You had Bill Bottoms. All them kind of names. Bill Bottoms...
That was a Chicago cat. He had a cabaret out in...
Yeah!
What was the name of that (?) in Chicago?
Yeah, but he owned the Royal...not the Royal Garden... Yeah, the Royal Garden.
He did?
Barker - IV-40
Yeah, Bill Bottoms was the manager of the Royal Garden. And that little-bitty guy, what's his name...Jones -- King Jones. "La-deez on gentlemen!" You know Little King Jones, the MC?
Yeah.
You've got to remember him.
Yeah, I remember him.

King Jones used to announce King Oliver and Freddie Keppard, who at one period they both played in the band together. He said, "Two kings on one throne. First time you ever seen that, la-deez on..." Paul used to laugh. He said, "La-deez on gentleman." And these ladies were sitting on (?), grabbing his head. He used to do that every night. Yeah, I saw him. And later on, he was around the Savoy; he had Something with King Jones.
Right. I remember him.
He was a legend.
Sure.
Yeah, King Jones was the first MC. As Paul said, he was the MC that they had that would out on the stage and announce with emphasis. Well, I had the pleasure of meeting him, you know.
But yeah, you had like Bill Bottoms, and the people up in Buffalo -- Ann Montgomery...
Barker - IV-41
Montgomery, yeah. They...
...and her husband. Yeah, they had two... They ran everything in Buffalo.
Yeah, they had a nightclub up there.
And the Cole Brothers. All them people was Night...
The Cole Brothers. That was in Cincinnati, wasn't it?

No. One of them was in Cincinnati and one was in Baltimore. There was a chain of them brothers. They was all hotel owners. And one had the... The Vendome in Buffalo, that was the Cole Brothers. And then I went through there with that little girl...
