Yeah, we were stuck, Black guys; we were stuck. We had to stay in the hotels, because we couldn't stay in the White hotels. And they treated us like a dog. Wouldn't clean up the rooms or nothin', boy. They sure gave us... You remember those hotels we used to stay at in the South?

Yeah, sure. They didn't care nothin' about nobody, and (?)you'd pay them(?). But they had a group of musicians that would go through and ransack a hotel. They would do so many ungodly things. I mean...
Barker - IV-42

Yeah, anyway each town had these people with these names, and they were Night People. And they'd talk different from day people. Now, Jelly Roll would stand on the corner, like I mentioned before, and talk to a bunch of day people, a bunch of cats who'd come off the plantation in Trinidad or something, and they'd come to New York and you'd see them with their little hats they had on, and other cats out of Georgia -- people that had nothing to do with show business. But they'd come around because of the excitement around musicians and show... And they'd stand up there, and Jelly Roll was lecturing them. See, half of them don't know what Jelly's talking about.

And Jelly's signifying, saying "Yeah, I did this and I did that." And he opens his mouth, and he's got that diamond in his tooth, and they're looking at that: "Watch when he's opening his mouth? You can see his diamond." They should have asked permission or paid, said, "Let me see your diamond" or did one of them things. But they had never seen no man stand on a corner like that, talking with his sleeves rolled up, with them nice, pretty shirts on and good clothes. Of course, he was a little dated, you know. But he was class.
Yeah. He had a new car.
Barker - IV-43

Yeah. And he believed in himself. And that's what it took in them days. You had to believe in yourself. Just like me to survive in New York. I didn't say nothing, but I used to say to myself, 'Goddamn, they ain't gonna to starve me, hell or high water.' That's the attitude you had. If you didn't...
Well, remember, you saved me there in New York. You took me around with you...

Well, you make the big ones and the small ones. Just like today in New Orleans, right now today, I'll play a little cheap gig and I'll play a big one. But I go on just to keep active. Because you keep sharp on your instrument; whatever you're doing, you're sharp. If you're going to lay around and wait for the big one, the big one might come next year. And in the meantime, you're dependent on somebody to help you over the times. So you just have to determine to exist, until you drop dead. But if you sit around and mope, 'I can't do this and I can't do that...' I played with all kinds of people in New York. Great artists.

After the Nest Club, I went with Tommy Jones. We went over and played at a little club for about a week, across the river in West New York, called The Silver Grill, which was run by racketeers, the West Side Mob -- and stayed over there. And one night when we went to work, they said, 'The
Barker - IV-44
club is closed." They had trouble with the police. We come back with no salary, and we'd worked almost a week.
From there I go in the Fordham Club up in the Bronx. It was college kids -- a different atmosphere of people altogether.
And between that, I worked what you call floating dice games.
What is that?

That's Italian racketeers, Spanish racketeers, they have floating dice games. They gamble like crazy. They don't stay in one spot. They'll rent an apartment like on the fourth or fifth or sixth floor, and they stake it out, and... The real estate, they've got a deal with the guy. And they come up over there overnight before the police can detect it. They've this dice game. These guys come there loaded with money, and be shooting high stakes, thousands of dollars shooting dice. And they lose, and they come out arguing. And they're borrowing money. You see them transacting money like at the stockyards. You know like you see in Guys and Dolls? The stock is going up and down...
Yeah.
That was a furious dice game. Guys from Brooklyn, from the Bronx and New Jersey, they're shooting
Barker - IV-45
dice. And we were over there playing music with a trio or duo.

I played with guys like Bill...I can't think of Bill's name right... Bill Douglas, played bass. He fists the bass. He never played a note on the bass yet. He just fists the bass and plays and smiles. And some of them Italians know music; they know that he ain't playin' nothin'. But they like him for his gayness(?). See, racketeers love you for your gayness. And they'd say, "Go and play us a solo, Bill." And he's just fistin' the bass. The bass ain't even in tune. And I'm playing. Now, to conquer him, I say, "Now, imagine he is a tom-tom. Don't wait for no note out of him." This is what it sounded like. [SINGS, HITS TABLE IN FOUR] Same thing on either string.

Curly Russell... We were working a joint in the Bronx. Curly Russell came over and looked at me on the stand with Bill. There was two of us playing this little joint. The Italians love him. Over there is a big old crate of lamb heads. First time I've seen it. This is real mafia, in the Bronx. Lamb skull. You know the skulls?
Yeah.
They were going to boil the brains. It's an Italian delicacy, the Sicilians. They boil these brains and they eat that. That's the real Cosa Nostra. So I seen all
Barker - IV-46
these lamb heads fresh, and they're going to boil that later in the morning and have this Italian feast. That's a delicacy.

So Curly Russell is in front of me... It's a nice little cabaret. We're on the side in a trunk(?) in the back -- a dive. Me and Bill are playing for this game they've got going back over there. So Curly Russell came and looked... I never knew Curly personally. Never was introduced. I've seen him, rubbed elbows with him, but never to speak to him. He never searched me out and I never searched him out. But he came to the stand, he looked at me, I looked at him. And he looked at Bill, like, in amazement. And I'm playing [SINGS] "Heart of my heart/I love that melody/Heart of my heart/Brings back fond memories./When we were kids on the corner of the square..." That's a gangster tune.
Yeah.

"We were rough and ready guys,/But oh, how we could harmonize./Heart of my heart..." And Bill's just hitting the same note, and just looking at his partner, proud like he's just... You know, like he's playing the right notes. He ain't playing nothin'. And he told me, he says, "You sound great, Danny. I ain't playin' nothin'" Some nights I got... "Man, I'm disgusted. Don't come get me
Barker - IV-47

ny more." He said, "I'm there, letting you make a living." So Curly Russell and I looked at him in amazement and he asked him, "Who was your teacher, man?" "Teacher?" he said. "I taught myself. Just I taught myself." That's what Bill told Curly Russell. If you ever see Curly Russell, you ask him about this bass player in the Bronx, in the joint... Curly walked away. Because he had a modern trio out there that was cookin'; a quartet, I think, with horns. He just walked away and shook his head. And he came back later and looked, because he wasn't sure what he saw. And Bill was doing...
The same thing!

I was doing "St. James Infirmary," and Bill was playing nothing. I could get high with Bill, see. See, he gave us all the whiskey we'd want. One time I said, "Brother, I'm finished. I'm tired. I don't want to work with you any more. You get you somebody else." No, he would tell me, when we were coming back from a gig(?), "See the money you're making with me? You see, I'm making it possible for you to make a living." He started insulting me. "Now, we've made some money together. Now, if you stick with me, I will keep you in money..." Drinkin' and braggin'! "I'll keep you in money." He was drunk; that night he'd had a few drinks.
Barker - IV-48

And we'd up all up in the Bronx, you know, them clovers and them highways, all going around. I said, "Man, let's go home." He said, "No, let's let the air blow on us. Let's scratch this out." He wanted to speak. He didn't want to go home. He was lonesome. "You see, if you stick with me, we will go anywhere in the world. You and I is a wonderful combination." I said, "Man, I don't want to hear that. Man, just bring me home." And he was zig-zagging... I said, "Man, let out of this goddamn car." Way up in the Bronx somewhere, up in an exclusive section, up where all them mansions and all that, driving..." I said, "Man, let's go on home." "Man," I said, when we... He provoked so, when I get home, I said, "Don't you never call me no more, nor never come here, nor ask my wife if I'm home or nothin'. Don't call me no more!" Slammed the goddamn door and walked in the house. Be mad, man.

That night, around seven o'clock, Lu said, "Bill Douglas called. He done called here three times. And he asked me to talk to you, because he was drunk, he didn't realize what he was saying this morning." I said, "No, I ain't doing it." Then he gets, like...what's that boy, that guitar player around...
Smitty?
Barker - IV-49
No, he used to be around Beefsteak Charlie's. Lucky Fowler.
Lucky Fowler!

Yeah, he's getting Lucky Fowler. He got Lucky Fowler. And Lucky Fowler played a whole lot of guitar, see. And Lucky Fowler could sing and entertain. And ...(?)... couldn't get Lucky. Lucky threatened to kill him. When Lucky found out what he was doing with that bass, Lucky threatened to kill him. And they fell out.

He fell out with the guitar players. He comes back to me and he begged me... Comes to my house and begged me. "Man, forgive me. Let's go and make this little money. These are some nice people. These are some racketeer friends of mine up in the Bronx. If you was to meet me tonight at eleven o'clock, man, we'd go up there and make this money. You don't even have to do nothin'; you know how easy I work. Let's just go in there and cooperate like two Black people, mann. Let's try to get somewhere in this world." He gave me all this... [LAUGHS] "Let's go up there and make this money."

I said, "Okay, I'm going to do it. But don't give me this... Just get me home in the morning, man."

We go up in the Bronx, and we go up to a lounge way up in the East Bronx. And it's one of them lounges, looked
Barker - IV-50

just like the lounge (I think that must have been it) that they did with The Godfather. There's a restaurant on the side and the lounge. It's a Sicilian joint if there ever was one. And we go on in there in the back, another room that has a floating dice game in there. I say "floating"... They moved, them people, because the Police... And they don't want other racketeers to know where they are to get robbed, with them real bad cats, see. And we played there.

Then he said, "I've got another one." And we go to another place. And we parked in front of a house. And we parked in front of a house, and there is an apartment in another building, another (?). And we wait. I said, "Man, I'm scared up in this dark neighborhood. Man, the (?) people looking at some Negroes up in this quiet neighborhood." He said, "I'm doing what the people told me to do." I said, "What people?" He said, "I was here today. The man showed me just how to come in the place. Do you understand?" Leave it to me. I know what I'm doing.

A police car comes. The police car comes and they look. Then they stopped even with us, and they looked us in the face and we looked them in the face. I was (?)... He said, "Don't worry about them son-of-a-bitches. They know what we're doing. They're just checking us out." "I said, "Okay." Them guys leave. At a certain time on the dot he
Barker - IV-51

said, "Okay," got in the back and grabbed his bass, "get your guitar and let's go." He slammed the door, and he went right to the gate, and right at the gate there was a guy. The guy opened the gate, and we went in.
Right on time.

Yeah, right on time. Then we went in, went in the back, and there in the back, man, chicks in there, fast chicks, and them cats are shootin' dice like crazy -- the whole scene. Then we go in, and they go, "Hey, Billy, daddy. Hey, Billy the Dag. Yeah, Bill, how you doin', Billy?" He says, "How you doin', Salvatore, how you doin', Dominick" -- all that. He went right along with them. We'd go in the back, and the man's saying, "Give-a Bill-a drink. Get him..." I don't know what... He had something with them people. They loved him. He still must be doing it!
That's great.

We go in the back, and we sit back there: [SINGS] "(?) Marie, (?) Marie..." And he sings it wrong, and they look at him. And they help him. "No, Billy, that's not it." [SINGS REFRAIN]...whatever that is. And he says, "You're right, Sal. Well, excuse me. I'm getting old, and I kind of forget" -- something, you know. But they loved him, man. We'd eat that artichoke, and we'd get that spaghetti that comes in big old tub -- a tub of spaghetti
Barker - IV-52
and meatballs.
[COUGHS, MOVES AWAY, COMES BACK...]
So we worked these joints...

You know, that Lucky Fowler was a weird guy. He would come out of Beefsteak Charlie's. I never did know what he did. I knew he played guitar. But he always had lots of money, he always had the finest cameras, and I never knew...
See, I gave him the break. I gave him the break. He was going backwards.
Yeah?
And he'd be around there, and he wouldn't be doing nothin'. At the Gaslight Club...
Right!

A guy called me, Milt Mackler(?), who was a friend of mine, who I used to go in the Village and hang out with -- a White boy. He was a friend of the guy that owned the Gaslight Club, the manager. I can't think of that man's name. He said, "Danny, I've got a good job for you." I said, "What is that?" Milt said, "At the Gaslight Club." "Well, I'm working." I didn't know nothin' about what's happening at the Gaslight Club. He said, "They want a banjo player." I said, "I can't make it. I got this gig" -- or whatever it was; something I had. I said, "But I've got a
Barker - IV-53

friend of mine I'll send you." He said, "All right." So I told Lucky Fowler to go up there to (?). He went there, and they sent him home. They said, "You need a banjo. We want a banjo player." So he comes dead straight to my house the next day, and I loan him my banjo -- I've got a second banjo. He went there... I showed him how to tune it up, because it's pitched high. And he went there and he made the gig. That's where he started making this money and buying his cameras.
Yeah!
He stayed there about two years. The guy who owned that club is called Burton Brown. Later...that boy's name who used to play like Benny Goodman, he went up there.
Sol Yaged. I think he's still there.

Then, when Burton Brown fired the group that Lucky Fowler had put ...(?)... Lucky Fowler sort told me that he started taking pictures of everybody in the place, and going to these people's homes -- going to this place, and come back and spend a whole lot of money photographing people. He figured that would get him a gig. That gave him a standby. He was averaging about four bills a week because of tips.
Yeah. Keg was heavy on the cameras; Keg Johnson was really heavy on the cameras. And they would do
Barker - IV-54
all that. Because I learned most of that stuff from Keg -- you know, about good cameras. Keg wouldn't have anything that wasn't good.
And they knew all about the lens and all the different filters....
Yes. You know, he had to do it right. He was by the book.
The first time I seen a filter, you had one.

Yeah. He showed me about it. And he was by the book, and he gave me a book. I've got a lot of books at home now with his autograph in them. "To my friend, Milt" -- you know, if he'd see something he thought I should know about.
So that was at that period. Now, that's the late period. That's in the Sixties, before I come down here.

All right. So I go with Danny Love(?). We go to Baltimore and we play a couple of towns. Then I go down south with Billy Fowler's band, which is a band. We get stranded in North Carolina, and I'm around there. We stayed around there about four or five weeks, a little longer. We went there anticipating that somebody is going to book us around there. We through all that part of the country. When we get down there, there's quite a few bands around
Barker - IV-55
there. The Carolina Cotton-Pickers, and other bands coming through there, and Billy Fowler... We just had a New York band of aspiring musicians and some defeated musicians, you know. We were just...

Yeah, a lot of them bands just was nothing. They were just a bunch of musicians together going through the motions, and trying and figuring that there was no future. Because there was no future for Billy Fowler because he was middle-aged. But you never know, because everybody, regardless of the age, aspires to make...to get famous. Billy Fowler could have made a hit record, regardless of who you are, and keep going. Like (?)Dan Garber(?), with middle-aged people. But they're smart enough to try to always make a record. Dan Garber(?) made a record...
Danny Barker & Lu Barker with Milt Hinton (4-30-80):
I'm sitting here in the lovely home of Danny Barker and Lu Barker, and I'm sitting here talking to Lu. Today's the 30th, isn't it, Lu?
Mmm-hmm. April the 30th.

April 30, 1980. We've been talking to Danny, rappin' with him, and we've been down here for a couple of weeks and just enjoyed it. We've out here a couple of times to talk to you, Lu, and it's nice to see you doing so well. Danny made out a list of...what do you call it...? A genealogy which he's supplied. People in general that you're all related to. And I'm just looking down this list. What's your real name, Lu?
My Name is Louisa DuPont.
Louisa DuPont. That's beautiful. What was your mother's and father's name?
My father's name was August DuPont, and my mother's name is Louisa Hurley DuPont.
Hurley.
Yes. Uh-huh.
And you were born in New Orleans.
I was born in New Orleans, and so was my mother and father. My mother is half-Irish and my father is half-French. He's Negro and French, and my mother is Negro and Irish.
Barker - V-2
So that's amazing. So you just grew up right around here. When did you start singing, Lu? What were your school days like? Did you start to sing when you was in school?

I had just started going to school. I started singing when I was about seven years old. See, around here we always played concerts. And one day we were playing a concert back at Pollard Land, they called this section, you know...
What did they call it?
They called it a long time Pollard Land. This man named Pollard who owned all this land at one time, so they called it Pollard Land.
Oh, I see.

So we were playing concert, and the girls across the street heard me sing. See, they were going to have a concert. So they said, 'We're going to have a concert, and we want you to come and sing in our concert.' I said, 'All right.' So they came and asked my mother could I sing in the concert. So I was seven years old. So I was singing 'Sweet Papa's Seen(?) Marie' in the concert and doing the shimmy. And from then on, I would go... You know, they had the yard concerts that they was doing; I'd sing in the concerts... You know, pretty (?) around here.
Barker - V-3

So one time we went to sing a little further(?)... Miss Fanella gave a concert. And that was out of Pollard's Land then, you know. And when I got out on the stage and I saw all these strange people, I got kind of cold feet. So a girl named Woods, she said, "Well, if I go stand on the stage with you, would you sing?" I said, "Yes." So she just stood up there whilst I sang my song, you know. And the next time they had a concert, well, I wasn't ashamed.

So I sang until I was about eleven years old. Not about; I know I was eleven years old. So my mother said to me, "If anybody asks you to be in a concert, tell them you know how to dance. Don't tell them you know how to sing." So I said, "Why?" She said, "Because those songs that you're singing, people think you know what you're saying." I said, "Well, what's wrong with them songs, Mama." She said, "Well, never mind what's wrong with them. They are not for a little girl to sing." She said, "But you tell them that you can dance, that you can't sing."

So the next day I started playing those records, you know. And I was singing "I got everything that a woman needs and makes a good man fall;/I knows just what to do to back 'em in my stall." Well, at that time I couldn't see, you know, nothin' wrong... You know, I wasn't sayin' nothin' wrong because I didn't understand.
Barker - V-4

So a (?) at Ann(?) Street(?) asked me, "Do you know how to sing?" I said, "No, I don't know how to sing, but I know how to dance." So they said, "All right." So he said, "All right. Come on and be in the show with us." They called themselves the Merry-Makers. So every time we got an opening and closing chorus, I would get so scared that they would find out I knew how to sing, I would just come out in the wrong key, you see. Until the night of the concert. The night of the concert, I didn't make no mistakes. They would all be backstage making the sign of the cross that I wouldn't make a mistake, and I never made no mistake on the night of the concert. So they knew that I could dance, but they didn't know that I could sing, and some of them didn't know until in '75 we were sitting around talking about it, and I told them that I could sing along. I said, "I'd make those mistakes because I'd get so scared because my mother said if I was going to sing I ain't gonna be in the concert, and I didn't want you'all to find out." So they laughed about it. And that's how I started, you know, singing.
When did you meet Danny?
I met Danny... I had just made thirteen years old. I made thirteen in November, and I met Danny in December, around the first week of December.
Barker - V-5

And how I met him, his Aunt, Louis Barbarin's wife, and her sister, she said to me, "You know something? I've got a nice little boy I want you to meet." So her sister Gladys said, "What little boy, Marguerite?" So she said, "Daniel." She said, "Louis' little nephew. You'd be a nice girl for him." So she said, "Bring her by my house Sunday. I want her to meet Danny." So Sunday after church, Gladys and II went to his Aunt's house, and they introduced me to him.

So that night we were going to a dance. So Gladys told me that we were going to this dance at the Lion's Club. And I had just made thirteen years old, so I was going to the dance. My mother was at the dance, too. And Danny came to the dance. So he stayed until 12 o'clock, because he had to go to work the next day.

So about two days later, we saw Danny coming. They called him Sundu then. So Gladys said, "Well, look at Sundu coming." I said, "Yeah." So he came by Gladys' house. And he was supposed to be coming to Gladys, but I must have looked good to him, because he'd come to see me.
So a couple of nights afterwards he come again. So we get on the steps, you know, and we didn't know her mother was watching...
[PAUSE]
You didn't know your mother was watching, huh?
Barker - V-6
That wasn't my mother...
It wasn't your mother.

Her mother. So her mother told my mother that Louis' nephew was coming there to see me. So my mother said, "Well, you tell that boy that if he wants to (?), he can come to your house. See, I don't want you to be meeting boys on the street or sitting on somebody else's steps. See, I know you're too young; you're thirteen years old. But rather than have people talking about you, have that boy come...you know, he could come to the house."
So he started coming to my house. And three years after, when I was sixteen, we got married.
I'll be darned. That is beautiful. And you've got one daughter.
I have one daughter.
What's her name?
Her name is Sylvia Barker.
What's her husband's name?
Well, she had two husbands. Her first husband was Rene Browner(?), and he passed away. She had one son for him, Larry Browner. And Larry has a little boy, Christopher, and now got one on the way.
Is that so?! I didn't know that. That's great.
Barker - V-7
Uh-huh. And years ago, she married Leonard Jones. Leonard Jones is her new husband.
Oh, that's wonderful. I wasn't aware of that. Was there anybody in your family that played music, Lu?
Oh yes. My ....(?).... played saxophone, my Daddy...
That's the one, August, huh?

August Du Pont is his name. They called him Dimes. All the musicians would call him Dimes. He played. And my cousin Hersey(?), he played drums. And he has a son, they call him Bib, but his right name is [INDECIPHERABLE]
He plays drums, too, huh?
He plays drums, too. And I have a cousin named...
Gil Thomas?
...Thompson...Thomas... Gil Thomas, yes. They call him Brother Cornbread.

He played clarinet.
I know you were around in New York with Danny. When did you first come to New York with Danny?
I came to New York in 1930. We had been married eight months.
Is that so?
Barker - V-8
When I came... You know, he sent for me. He was there a month and then he sent for me.

I know we were with Cab, and it was just a miracle and just wonderful, the things that you did. All of the musicians that came out of the South... Danny was always bringing... Everybody knew they could come by Lu's...
He was bringing them in!
...and get something to eat.
Yeah!
You fed a host of them. I really saw that myself.

Mmm-hmm. Now, I didn't like to wash dishes. So he'd tell them, "Well, man, I'll bring you to eat, but you've got to wash the plates." Because I told them I was tired of washing all them dishes now. They could eat, but they'd have to wash the dishes. Anybody Danny met, he'd tell them to come to my house and eat. And he was so proud of my cooking. Well, now, today I don't want to cook. It's fifty years now! I don't want to cook now!
Well, you deserve a break.
I deserve a break, yes.
Tell us about them times around New York, Lu. It was some good days... I remember when you were with Cab... Danny, how long were you with Cab?
Barker - V-9
A little over seven years.
Almost eight years...
A little over seven years.
We had some good times there in that band. When did you make that record, "Don't You Feel My Leg."
When did I make it?
Yes.
I made it in 1938.
Is that around when you started singing professionally? Were you singing before then?

Not in New York. You know, I sang around here in the bands. But in New York in 1938... I used to sing when Danny would be playing his guitar. So they told him as good as I can sing, why don't you bring me...you know, let them hear me sing. So they brought me down to Vocalion Records.
Vocalion.

Yes. So at Vocalion I made "A Tisket, A Tasket." They wanted to try out a Hammond organ, and they was tryin' me out, too, see. And Cozy was there, Cozy Cole, and Erskine Butterfield was playing the new Hammond organ. And what's that trumpet player...?
Johnny McGee.
Johnny McGee.
Barker - V-10
He was a noted White trumpet player.
Johnny McGee. Yeah, sure.
So we made "A Tisket, A Tasket." And it took us so long to make this one side, because the organ...you know they couldn't get the right sound with this organ. So we only made one side.
And about two weeks after that, somebody heard about it, and spoke to Danny about it that Mel Williams wanted to see him.
Who?

Mel Williams. To bring me to Decca. So when I got to Decca, they asked me to sing, and I did -- and sang them old songs. He said, "How old you are?" I don't know if I was 23 or 24. He said, "How do you know all those songs?" So I told him how long I had been singing, you know, trying learn off them old records and things like that. So he told Danny that he wanted me to make a recording date.

So the day we made the first recording date with Decca, well, I wasn't so familiar with downtown -- so I got lost on the subway. And finally I found my way back there, but everybody thought I had went back to Vocalion instead of coming to Decca. They were very happy to see me when I finally got there! [LAUGHS] So that's when we made "Don't
Barker - V-11
You Feel My Leg," and that was my first recording date in 1938. Because Danny and I had written the song.
He said you had had your mother singing with the words...
I don't know where he got that from.
Where did you get them words from?

See, because I sing "Don't you feel..." So he'd say, "Well, what goes next?" I said, "(?) Danny," and I'm hum the rest. I said, "It ain't got not next." He said, "What's the channel?" I said, "What's a channel?" He said, "Well, the song's got to have a middle." I said, "Well, this song ain't got no middle." And I was real mad with him! So he said, "Go get a paper and a pencil." So I went to get the paper and the pencil, you know, and then we got the channel together. And that's how that was created.
Well, even this year, it's 1980, and you were out there at... What do they call this Festival here? The Heritage Festival.
The Heritage Festival.

At the Jazz Tent.
At the Jazz Tent, you and Danny performed there.

Yes, we did.
Because I know last year I was down...
There was only one year we didn't perform this.
What's that?
And there was... The first one... There was one before the Heritage Festival. Tell him about that one, Danny, the first Jazz festival here...
Was that the one that was down at the...

That's the one held(?) at the Roosevelt(?). That's about twelve years ago. We put on the first festival here. So they held it in the hotel. Leon Andrews, who is a local lawyer here, he decided to have a festival. And he had seven thousand dollars to play with, and he had this festival. It was the first New Orleans Festival. But it was in the hotel here. And later on, they got the idea that we should have a festival.
Well, I came down here eleven years ago, but it was over where Louis Armstrong Park is over there. Is that an auditorium or something...?
An auditorium, yes.
You remember that one?
Yes.
That was eleven years ago.
Yes.
Barker - V-13
That was a pretty big one, I thought.
Well, that was the first big one. Our was located in a hotel; three days, a weekend they had this festival.
They brought a bunch of us down at New York, and I remember you-all met us out at the airport with a band.
Yeah. You all was the official band for the festival.
I think I came with Benny Goodman, wasn't it?
Yeah, Benny Goodman.
Yeah!
And you and Clark Terry, I think you all went around playing various spots.
That's right. We played at Beau's(?).
Yeah. You-all were the nucleus of the whole thing. It was built around...
See this thing I got around my neck? They gave us a little key to the city. I said, 'I've just got to wear this little thing.' That was a great festival. I really enjoyed that.
Yeah, it was nice of you to...
But this is monumental now, man! You've got this thing out at the Fairgrounds!
Barker - V-14
If you look at the list of the people that they've booked, man, it must be about two hundred very different artists, different groups, all kinds of groups.
Those Cajun groups. I really got turned on to that Cajun music.
Yeah, yeah...
Those Gospel singers, man!
That Gospel Tent, that's where you will hear some mean competition, with them different choirs and them different vocalists.
They was really hittin' it, man.

Yeah, they swing out there. That's the jumpin'est place on the whole place. There's Whisperin' Doopsie...Doxy...Rockin' Dopsie! One of the wildest bands you ever heard. It's a Black Cajun band, and they play funky Black music with the French thing up in it. And them Cajuns out there around the swamps, around Lafayette and all up in there, they are wild about Rockin' Dopsie. It was something else.
Well, I'm just sitting at your genealogy, Danny, of you and your family and Lu...
Well, it should have had about six more. There's Lucien Barbarin, Junior; Charlie Barbarin, Junior, and their little nephew, what's his name...
Barker - V-15
Well, let me just start out here. I see you've got up at the top of the page, Louis Arthadeaux(?)...
Louis Arthadeaux(?). That was my grandmother's brother. He was a virtuoso. As a young man, he played in an Army brass band, which at that time...
Played what instrument?

Clarinet. Clarinet virtuoso. He was acclaimed. But he got involved with some people, and he got sick with sort of a wasting disease. And he didn't tell his people that he was sick until it was too late, and then they brought him to fine doctors, but it was too late. They wanted too late to tell him what was wrong with him. It was one of them social diseases of that time...
Yeah. That's from 1884 to 1905. He died about 1905, huh?

That's right. My Uncle Paul even heard him, and he told how he had wrote waltzes. He was into serious, serious music. And he wrote these things, but they don't know what happened to the music. He said that's what inspired him to write. Because he remembered seeing his Uncle sitting down playing his clarinet and running over this beautiful music he had written, and he said that there was a beautiful waltz he wrote that the bands were beginning to play around here.
Barker - V-16
And that's my Grandfather's brother-in-law, Isidore John Barbarin, who married Louis Arthadeaux's sister, Josephine. And it goes on down from there.

Paul Barbarin is my godfather. That's my mother's oldest brother. There's four brothers, and you had four brothers and five sisters. And Paul Barbarin was the oldest brother who was a drummer, and Louis was a drummer, Lucien's a drummer, and Willie's a trumpet player. There was four brothers. Paul coming down two years younger, Louis two years younger, Lucien two years younger, Willie... And then there's a girl stuck there two years younger than Willie. And I am two years younger than Willie. And the youngest sister, my aunt, we were born the same year, the youngest Barbarin daughter.

And from that, you can see the four boys beatin' around the house on drums, and the old man walkin' up and down the house with his mellophone and his baritone horn -- and there was music all the time.
What was the old man's name?
They called him Isidore, Isidore Barbarin.
Are any of the Barbarin brothers living?
Barker - V-17
Yes. There is one, Louis Barbarin. He works with the Preservation Hall Band, one of the bands.

Yes. Paul left here and joined King Oliver's band at the Plantation. After Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds left him, King Oliver formed an orchestra, a ten-piece orchestra for the Plantation. And that's where Paul joined that band. And that was, like, 1923 or '24. That's the band that King Oliver was taking to New York in ...(?)... ...(?)..., asked for more money, and he couldn't get it, and the man took Duke Ellington instead of King Oliver to go into the Cotton Club. And that was the beginning of Duke's success.
I see another great name which comes up in your genealogy, because Jimmie Noone and your Uncle Paul married two sisters.
Yes, married two sisters.

Barker - V-18
And now I can't recall Jimmie Noone's wife's name.
Yeah, Paul's wife's brother was T.J. Thomas.
That's right, T.J. Thomas. You knew T.J. from around Chicago.
I think I did, yeah.
A little quiet saxophone player who later went to Milwaukee. He lived in Milwaukee, and he had a pressing business in Milwaukee. That's standard now.
Sure. So you've got this tie-in here with your Uncle and Jimmie Noone married to two sisters...
And they were very close friends, Jimmie Noon and Paul. They were real close.
Yeah, Jimmie Noone was a great clarinet player.

Yeah. And he came to New York and he organized a band and went into the Savoy, we went there to meet him, and he went there -- and it lasted around two weeks, and he went back to Chicago. That's around 1932, 1931... [June 1932] Things were slowing down in Chicago, so he came on through. And he had Vincent/Richard(?) (?) in his band.
Piano player. He was a great piano player.

Niece.
...niece.

Matthew.
That's the genealogy of Jesus Christ, I think it is, Matthew. It starts that way, telling everybody...
He's got who did...who's who...
Like the first part of the Bible.
Yeah, the first chapter.
Well, that's how it is here. Well, the Santiago family is involved the same way. The Marrero family is involved the same way. The Marrero's, the Williams and the Fraziers.
My brother played the piano.
What was his name, Lu?
His name was August DuPont. There was five Augusts in our family.
Really?

My father was named August. My brother was named August. He named his son August. And then his son is named August. So now we've got five. We've got August, Senior, August, Junior, August the Third, August the Fourth and August the Fifth.
Wow, that's great!
When my brother was young, he got a job on the railroad, and he would be out six days and he'd come home
Barker - V-21

six days. So when he'd come home, he'd say to me, "What's the new tune?" So anything I could hum, he could play on the piano. So I'd hum anything, and he'd give me a dime! "Oh," I said, "they live back of the tracks. They don't know those new tunes." I said, "That's a new tune. Give me my dime!" So he'd give me the dime. I'd give him sometimes the dime back to show me some Blues chords on the piano, you know. So that's how I... I'd always have a new tune for him after those six days....
Yeah, get your dime.
So I could get that dime, yeah.

Well, Paul Barbarin, I knew his name and knew how famous he was. And one of the greatest things that happened to me as far as New Orleans Jazz History is concerned is, Danny, you got me on a record date with him in New York City. That's a great record. It's a collectors' item, isn't it.
Good record.
You were on that also.
Yes.

Atlantic.

Five Augusts.
Yeah, that's beautiful.

And you know, it's funny, just lately... You know, my father died, and so there's four of them living, and they live next door to each other. So somebody says, "August" and they say, "Which one do you want?" My father called them Duke, so they were called Duke, because we wanted dimes... So they had little names to distinguish...
Yeah, nicknames.
Nicknames to distinguish which one they wanted to see.
Dimes, huh?! What were you trying to say, Danny?
Oh, like she said, her blind uncle, he played...
Barker - V-23
Yes. My great-uncle. And he had one of these big, great baby grand pianos.
What was his name, Lu?

His name was Alexander Augustine. And my cousin Clarice was working for some people, and they gave her a piano. Well, her place was too small for a piano, because it was one of these big concert pianos. And my mother, she had a great big room. So she had to give the piano to my mother, because she couldn't fit it in her house. And that's how my brother learned to play the piano. And Miss Nelly, she was a lady in the neighborhood, she used to come and play "Salty Dog" on the piano. And Blind Santi(?) would get his guitar with one string on it, and he'd play that, and Mr. Reese, Reese Scovette(?), he'd play his saxophone...
He was in the neighborhood.

Yes. But Mr. Reese's father used to play the bass on the table with the broomstick, with his finger. He would rub that stick across his finger and play the bass. Reese Scovette(?) played the bass, and that's the band they had. And then my mother or my father, they'd be singing or playing the comb. They'd put some grade(?) paper... At that time they'd put grade(?) paper on that comb or put some cigarette paper on the comb, and blow it across.
Barker - V-24

So we always had music. And when the company would come, I would always be waiting, because they'd call me to come do the Shimmy. So I had to do the shimmy, so somebody's going to give me nickels, dimes, something like that. Then Mama said, "Now you can go."
So you were a professional from that start.
That's right.
It's always an incentive, that loot.
That's right.
It's a way to make some money. She said she waited on her brother to give her that dime, she waited for the company... And they gave you something to encourage you with music, didn't they.

My first recollections of music was in Vicksburg, Mississippi. Late at night, after we'd gone to bed, a guy would come by with a bass fiddle and maybe a clarinet or a guitar, and he would play softly. And the bass fiddle would be bowing, see. I'd wake up and I'd hear this, and people would come to the door and give him that money so he could go get him some wine or something. And they just did two or three pieces. And they used to go through the neighborhood. I want to ask you this. My grandmother had one of them big pianos in our house in Vicksburg, Mississippi. How did them people get them
Barker - V-25
pianos, Danny? They didn't have no money.
They had ...(?)... getting them pianos, get rid of them sometimes...

See, most of the time the people would... Like, they'd be working for somebody, and they'd give it to them. And you'd see them old baby grand pianos. The legs used to come off, see. And if you had a high door, and the houses had high doors...

They'd take the legs off. See, the legs used to come off. And they would just bring it through sideways. Because we had big doors, and most of the houses had big ceilings, you know...
Would you say it was gold-looking?
Yeah, it looked... Do you see that picture frame over there?
Oh yeah, the gilt...
Gilted like. And that's how that piano looked. And today... That must have been a real, you know, good piano.
Sure! A grand piano generally costs a fortune.
Barker - V-26
A baby grand. Mmm-hmm.

I wondered about that, and I never had... When I was younger, I never had the nerve to ask my grandmother, and I should have. I really should ask my mother right now; you know, she's still living. But I never understood how come we had this little old house, two rooms and a kitchen, and there was a great big piano sitting in there. And this is where everybody met on the weekends, they was around that piano for choir rehearsals, and Friday evenings when folks would get off of work, they'd sing them songs like "Dear Old Girl, The Robin Sings About You," harmonizing... So there was always a congregation in our house, because wherever the piano is, that's where you go have your action.
Yeah, that's right.
But how did they get it? I know they didn't have no money.
They went and bought it second-hand at about 50 cents a week or 50 cents a month...
Isn't that somethin'?
They bought it second-hand, used. And people... It was a prestige thing to have a piano in your house.
That's right.
Because people came over...
Barker - V-27
See, when Danny and I were courting, we didn't have a bedroom set, but we had a piano.
That's right.
He used to come in in the evening, and he'd put his hat, his cap he wore on top of the piano. We had no living room, but we had a piano!

A lot of people had melodions, which is similar to a piano. It's a thing like an organ you pump with your feet, so somebody would get that before the modern organ. they was around in people's houses. People... Whites would get tired of something, or some Blacks just had enough money to go and buy one...
I can't conceive it. Because pianos nowadays cost nine or ten thousand dollars. I can't conceive of them poor Black people having them. Some of them White folks had to give it to them or something.
Sometimes.
In New Orleans, there was many pianos. His mother had a piano, too. You could always find a piano!
You really had to have some love for music to want to keep something like that around.
So go on, Lu. What were you telling me about your family?
Brother Cornbread, your cousin.

Oh yeah, we mentioned Brother Cornbread, Joseph Thomas.
Yes.
Great clarinet player. Great artist.
Who was this Boy Bijou?
Esther.
Huh?
Esther Bijou and Boy Bijou. That's her brother. Boy Bijou playd kazoo and the clarinet. He was a ballroom musician, played the ballroom with a band called the Rootie-Dooty sometimes.
Well, how did he get in this band? Where was he in the...
Well, that's Esther Bijou's brother, and Esther Bijou is a cousin, a second or first cousin to Isidore -- Isidore Barbarin, Paul's father.
Oh, I see. His father. So on the Barbarin side.

Yes, but the Bijous were in there. And the Bijous and the Barbarins were related. And you'd have to get some old folks, some old person to tell you how that relation went on. But they're all dead now, so that's lost, unless you go to City Hall.
Barker - V-29

Sure.
She toured with me.

Yes. So if you see a tall, slim guy... Huh? That's the one?
Yeah. The tall, slim one.
If you see him, ask about Esther Bijou in relation to New Orleans. Because it's your interview... Because you can bring it in...
No, no. I want everybody together here.

I'll tell you what happened. Before Sylvia was born... Well, we were married five years before we had any kids, you know. And we was living with Lizzie Niles. Now, Lizzie Niles, you know, she was a great singer...
I know that name, Lizzie Niles.
Lizzie Niles, yeah.
Spencer Williams' wife.
Oh, she's Spencer Williams' wife, huh.
That was his old lady.
Barker - V-30

So one day... See, I heard Lizzie sing, and Lizzie sang so pretty, you know -- and I would never sing around Lizzie. So one day I forgot that Lizzie was home, and I was making the bed, and she was... She used to sing this song, "Don't You Remember Me." Well, I had heard her sing it, and I had learned the song. So I was making the bed, and I would get to singing "Don't You Remember Me?" And Lizzie was quiet. So when I came to singing, she came by the door and she said, "Who learned you how to sing that song?" I said, "Well, Lizzie, I heard you sing it." She said, "Yeah?" I said, "Yes." Well, from that day on, Lizzie never sang when I was around the house no more. I never heard Lizzie sing no more, after she heard...you know, I sang her song.
She was White?
No.
No, she was Colored.
But she was real light.
She was a (?). I think her father was a (?)tap dancer(?). Anyway, I never heard...
She wasn't going to sing, huh?
And Lizzie, she said... I said, "I heard you sing that, Lizzie." And from that day on, I remember I didn't hear Lizzie sing no more around the house.
Barker - V-31
Yeah, Lizzie wrote "Basin Street Blues."
She did?
Yeah. Spencer, her old man, he was a songwriter, he wrote "Mahogany Hall Stomp" and a whole lot of things. And he took it and published it himself.
Spencer Williams, he was a big publisher...
He was a big songwriter..
In my neighborhood, Danny (you've got to see it when you come there), a fellow just took me around and showed me his house. He's one of the first guys to buy a house out there in Long Island.
He was?
Yeah. He bought some property. Evidently, he had a little money. And he bought... He was going to try to set up a musicians' settlement, songwriters.
It wasn't Clarence? You say it was Spencer.
Well, maybe it was Clarence.
Clarence lived out there.
Clarence lived out there, Spencer lived there, and Perry Bradford, too. I think Fats Waller, too...
And James P. Johnson.
James P. Johnson.
Yank Porter.
Yup.
Barker - V-32
A whole slew of musicians moved out there.
Yes. Well, I know where all the houses are. Now we're putting plaques up on them and making them...what do you call it for the neighborhood...?
Historical.
Historical.
Yeah, because they were important.
They were very important. And the houses are really in good shape.
I think Handy lived out there a while.
I didn't know anything about Handy, but...
Oh, sure.
I think he did.
Yeah.

But that same neighborhood is where the White sportsmen used to live. Babe Ruth and Earl Sander, the great jockey. And I think I told you about Fats Waller was the first Black man to move into that St. Albans neighborhood.
Yeah. Well, they called it Jamaica in them days.
It was Jamaica, right.
All right. And Jamaica Track was there.
Barker - V-33

That's right. Jamaica Track was there. That's where Charlotte and Tessie lived. They tore that track down and built them buildings, condominiums in a big apartment building when you buy them. That's where they lived, right where Jamaica Track was. But over where I lived was near Jamaica Avenue, or Jamaica. That's where these guys had all their homes.
Where is Corona?

He would write songs and then got a deck of cards, and he would take this deck...you know, the words of the songs, and paste it on these cards and put it on his guitar -- and he would sing from that, you know. So one night I told my girlfriend, Rosie, and I said, "We're going

to Hoboken where Danny works." So she said, "Yes." So when we got there, I said, "Now, Rose, now Danny's going to sing all night." So she says, "All right, I ain't gonna laugh." A card about this big.

Playing cards, yes.

And when we got through fixing that bus and painting it up, it cost nine hundred dollars! But we used to go on
Barker - V-71
the...
Because (?) wanted to travel easy.
I remember that, Danny. Sure.
We would go with this bus. And Danny never did learn how to drive the bus, so we had pay somebody ten dollars every time we'd go out to drive the bus. And we took that bus up to New York...
With full brand-new tires. Remember them heavy-duty tires?

And we got three hundred dollars for it when we sold it. But it served the purpose, because it took us, you know, a lot of places. And each time, the first thing you know, the bus would stop, and I'd say, "What happened?" "No gas." Because the what'cha call it didn't...
The speedometer didn't register.

Yeah, it didn't work. And oh, I'd get so mad. I'd say, "Didn't I tell you'all to get some gas?!" You know, we'd always be talking about the bus done stopped on the road. It was something riding that bus.
How does that tune go, Danny? "I know a little girl from..." -- where did you say...?
"This Little Girl From Jacksonville."

Patent medicine.
But it wouldn't cure nothin'....

Yeah. That means wine.

So the "hadicol"(?) in the song, that was (?). And you'd say, "She can do the ring-dang-do," and I was straight(?), you know... Everything, like they're doing now, was supposed to be a new thing, that was in that tune.

The Hadicol(?) man. We sent it to Dudley Lebeau. He was a Louisiana State Senator who had a patent

You had a disk jockey here named Papa Stoppa(?) who used to take just that part when he was publicizing the Hadicol(?) thing. "You know, you can do a lot of Hadicol..." -- and he'd play that over and over and over and over, see.

So somebody found out I was here. So they sent for me, and they said, "Senator Lebeau wants to see you. He wants to thank you for making that record." Because they wanted to get off the hook, because I guess the government was suing them for using that as a gimmick. So he said, "Senator Lebeau..." He called me, Papa Stoppa. "He appreciates this thing. He's been looking for a jingle, and he's finally found something that's perfect for his Hadicol program." He said, "When he comes in town, I'll call you."

So Senator Lebeau was living at the New Orleans Hotel. Papa Stoppa said, "You go to the New Orleans Hotel, and he's there." I go to the New Orleans Hotel, and you're not allowed to go through the front elevator. So me and Paul...

Me, you and Paul. Because they wanted him to bring me, because he was supposed to bring me a watch. So we go to the hotel, and we couldn't go through the front door. So we had to go around. So we're finally in the basement. I'm all sharp, you know, and I was young...
Sure!

Around the garbage cans. We're standing up there waiting for the Senator to send for us. So we were there, I don't know, about two hours, maybe three hours waiting for him to call. So I told them, I said, "Look, you'all can stay if you'all want, but I'm going." They said, "Well, the Senator said..." So we told them that we were going. So the next day I told Paul and Danny, I said, "Now, if you'all want to go amongst them garbage cans down there

waiting for the Senator, you'all can do. But I ain't goin'. I'm gonna stay home." Now you can take over.

He thought she was White.

Well, I'm determined, see, because Paul was telling me, 'Maybe you can get the Senator to let you have one of them station wagons, since you advertised for Hadicol(?) so well' or something. There's an old abandoned firehouse I've been trying to get, right in the middle of the Black neighborhood that I was born and raised in, and I want to use that as a little opera house, something like that Nashville thing that they have for opera [sic: Grand Old Opry], have a little place where young Blacks or any Black can come in and hear traditional music, and keep the tradition. A little place where you can come there and hear youngsters playing it. Because youngsters are still interested in the music. When they're hear it in the parades, on the street marching along... outside." So he came to me and said, "Come in." So I went in, and he said, "Now, why did you send Jack to ask me to autograph those pictures for you. Why didn't you come in here and ask me yourself?" This is just a little aftermath. We were talking with Lu, and you talked about when you used to dance. You had a partner or something?

Yes. You see, when I was eleven years old, my mother told me that I couldn't sing no more, and that if anybody asked me to be in a concert, to tell them I could dance. So I had a partner called Doug DeLille(?) and I was Louise DuPont. We were partners together, and we did our dance, you know. And I did the Georgia Grind, and I would shake down to the floor and all this kind of movement with the Shimmy and everything. And we did a routine tap dance, you know.

Because we used to dance... You see, everybody would dance in a show. When we would be rehearsing, they would be up there rehearsing, and we'd do everybody's song and everybody's dance -- and you could look at 'em. We'd know everybody's routine. So that was the deal.
And Gladys used to sing the Blues.

Yeah. Gladys used to sing the Blues, too.
And you got involved with your sisters.

And Eunice. And what they used to do, when we was in a concert, they would take me, and we'd learn some new steps... They'd take me for a guest at the Orpheum. See? The Orpheum used to have vaudeville, see. And in the ladies rooms, they'd change their clothes, see. And we would go in (?), and they'd say, "You all look good now." So we'd say, "All right." And then, "Have you got that step?" You'd say, "Yes." So we ran back in the ladies room and rehearse it! You see? Then we'd have a couple of new steps for the next concert, you know.

And it was called the Merry-Makers. And there were seventeen of us. We used to get three dollars for the concert. But actually my mother (?), because we'd have to wear new shoes and we had new dresses, and they'd be coming in the halls, you know, with these big dresses... Everybody had a big dress like they were (?) in New York or something! A great big dress, and after the concert was over, you got three dollars.

My mother said one night, "I bought you new shoes, I had to make a new dress for the opening, you had an opening dress" -- you had an opening dress and then a dress to dance in and put some taps on the shoes and all that kind of

stuff. And you didn't make no money. But we had a whole lot of fun.
What do you think your mother... You used to tell me about your mother taught you some of them steps at first, when you was a little girl?

What did you call them? A big what?
An [PHONETIC] 'armor.'
Armoire. See like this?
Oh yeah, I see.

But it had a mirror on each side. See, so she'd get on one side and I'd get on the other. And we'd sing, you see. And we'd get in the mirror, and then she would show me how to shimmy, you know, and what to do. And I was singing the Blues...
